=== NOTES 4:36 | Himalayan Drainage System – Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra Basins
## SUB 0 | Ganga Tributaries – Yamuna, Son, Damodar, Kosi and the Left Bank
[36:0:0] # Left bank vs right bank
[36:0:1] TABLE head: Bank | Tributaries
  [36:0:1.0] Left (Himalayan) | Ramganga, Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Mahananda
  [36:0:1.1] Right (mostly Peninsular) | Yamuna (longest), Son, Tons, Punpun; Damodar joins the Hugli (right bank)
[36:0:2] - **Yamuna** = **westernmost and longest** tributary of the Ganga; **Son** = the largest right-bank tributary from the Peninsula.
[36:0:3] - **Mahananda** = **last, easternmost** left-bank tributary; joins in **West Bengal**.
[36:0:4] - **Son** is the main right-bank tributary that **flows northwards** (from Amarkantak) and **joins the Ganga directly** near **Maner (Patna)**; Gomti, Ghaghara, Kosi join from the **left**.
[36:0:5] - **Chambal, Betwa, Ken, Sindh** join the **Yamuna**, not the Ganga; the Chambal therefore lies in the **Ganga basin** (not Narmada/Sabarmati/Godavari).
[36:0:6] # Order of confluence below Prayagraj (west → east)
[36:0:7] - **Gomti** (near Ghazipur, Kaithi) → **Ghaghara** (near **Chapra**, Revelganj, Saran) → **Son** (R, near Maner) → **Gandak** (Hajipur/**Sonpur**, opposite Patna) → **Kosi** (Kursela, Katihar, below Bhagalpur) → Mahananda.
[36:0:8] > UPSC 2024 (asked twice): Himalayan rivers joining below Prayagraj, west → east = **Gomti – Ghaghara – Gandak – Kosi**.
[36:0:9] # Left-bank (Himalayan) tributaries
[36:0:10] TABLE head: River | Facts
  [36:0:10.0] Ramganga | Rises in the Dudhatoli ranges (Pauri Garhwal, near Nainital); joins near Kannauj/Farrukhabad; Kalagarh Dam; a Ganga tributary, not the Yamuna's
  [36:0:10.1] Ghaghara | Mapchachungo glacier / Gurla Mandhata, south of Mansarovar (Tibet); Karnali in Nepal; receives the Sharda (called Kali/Mahakali in its hill course); joins at Revelganj (Chapra)
  [36:0:10.2] Gandak | Narayani / Gandaki in Nepal; Sadanira of the Shatapatha Brahmana; streams Kali Gandak and Trishuli; enters India at Valmikinagar (not Raxaul); joins at Hajipur/Sonpur
  [36:0:10.3] Kosi | "Sorrow of Bihar"; maximum shifting of course; seven headstreams – Arun most important (Sun Kosi, Tamur Kosi); changed course in Aug 2008 (Kusaha breach) → Bihar flood calamity
  [36:0:10.4] Gomti | Rises at Gomat Taal (Fulhar lake), Pilibhit – the only Ganga tributary rising in the plains; Lucknow
  [36:0:10.5] Mahananda | Easternmost/last left-bank tributary
[36:0:11] - **Kosi and glaciers:** the Bihar Kosi has glacier-fed headwaters (NextGen); in the Uttarakhand (UKPSC) question the **Kosi of Kumaon** rises near **Kausani** (rain-fed), so "Kosi" is the river **without a glacier source** – Yamuna (Yamunotri), Alaknanda (Satopanth) and Mandakini (Chorabari) are glacier-fed.
[36:0:12] - **Mahakali Treaty** – India–**Nepal**, **Feb 1996**; Mahakali = **Sharda**; Sharda and Tanakpur barrages, Pancheshwar project.
[36:0:13] - **Gandak Project** – India–Nepal agreement **4 Dec 1959**; Bihar and UP.
[36:0:14] - **Catchment (sq km):** **Son ~70,055** > Gandak ~45,700 > Ramganga ~30,800 > Mahananda ~23,700.
[36:0:15] # Yamuna and its tributaries
[36:0:16] - Rises at **Yamunotri glacier**, western slopes of **Bandarpunch (Banderpunch)**; joins the Ganga at **Prayagraj**.
[36:0:17] TABLE head: Bank | Tributaries of the Yamuna
  [36:0:17.0] Right (west → east) | Chambal (joins in Etawah) → Sindh → Betwa (joins at Hamirpur) → Ken
  [36:0:17.1] Left | Tons, Hindon (Hindan), Hanuman Ganga, Sasur Khaderi
[36:0:18] - **Chambal:** rises at **Janapav hills near Mhow** (Dr Ambedkar Nagar), Malwa; **deep ravines** (badlands); tributaries **Banas** (left), **Kali Sindh, Parvati, Kshipra** (right) – the **Betwa does not join the Chambal**; Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar, Kota.
[36:0:19] - **Betwa** rises in the Vindhyas (Bhopal plateau) and joins the **Yamuna** at Hamirpur.
[36:0:20] - **Yamuna between Delhi and Agra** is almost a "dead river" for much of the year because of heavy abstraction and pollution – but the Yamuna itself is a **perennial** Himalayan river.
[36:0:21] # Son, Damodar and the Chota Nagpur rivers
[36:0:22] - **Son:** Amarkantak → north through Baghelkhand → Ganga near **Maner (Patna)**; tributaries Johilla, Banas, Gopad, **Rihand**, Kanhar, **North Koel**.
[36:0:23] - **Kaimur range** = water divide between the **Yamuna (via the Tons) and the Son** (MPPSC).
[36:0:24] - **North Koel:** rises on the **Ranchi plateau**, flows through the **north of Betla NP** (Palamu), joins the **Son** → part of the **Ganga basin**; **Mandal dam** on it. **South Koel and Sankh** go to the **Brahmani** (not Ganga).
[36:0:25] - **Damodar:** Khamarpat hill/Tori, Chota Nagpur; flows in a **rift (fault) valley**; "**Sorrow of Bengal**" (before DVC); joins the **Hugli (Hooghly)** south of Kolkata; main tributary **Barakar** (also Konar, Jamunia, Barki).
[36:0:26] - **Rajarappa** (Ramgarh, Jharkhand) – confluence of **Damodar and Bhera (Bhairavi)**; Chhinnamasta temple.
[36:0:27] - **Bansagar Accord, 1973** on the Son: 7.75 MAF; the **2026 Bihar–Jharkhand MoU** gives **Bihar 5.75 MAF, Jharkhand 2 MAF** (as of 2026).
[36:0:28] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.10-12; Rocket Indian Geography p.2, p.9-14; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.23; app notes 4:36 (sub 4)
[36:0:29] - **Tropic of Cancer** crosses the Chota Nagpur plateau near **Ranchi–Lohardaga**; CGPSC 2021 key: **South Koel–Damodar** cut it twice (disputed – only the **Mahi** is standard).
## SUB 1 | Indus System
[36:1:0] # Course of the Indus
[36:1:1] - Rises at **Singge Khabab** (Bokhar Chu glacier) on the **northern slopes of the Kailash range** near Mansarovar (5,182 m); in Tibet = **Singi Khamban** ("Lion's mouth").
[36:1:2] - Flows west between the **Ladakh and Zaskar** ranges; **Leh** lies on its **right bank** (UT of Ladakh since 31 Oct 2019); **Zanskar** joins at **Nimu**.
[36:1:3] - Takes a southerly course at **Nanga Parbat** through a deep **antecedent gorge** → Pakistan → **Arabian Sea near Karachi**; flows through **north-western India and Pakistan**.
[36:1:4] - Length **2,880 km** (NCERT; NextGen 2,480 km), only **709 km** in India. Himalayan tributaries: **Shyok**, Gilgit, Zaskar, Shigar, Dras, Hunza.
[36:1:5] - **Panjnad:** the five Punjab rivers join the Indus a little **above Mithankot**: Jhelum and Ravi → Chenab; Beas → Sutlej; Sutlej + Chenab = Panjnad.
[36:1:6] > UPSC 2021 (asked twice): the river that "joins the Indus direct" = **Sutlej** (UPSC key, per PMF); strictly the Sutlej and Chenab merge as the Panjnad.
[36:1:7] # The five Punjab rivers
[36:1:8] TABLE head: River | Greek / Vedic | Source and facts
  [36:1:8.0] Jhelum | Hydaspes / Vitasta | Spring at Verinag, foot of the Pir Panjal (NextGen: Sheshnag); flows through Srinagar and Wular lake; main tributary Kishanganga (= Neelum in Pakistan); Tulbul project
  [36:1:8.1] Chenab | Acesines / Asikni | Chandra + Bhaga (rise near Baralacha La, flow in Lahaul) meet at Tandi (HP); largest tributary of the Indus; Salal, Baglihar, Dul Hasti; Tawi is a Chenab tributary
  [36:1:8.2] Ravi | Hydraotes / Parushni | Kalu hills/Rohtang, HP; joins the Chenab in Pakistan; Harappa lies on the Ravi; Upper Bari Doab canal
  [36:1:8.3] Beas | Hyphasis / Vipasa | Beas Kund near Rohtang; joins the Sutlej at Harike; whole course in India; Indus river dolphin (Beas Conservation Reserve, Punjab – the only Indian population)
  [36:1:8.4] Sutlej | Zaradros / Shutudri | Rakas Tal (Rakshastal), Kailash range, Tibet (Langchen Khambab); enters India at Shipki La; antecedent, Trans-Himalayan – cuts across all the Himalayan ranges; tributaries Spiti (joins at Khab), Baspa, Beas; Bhakra-Nangal
[36:1:9] - **North → south (also west → east):** **Jhelum → Chenab → Ravi → Beas → Sutlej**.
[36:1:10] - **North → south, upper Indus streams:** **Shyok – Zaskar – Spiti – Sutlej** (UPSC 2006).
[36:1:11] - **Ravi** is not a tributary of the Sutlej directly (it joins the Chenab); **Mahanadi** is a Peninsular river, not an Indus tributary.
[36:1:12] - **Doabs:** **Bist (Doaba) = Beas–Sutlej**; Bari = Beas–Ravi; Rechna = Ravi–Chenab; Chaj = Chenab–Jhelum; Sind Sagar = Jhelum/Chenab–Indus. "Panjnad/Punjab" = land of five rivers.
[36:1:13] - **Rivers of Himachal Pradesh:** **Beas, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej and Yamuna**.
[36:1:14] - **Sutlej identification (UPSC 2026):** antecedent, flows through **three countries** (China, India, Pakistan), rises on the Tibetan plateau, key for irrigation, forms **no distributaries** (it ends in the Panjnad).
[36:1:15] # Indus Waters Treaty, 1960
[36:1:16] TABLE head: Rivers | Allotted to
  [36:1:16.0] Eastern – Ravi, Beas, Sutlej | India
  [36:1:16.1] Western – Indus, Jhelum, Chenab | Mainly Pakistan
[36:1:17] - Signed 19 Sep 1960 (Karachi), **brokered by the World Bank**. India has held the treaty **in abeyance since 23 Apr 2025** (after the Pahalgam attack; MEA, still in force as of Jul 2026).
[36:1:18] - **Salal** (690 MW, NHPC, Chenab) – India's first project in the region under the treaty; **Baglihar** (Chenab, Ramban); **Dul Hasti** (390 MW, Chenab, Kishtwar).
[36:1:19] - **Chenab rail bridge** (Reasi, J&K, 359 m above the river) = **world's highest railway arch bridge**; under construction for years, **opened 6 Jun 2025**.
[36:1:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.7-9; Rocket Indian Geography p.6, p.13; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.23; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.6; rsis.ramsar.org/ris/2408; tribuneindia.com (Chenab bridge, 6 Jun 2025); thestatesman.com (IWT in abeyance)
[36:1:21] - **North → south:** Kishanganga (Kashmir) → Ganga → **Wainganga** (Seoni, MP) → **Penganga** (Buldhana) – UPSC 1996.
## SUB 2 | Ganga – Headwaters, Panchprayag, Course and Delta
[36:2:0] # Headwaters
[36:2:1] - **Bhagirathi** – **Gangotri glacier at Gomukh**, Uttarkashi district (**Uttarkashi is on the Bhagirathi**).
[36:2:2] - **Alaknanda** – **Satopanth glacier** above Badrinath = the **second glacial source** of the Ganga; **Badrinath** lies on the **Alaknanda**, **Kedarnath** on the **Mandakini**.
[36:2:3] - The two meet at **Devprayag** (Tehri Garhwal); the river is called the **Ganga** from Devprayag.
[36:2:4] # Panchprayag (on the Alaknanda, upstream → downstream)
[36:2:5] TABLE head: Prayag | River joining the Alaknanda
  [36:2:5.0] Vishnuprayag | Dhauliganga
  [36:2:5.1] Nandprayag | Nandakini
  [36:2:5.2] Karnaprayag | Pindar
  [36:2:5.3] Rudraprayag | Mandakini
  [36:2:5.4] Devprayag | Bhagirathi → Ganga begins
[36:2:6] - **Prayagraj (Triveni Sangam)** = **Ganga, Yamuna and the mythical Saraswati**.
[36:2:7] - Kedarnath is **not** one of Adi Shankaracharya's four mathas (Jyotirmath, Sringeri, Dwarka, Puri), so a statement calling it his "biggest seat" is false.
[36:2:8] # Course
[36:2:9] - Rises in the western Himalayas of **Uttarakhand**, enters the plains at **Haridwar**; navigable up to **Prayagraj**; towns: **Kanpur (largest city on the Ganga)**, Prayagraj, Varanasi, **Patna**, Bhagalpur.
[36:2:10] - In Bihar the Ganga touches **12 districts**; **Patna** district has its longest stretch (about 99 km).
[36:2:11] - At **Farakka** (WB): left arm **Bhagirathi–Hooghly**; right arm **Padma** enters Bangladesh – in Bangladesh the **Ganga = Padma**, the **Brahmaputra = Jamuna**.
[36:2:12] - Padma + Jamuna (at **Goalundo**) + Meghna → enters the **Bay of Bengal as the Meghna**; the delta ends in the **Sundarbans**.
[36:2:13] - **Length:** **2,525 km** – the **longest river in India** (NextGen gives 2,465 km, 2,071 km in India); basin ≈ **26%** of India's area, about 40% of its population.
[36:2:14] # Bengal delta
[36:2:15] - **Moribund delta** (old, inactive, Nadia–Murshidabad), **mature delta**, and **active delta** (still growing, **North and South 24 Parganas**, Sundarbans) – "moribund" is a sub-division of the **Bengal delta**.
[36:2:16] > Statement trap: "Burhi Dihing and Dhansiri are the Ganga's left-bank tributaries" and "it finally merges with the Padma" are NCERT lines about the **Brahmaputra**, so both are false for the Ganga.
[36:2:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.9; Rocket Indian Geography p.2, p.7; app notes 4:36 (sub 3); gktoday.in (Ganga in Bihar)
[36:2:18] - **Ganga pollution** – chiefly untreated urban sewage and industrial effluent (not its sanctity); Namami Gange programme.
## SUB 3 | Character of Himalayan Rivers – Antecedent, Perennial, Inland Drainage
[36:3:0] # Four groups of Indian rivers
[36:3:1] TABLE head: Group | Example
  [36:3:1.0] Himalayan | Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra
  [36:3:1.1] Deccan (Peninsular) | Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi – seasonal, not perennial
  [36:3:1.2] Coastal | Short west-coast streams
  [36:3:1.3] Inland drainage | Western Rajasthan – Ghaggar, Luni (into the Rann; the river of the "Great (Thar) Desert"), Rupen
[36:3:2] - **Inland drainage:** the river does not reach the sea – e.g. **Ghaggar** (not the Ghaghara, a Ganga tributary).
[36:3:3] - **River Khari (Rajasthan):** the main **Khari** is a **Banas tributary** (Rajsamand → Deoli) → Banas → Chambal → Yamuna → Ganga → **Bay of Bengal**; other streams named Khari feed the Luni (Arabian Sea) and Sambhar lake (inland).
[36:3:4] # Antecedent rivers
[36:3:5] - **Definition:** a river that **existed before the Himalayas rose** and kept its course by **cutting deep gorges** as the land rose.
[36:3:6] - Marks: **valley-in-valley**, **paired terraces**, **entrenched (ingrown) meanders**.
[36:3:7] - Examples: **Indus** (gorge at Nanga Parbat – the river most cited for **gorges**), **Sutlej**, **Brahmaputra** (Dihang gorge) – the **Brahmaputra is "older than the Himalayas"**; the Yamuna, Kosi and Ganga are not the answer to that question.
[36:3:8] - The **Ganga** is usually listed as an **antecedent** river in exam keys; it rises at Gangotri **within** the Himalayas, unlike the Indus, Sutlej and Brahmaputra which rise **beyond** them in Tibet (**Trans-Himalayan**).
[36:3:9] # Perennial character and work in the plains
[36:3:10] - **Perennial:** fed by **rain + snowmelt** (rainfall and melting ice); Himalayan rivers are **not dry in winter**.
[36:3:11] - In the plains: gentle slope → **meanders, shifting channels, ox-bow lakes, floodplains**, braided channels and riverine islands.
[36:3:12] - Himalayan rivers show **all three stages** of the erosion cycle (youth, maturity, old age); **Peninsular rivers have reached maturity**.
[36:3:13] - The Northern Plain (not the "Western plain") is formed by the interplay of the **Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra**.
[36:3:14] > A–R pattern: "Himalayan rivers are perennial" + "Kosi changes its course" → both true, R does **not** explain A; + "Himalayas get rain from the SW monsoon" → both true, R does not explain A (the snowmelt part is missing).
[36:3:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.7, p.13; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.2-6; rajras.in (Khari, rivers of Rajasthan); app notes 4:36 (sub 0)
## SUB 4 | Brahmaputra System
[36:4:0] # Names and course
[36:4:1] TABLE head: Region | Name
  [36:4:1.0] Tibet | Tsangpo / Yarlung Zangbo / Sanpu
  [36:4:1.1] Arunachal Pradesh | Dihang / Siang
  [36:4:1.2] Assam | Brahmaputra (after the Dibang and Lohit join near Sadiya)
  [36:4:1.3] Bangladesh | Jamuna (below Dhubri); joins the Padma at Goalundo
[36:4:2] - Rises at **Chemayungdung glacier**, east of Mansarovar (Kailash range); also traced to the Angsi glacier.
[36:4:3] - Flows east, then makes a **U-turn at Namcha Barwa** and enters India through the deep **Dihang gorge** – "**born before the Himalayas**" (antecedent).
[36:4:4] - Length **2,900 km**, only **885 km** in India; catchment **Tibet (China), Bhutan, India, Bangladesh**; navigable **1,280 km up to Dibrugarh**.
[36:4:5] - **"Sorrow of Assam"** – floods; **Majuli** (upper Assam) = **largest riverine island** in the world.
[36:4:6] - **China's dams:** **Zangmu** (construction from **Nov 2010**) on the Yarlung Zangbo, Tibet.
[36:4:7] # Tributaries
[36:4:8] TABLE head: Right bank (north, Himalayan) | Left bank (south)
  [36:4:8.0] Subansiri, Kameng (Jia Bharali), Manas, Sankosh, Teesta | Burhi Dihing, Dhansiri, Dikhu, Kopili
[36:4:9] - Also: **Dibang, Lohit** (headstreams in Arunachal). **Lohit and Subansiri** flow through **Arunachal Pradesh**; the **Barak** does not.
[36:4:10] - **Sankosh** – rises in northern Bhutan; forms the **Assam–West Bengal** boundary.
[36:4:11] - **Teesta** – rises at **Tso Lhamo** lake, North Sikkim (**not** the Brahmaputra's source); largest tributary **Rangeet** (rises in Sikkim); joins the **Brahmaputra in Bangladesh**, not the Bay of Bengal.
[36:4:12] # Barak (Meghna) system
[36:4:13] - **Barak** rises in the **Manipur hills**; the **important river of Manipur and Mizoram**; headstream of the **Meghna**.
[36:4:14] - Tributaries of the Barak: **Katakhal, Jiri, Chiri, Madhura (Modhura)**, Sonai, Dhaleswari.
[36:4:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.12; Rocket Indian Geography p.3, p.10-11; app notes 4:36 (sub 5)
[36:4:16] - **Teesta hydro projects:** stages III, V, VI in **Sikkim**; **Teesta Low Dam III and IV** in **West Bengal**.
## SUB 5 | Sources – the Mansarovar Group and Others
[36:5:0] # Rising near Mansarovar (Tibet) vs elsewhere
[36:5:1] TABLE head: Rise in the Mansarovar–Kailash area (Tibet) | Rise elsewhere
  [36:5:1.0] Indus – Singge Khabab | Ganga/Bhagirathi – Gangotri (Gomukh), within India
  [36:5:1.1] Sutlej – Rakas Tal (Rakshastal) | Yamuna – Yamunotri
  [36:5:1.2] Brahmaputra – Chemayungdung | Chenab – Baralacha La
  [36:5:1.3] Karnali (Ghaghara) | Jhelum – Verinag
  [36:5:1.4]  | Beas – Beas Kund, Rohtang
  [36:5:1.5]  | Ravi – Kalu hills/Rohtang
[36:5:2] - Near Mansarovar lie the sources of **all three – Brahmaputra, Sutlej and Indus**; the **Brahmaputra and Indus** rise at almost the same point.
[36:5:3] - **Rivers not rising in Indian territory:** **Brahmaputra**, **Sutlej** (only one of Beas/Chenab/Ravi/Sutlej), **Ghaghara**; Chambal, Jhelum, Ravi, Beas, Mahanadi, Ganga, Yamuna rise in India.
[36:5:4] - The Sutlej rises within about 80 km of the Indus source and enters India at Shipki La.
[36:5:5] # Other sources
[36:5:6] TABLE head: River | Source
  [36:5:6.0] Teesta | Tso Lhamo lake, North Sikkim
  [36:5:6.1] Barak | Manipur hills
  [36:5:6.2] Ramganga | Dudhatoli ranges, Pauri Garhwal
  [36:5:6.3] Chambal | Janapav hills near Mhow
  [36:5:6.4] Son | Amarkantak
  [36:5:6.5] Damodar | Khamarpat hill, Chota Nagpur
  [36:5:6.6] Gomti | Gomat Taal, Pilibhit (plains)
  [36:5:6.7] Narmada | Amarkantak plateau – a Peninsular river that does not rise from a glacier
[36:5:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.7-12; Rocket Indian Geography p.2-3, p.6; app notes 4:36 (sub 1)
## SUB 6 | Himalayan Lakes and the Terai Arc
[36:6:0] # Lakes
[36:6:1] TABLE head: Lake | State/UT | Type / note
  [36:6:1.0] Pangong Tso, Tso Moriri | Ladakh | Brackish, high-altitude; formed by tectonic activity; Tso Moriri is a Ramsar site
  [36:6:1.1] Yaya Tso | Ladakh | First biodiversity heritage site of Ladakh (Biological Diversity Act)
  [36:6:1.2] Wular | J&K | Largest freshwater lake of India; on the Jhelum
  [36:6:1.3] Loktak | Manipur | Freshwater; floating phumdis; Keibul Lamjao NP
  [36:6:1.4] Bhimtal | Uttarakhand (Kumaon) | Freshwater
  [36:6:1.5] Roopkund | Uttarakhand | Glacial "skeleton lake"
[36:6:2] # Terai Arc Landscape
[36:6:3] - An ~810 km India–Nepal tiger landscape **between the Yamuna (west) and the Bagmati (east)** (WWF India); about 49,500 sq km, 30,000 sq km in India.
[36:6:4] ~~ Sources: wwfindia.org (Terai Arc Landscape); app notes 4:36 (sub 6)
[36:6:5] - **Kolleru** (AP) is fed by the **Budameru and Tammileru**, not directly by the Krishna; **Kanwar lake (Kabar Tal, Bihar)** = oxbow of the **Burhi Gandak** (UPSC 2023).
[36:6:6] - **Ghepan (Ghepan Gath)** – glacial lake in the **Lahaul valley, Himachal Pradesh**.
[36:6:7] - **Sambhar** (near Jaipur, Rajasthan) = **largest inland salt-water lake** of India; Chilika is a coastal lagoon.
[36:6:8] - **Yaya Tso** (Changthang, ~4,820 m) = '**bird's paradise**'; not fed by the Sutlej.
[36:6:9] - **Pangong Tso:** name = '**high grassland lake**'; **brackish**, not freshwater; most of it lies in **Tibet (China)**; ringed by arid mountains.
[36:6:10] - **Tso Kar** is also in **Ladakh**; **Tsomgo (Changu)** is in **Sikkim**.

  [36:7:0.0] Bhakra–Nangal | Sutlej | HP; Gobind Sagar
  [36:7:0.1] Pandoh | Beas | HP
  [36:7:0.2] Pong | Beas | Maharana Pratap Sagar bird sanctuary
  [36:7:0.3] Baglihar, Salal, Dul Hasti | Chenab | J&K
  [36:7:0.4] Tehri | Bhagirathi | Uttarakhand
  [36:7:0.5] Tilaiya, Maithon | Barakar | DVC
  [36:7:0.6] Panchet | Damodar | DVC
  [36:7:0.7] Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar | Chambal | MP, Rajasthan
  [36:7:0.8] Matatila, Rajghat | Betwa | UP–MP
  [36:7:0.9] Mandal | North Koel | Jharkhand
  [36:7:0.10] Rihand | Rihand (Son system) | Uttar Pradesh
  [36:7:0.11] Kishau | Tons | Yamuna system
  [36:7:0.12] Kalagarh | Ramganga | Uttarakhand
[36:7:1] - **Multi-state projects:** **Chambal Valley – MP and Rajasthan**; **Kosi – Bihar and Nepal**; Gandak – India–Nepal (1959); DVC (1948) – Jharkhand and WB.
[36:7:2] - **Canals:** **Sirhind – Sutlej** (Ropar); **Upper Bari Doab – Ravi**; Indira Gandhi – Harike (Sutlej–Beas).
[36:7:3] - **Peninsular projects (for contrast):** Srisailam – Krishna; **Hirakud – Mahanadi**; **Jayakwadi – Godavari** (not Cauvery); Shivasamudram – Cauvery.
[36:7:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Geography p.12, p.14; app notes 4:36 (sub 7)
[36:7:5] - **Eden canal** (1873, Bardhaman, WB) is taken out of the **Damodar**.
[36:7:6] - **Kishau dam** (Tons, HP–Uttarakhand border): water mainly for **Haryana**, Delhi, UP, Rajasthan; power to HP and Uttarakhand; six-state agreement **Sep 2026**.
[36:7:7] - **DVC (7 Jul 1948)** = **first multipurpose river valley project** of independent India (modelled on the TVA).
[36:7:8] - **Tilpara barrage** (Suri, Birbhum, WB) is on the **Mayurakshi** (Massanjore/Canada dam upstream).
[36:7:9] - **Farakka barrage** (1975) – main aim: divert Ganga water to **augment the Bhagirathi–Hooghly** (flush silt from Kolkata port).
[36:7:10] - **Indira Gandhi canal** (started 1958) carries water of the **Sutlej, Beas and Ravi** from **Harike**.
[36:7:11] - **Saran and Triveni canals** – both from the **Gandak** (barrage at **Valmikinagar**, West Champaran, Bihar).
[36:7:12] - **Tehri dam** is on the **Bhagirathi** just below its confluence with the **Bhilangana** (old Tehri).
[36:7:13] - **Gang canal (Bikaner canal)** – from the **Sutlej** (Hussainiwala, Ferozepur); built by Maharaja **Ganga Singh**, opened **1927**.

=== NOTES 4:37 | Peninsular Drainage – East-flowing and West-flowing Rivers, River Basins, Watershed
## SUB 0 | East-flowing vs West-flowing Rivers – Deltas, Estuaries and Direction
[37:0:0] # Why most Peninsular rivers flow east
[37:0:1] - The **Western Ghats** are the main water divide; the Deccan Plateau is **higher in the west and slopes east** to the Bay of Bengal, so most large rivers flow **east**.
[37:0:2] - The Peninsular block was **tilted north-west → south-east** (Himalayan upheaval), giving the whole drainage a Bay of Bengal orientation.
[37:0:3] - **Narmada and Tapi** are the only major Peninsular rivers flowing **west** – they occupy **trough faults (rift valleys)**.
[37:0:4] # Comparison
[37:0:5] TABLE head: Feature | East-flowing (Bay of Bengal) | West-flowing (Arabian Sea)
  [37:0:5.0] Rivers | Subarnarekha, Brahmani, Baitarani, Mahanadi, Vamsadhara, Nagavali, Godavari, Krishna, Pennar, Palar, Kaveri, Vaigai, Tamraparni | Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati, Vaitarna, Mandovi, Kali, Sharavati, Netravati, Periyar, Bharathapuzha, Pamba
  [37:0:5.1] Size | Long and large, dendritic tributaries | Short and swift (except Narmada, Tapi)
  [37:0:5.2] Mouth | Extensive deltas | No deltas – long, deep estuaries (natural harbours)
  [37:0:5.3] Use | Irrigation | Hydropower
[37:0:6] - **Why no deltas in the west:** steep Western Ghats slope (rapid flow), **short courses**, **hard rocky terrain**; Narmada and Tapi filled their fault troughs, so there is little alluvium – sediment is carried away by waves.
[37:0:7] - **Mahanadi** (delta near **Paradeep**, Odisha), Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri build deltas; **Narmada, Tapi, Mandovi** end in **estuaries** (Narmada estuary ~27 km, south of **Bharuch**).
[37:0:8] - **Subarnarekha** forms an **estuary** between the Ganga and Mahanadi deltas.
[37:0:9] - About **600** short, swift rivers drain the west coast.
[37:0:10] # Classic odd-ones
[37:0:11] - **Kali (Kalinadi)** of Karnataka is **west-flowing** (Diggi, Uttara Kannada → Arabian Sea at Karwar) – not east-flowing.
[37:0:12] - **Periyar** – west-flowing, reaches the Arabian Sea via **Vembanad**; **Pennar and Palar** flow east to the Bay of Bengal.
[37:0:13] - **Krishna** rises ~64 km from the Arabian Sea but flows ~1,400 km east to the **Bay of Bengal**.
[37:0:14] - **Tamraparni** flows east into the Gulf of Mannar – not west-flowing; **Brahmani** is east-flowing.
[37:0:15] - **Betwa** is a Yamuna tributary (flows north-east); **Rapti** is a Ghaghara tributary (NW → SE) – neither is west-flowing.
[37:0:16] - **Tungabhadra, Penganga** flow east (Krishna / Godavari systems).
[37:0:17] - **Kerala:** all major rivers flow west, but the **Kabini** (Wayanad) flows **east** to the Kaveri; **MP:** most rivers flow east but **Narmada and Tapi** flow **west** – so "no east-flowing river in Kerala" and "no west-flowing river in MP" are both **false**.
[37:0:18] > A–R (UPSC 2004): "West-flowing rivers have no deltas" / "they do not carry any alluvial sediments" → key (a), both true and R explains A; PMF calls this debatable because "do not carry any" is too absolute.
[37:0:19] > A–R (CDS 2010): "East-flowing Deccan rivers have deltas" is true, but "because they flow through soft rocks" is false – the Deccan is hard rock.
[37:0:20] > A–R (UPPSC 2014): "Western Ghats rivers do not form deltas" / "short courses, high speed over hard rocks" → both true, R explains A.
[37:0:21] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.13 (book p.97); PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.16-20, p.47-48, p.55-56; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.11-13; Rocket Indian Geography p.6-7; app notes 4:37 (sub 1)
## SUB 1 | Krishna System
[37:1:0] # Course
[37:1:1] - Rises near **Mahabaleshwar** (Sahyadri, Maharashtra; ~1,337 m) → Maharashtra (**Sangli**), Karnataka, Telangana, AP → Bay of Bengal at **Hamsaladeevi**.
[37:1:2] - **~1,400 km**; **second-longest Peninsular river** and second-largest east-flowing river; basin ~**8%** of India; one of India's largest deltas.
[37:1:3] - Splits into two branches at **Puligadda**, **64 km below Vijayawada**; **Diviseema** lies between them.
[37:1:4] - Cities: **Sangli, Vijayawada, Srisailam, Kurnool (Tungabhadra), Hyderabad (Musi)**.
[37:1:5] # Tributaries
[37:1:6] TABLE head: Bank | Tributaries
  [37:1:6.0] Right | Tungabhadra (largest), Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Koyna, Yerla, Varna (Warna), Panchganga, Dudhganga
  [37:1:6.1] Left | Bhima (largest left-bank; Chandrabhaga at Pandharpur), Dindi, Musi (Anantagiri hills; Hyderabad), Munneru
[37:1:7] - **Tungabhadra** = **Tunga + Bhadra**, both rising at **Varaha Parvata (Varaha hills), Western Ghats**; 531 km; joins the Krishna at **Sangameswaram** (Kurnool); **Hampi** on its bank; **Hagari (Vedavathi)** is its biggest tributary.
[37:1:8] - **Raichur Doab** = wedge between the **Krishna and Tungabhadra**.
[37:1:9] - **Not Krishna tributaries:** **Tel** (Mahanadi), **Gomati** (Ganga). **Panchganga** and **Koyna** belong to the Krishna, not the Godavari; Mand, Warna, Tungabhadra are Krishna tributaries.
[37:1:10] # Dams and projects
[37:1:11] TABLE head: Project | Place / note
  [37:1:11.0] Nagarjuna Sagar | On the Krishna near Nandikonda; multipurpose; then in undivided AP – now on the Telangana (Nalgonda)–AP (Palnadu) border
  [37:1:11.1] Srisailam | On the Krishna (not Tungabhadra); HEP; heart of the Nagarjuna Sagar–Srisailam Tiger Reserve
  [37:1:11.2] Almatti (Lal Bahadur Shastri Dam) | Krishna, Bijapur/Vijayapura, Karnataka; main reservoir of the Upper Krishna Project
  [37:1:11.3] Tungabhadra (Pampa Sagar) | Near Hosapete
[37:1:12] - **Krishna Raja Sagara (KRS)** is on the **Kaveri**, not the Krishna, despite the name.
[37:1:13] > "Rises in Maharashtra, flows through Karnataka and AP, meets the Bay of Bengal on the Andhra coast" (also "passes Sangli, meets the sea at Hamsaladeevi") = **Krishna**; the Godavari does not enter Karnataka.
[37:1:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.14 (book p.98); NextGen AP Geography 02 p.18-19; Rocket AP Geography p.5-6, p.10; Rocket Indian Geography p.4, p.11-12; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.37-39; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.13
[37:1:15] - **Pune** stands on the **Mula-Mutha** (tributaries of the Bhima → Krishna).
[37:1:16] - Match: **Pandoh – Beas**, **Srisailam – Krishna**, **Matatila – Betwa**, **Nizam Sagar – Manjira**.
[37:1:17] - **Pune** – on the **Mula–Mutha** (tributaries of the **Bhima**, Krishna system).
## SUB 2 | Sources of Peninsular Rivers – Amarkantak, Western and Eastern Ghats
[37:2:0] TABLE head: Source | River(s)
  [37:2:0.0] Amarkantak plateau, Maikal range (Anuppur, MP) | Narmada (west) and Son (north to the Ganga); also Johilla and a small Mahanadi (Son tributaries)
  [37:2:0.1] Trimbakeshwar / Brahmagiri (Nashik, Maharashtra) | Godavari; Vaitarna rises in the Trimbak hills too (west-flowing, north of Mumbai)
  [37:2:0.2] Mahabaleshwar (Western Ghats, Maharashtra) | Krishna (also Koyna)
  [37:2:0.3] Brahmagiri / Talakaveri (Kodagu, Karnataka) | Kaveri – not AP
  [37:2:0.4] Sihawa (Dhamtari, earlier Raipur district, Chhattisgarh) | Mahanadi
  [37:2:0.5] Multai, Betul (Satpura, MP) | Tapi – not the Western Ghats
  [37:2:0.6] Minda, Vindhyas (Dhar, MP) | Mahi
  [37:2:0.7] Nandi hills / Nandidurg (Chikkaballapur, Karnataka) | Pennar, Palar, Ponnaiyar
  [37:2:0.8] Varaha Parvata (Western Ghats) | Tunga and Bhadra → Tungabhadra
  [37:2:0.9] Mahadeo hills (Satpura, Chhindwara) | Tawa
  [37:2:0.10] Eastern Ghats | Vamsadhara, Nagavali, Machkund, Sileru, Sabari
[37:2:1] - **Western Ghats** = "**Water Tower of Peninsular India**" – sources of the **Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri**.
[37:2:2] - **Amarkantak** is where two major rivers rise – the **Son** flows **north** to join the Ganga (Bay of Bengal) and the **Narmada** flows **west** to the Arabian Sea (UPSC 2009). **Damodar** does **not** rise at Amarkantak (Khamarpat hill, Chota Nagpur).
[37:2:3] - **Son – "actual" source:** usually given as **Amarkantak** (Sonmuda, ~1.5 km from Narmada Kund); the stricter view places its origin near **Pendra** – the village **Sonbachharwar**, Pendra tehsil (then **Bilaspur district**, now Gaurela-Pendra-Marwahi, Chhattisgarh).
[37:2:4] - **Bhedaghat** (marble rocks, Jabalpur), Shahdol and Hoshangabad lie **on the course** of the Narmada, not at its source.
[37:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.13-14, 08 p.1; Rocket Indian Geography p.2, p.5, p.13; Rocket AP Geography p.6, p.21; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.35, p.40, p.44, p.49-53; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.12-13; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sone_River; villageinfo.in (Sonbacharwar, Pendra)
[37:2:6] - **Radial drainage:** streams flow outward from a central height – **Amarkantak** (Narmada, Son, Mahanadi).
## SUB 3 | Mahanadi, Kaveri, Pennar and Other East-flowing Rivers
[37:3:0] # Mahanadi
[37:3:1] - Rises at **Sihawa** (Chhattisgarh) → Chhattisgarh and **Odisha** (does **not** pass through AP); **851 km**; basin **1,41,589 sq km** (~4.3% of India); **Cuttack**; **delta in Odisha near Paradeep**; second to the Godavari in water potential and flood capacity.
[37:3:2] TABLE head: Bank | Tributaries
  [37:3:2.0] Left | Seonath (Shivnath), Hasdeo (largest), Mand, Ib
  [37:3:2.1] Right | Ong, Tel, Jonk
[37:3:3] - **Hirakud Dam** on the Mahanadi, ~15 km from **Sambalpur** (Odisha) – longest earthen dam (main dam 4.8 km). **Kuakhai** (Bhubaneswar) is a delta branch.
[37:3:4] - **Tel** = right-bank tributary of the **Mahanadi** (not of the Krishna or any Bihar river).
[37:3:5] # Kaveri (Cauvery)
[37:3:6] - **Talakaveri, Brahmagiri hills, Kodagu (Karnataka)** → Karnataka, **Kerala** (Kabini catchment), **Tamil Nadu**, Puducherry → Bay of Bengal near **Poompuhar**; ~800 km; basin 81,155 sq km.
[37:3:7] - Called **"Dakshina Ganga" / "Ganga of the South"** (the Godavari is also called Dakshin/Vriddha Ganga).
[37:3:8] - **Cauvery delta = "South India's granary"** (Thanjavur).
[37:3:9] TABLE head: Bank | Tributaries
  [37:3:9.0] Left | Harangi, Hemavathi, Shimsha, Arkavathi
  [37:3:9.1] Right | Lakshmantirtha, Kabini (Kapila), Suvarnavati, Bhavani, Noyyal, Amaravati
[37:3:10] - **Kabini** – Wayanad (Kerala), flows east, joins at **Tirumakudalu Narsipur**.
[37:3:11] - Forks thrice: islands **Srirangapatna, Sivasamudram, Srirangam**; dams **KRS (Kannambadi)**, **Mettur**; most exploited river (highest share abstracted for irrigation).
[37:3:12] # Pennar and smaller rivers
[37:3:13] - **Pennar (Uttara Pinakini)** – Nandi hills (Karnataka) → AP (Anantapur, Kadapa – **Gandikota gorge**, Nellore) → Bay of Bengal; **lifeline of Rayalaseema**; tributaries **Jayamangali**, Kunderu, Sagileru (left), Chitravathi, **Papagni**, Cheyyeru (right).
[37:3:14] - **Palar** – Nandi hills → Karnataka, AP (Chittoor), Tamil Nadu. **Vaigai** – Madurai → Palk Bay.
[37:3:15] - **Brahmani** (South Koel + Sankh) and **Baitarani** – common delta at **Bhitarkanika** (Odisha). **Subarnarekha** – Ranchi plateau; estuary.
[37:3:16] - **Machkund** – Duduma falls; **Machkund HEP** (AP–Odisha) is on the **Machkund** river.
[37:3:17] # Hilsa
[37:3:18] - **Hilsa (Indian shad)** migrates up the east-coast rivers; in AP the **Godavari's "Pulasa"** (Jul–Sep floods) is the famous catch; the **Narmada estuary (Bharuch)** now lands the largest hilsa catch on the west coast; Hooghly and Mahanadi also have hilsa.
[37:3:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.13-14; Rocket Indian Geography p.4, p.12; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.8, p.40-46, p.58; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.12-13; sandrp.in (Pennar); downtoearth.org.in and core.ac.uk (hilsa)
[37:3:20] - City–river: **Lucknow – Gomti**, **Cuttack – Mahanadi**, **Jamshedpur – Subarnarekha (Kharkai)**, **Kota – Chambal**.
[37:3:21] - **Tiruttani** (Tamil Nadu) lies on the small **Nandi (Nandiyar)** river.
## SUB 4 | Godavari System
[37:4:0] - **Dakshin Ganga / Vriddha Ganga** – called so for its **length and the area it covers** and its many tributaries; **longest Peninsular river** (1,465 km), second longest in India; **largest Peninsular basin** (3,12,812 sq km, ~9.5% of India).
[37:4:1] - Rises at **Trimbakeshwar (Nashik)** → Maharashtra (Nanded), Telangana, AP → Bay of Bengal; basin also in Chhattisgarh, Odisha, MP, Karnataka, Puducherry (Yanam).
[37:4:2] - **Widest/extensive delta** of the Deccan (**Konaseema**); after Rajahmundry splits into **Gautami** (east) and **Vasishta** (west), which divide into **7 branches** (Sapta Godavari).
[37:4:3] TABLE head: Branch | Mouth
  [37:4:3.0] Gautami | Yanam
  [37:4:3.1] Vasishta | Antarvedi
  [37:4:3.2] Vainateya | Komaragiripatnam
  [37:4:3.3] Tulya, Bharadwaja, Kaushika, Athreya | Bendamoorlanka / Coringa area
[37:4:4] - **2.7 km** wide at Rajahmundry; **Sir Arthur Cotton's anicut** at **Dowleswaram** (1852).
[37:4:5] # Tributaries
[37:4:6] TABLE head: Bank | Tributaries
  [37:4:6.0] Left | Purna, Pranhita (Penganga + Wardha + Wainganga), Indravati, Sabari, Kinnerasani
  [37:4:6.1] Right | Pravara, Manjira (Manjeera), Maner (Manair)
[37:4:7] - **Pranhita** = **largest tributary** (biggest flow), joins near **Kaleshwaram**; Penganga reaches the Godavari **via the Wardha–Pranhita**, not the Ganga.
[37:4:8] - **Indravati** rises in **Kalahandi (Odisha)**, flows through Bastar (Jagdalpur; Chitrakote falls).
[37:4:9] - **Sabari** (= **Kolab** in Odisha; Sinkaram hills) is the **last major tributary**, joining near **Kunavaram** above the delta; its tributary **Sileru** (upper reaches **Machkund**) joins it at the **AP–Chhattisgarh–Odisha** tri-junction.
[37:4:10] - **Nizam Sagar** is on the **Manjira** (Kamareddy, Telangana).
[37:4:11] - **Not Godavari tributaries:** **Koyna, Ghataprabha, Panchganga, Bhima** (Krishna), **Vamsadhara, Pennar**, **Amaravati** (Kaveri).
[37:4:12] > The Godavari is **not** perennial everywhere: like other Peninsular rivers it is rain-fed and seasonal in its upper Maharashtra course; Narmada and Tapi (rift-valley rivers) have more sustained flow.
[37:4:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.13; Rocket AP Geography p.5, p.8, p.10, p.12; Rocket Indian Geography p.4, p.11; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.34-36; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.11-12
[37:4:14] - **Kandakurthi** (Nizamabad, Telangana) – Triveni Sangamam where the **Manjira and Haridra** join the **Godavari**.
## SUB 5 | Structure and Sequence – Older Drainage, Rift Valleys, Consequent and Superimposed Rivers
[37:5:0] - Peninsular drainage is **older** than the Himalayan – **broad, graded, shallow valleys**, **fixed courses**, no meanders, **non-perennial** flow.
[37:5:1] - **Consequent rivers** follow the general slope – **most Peninsular rivers**, e.g. **Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri** (Western Ghats → Bay of Bengal). **Subsequent:** Chambal, Sind, Ken, Betwa, Son meet the Yamuna/Ganga at right angles.
[37:5:2] - **Superimposed** rivers keep a course developed on a former cover rock – **Chambal**, Damodar, Subarnarekha, Banas.
[37:5:3] # Rift valleys
[37:5:4] TABLE head: River | Rift between / note
  [37:5:4.0] Narmada | Vindhya (north) and Satpura (south) – divides the Deccan Tableland from northern India; west-flowing
  [37:5:4.1] Tapi | Satpura (north) and Ajanta (south)
  [37:5:4.2] Damodar | Chota Nagpur – east-flowing rift valley due to down-warping (Gondwana trough); called a "biological desert" because of heavy industrial pollution
[37:5:5] # Sequences
[37:5:6] - East-flowing, **north → south:** **Subarnarekha, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Pennar, Kaveri, Vaigai** (UPSC 2002) – so south → north = Kaveri, Pennar, Krishna, Godavari, Mahanadi.
[37:5:7] - **North → south:** Godavari, Pennar, Kaveri, **Periyar**; **Penganga, Godavari, Bhima, Tungabhadra**.
[37:5:8] - Whole India N → S: **Indus – Ganga – Godavari – Krishna** (Ganga – Mahanadi – Godavari – Krishna is also N → S).
[37:5:9] - Main systems: **Himalayan** = Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra (the Indus rises on the northern slopes of the **Kailash range near Mansarovar**); **Peninsular** = Narmada, Tapi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi.
[37:5:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Physical Geography 03 p.13-16; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.19, p.48-50; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.5-6, p.11-12; Rocket Indian Geography p.2, p.5; app notes 4:37 (sub 0)
[37:5:11] - **Rectangular drainage:** right-angle bends along joints and faults – **Vindhyan region**.
[37:5:12] - **Dendritic** (tree-like) pattern on uniform rock: Ganga plains, **Godavari**, Krishna.
[37:5:13] - **N → S:** **Kishanganga – Ganga – Wainganga – Penganga** (UPSC 1996).
## SUB 6 | Narmada, Tapi and the West-coast Rivers
[37:6:0] # Narmada
[37:6:1] - Amarkantak (Maikal) → MP, Maharashtra (border), Gujarat → **Gulf of Khambhat** south of Bharuch; **1,312 km** – **longest west-flowing**; **Jabalpur, Bhedaghat** (marble rocks, **Dhuandhar**), Kapildhara near Amarkantak.
[37:6:2] - Tributaries: **Tawa** (longest; Mahadeo hills; joins at Bandra Bhan), Burhner, **Banjar**, Sher, Shakkar, **Dudhi**, Ganjal (left); **Hiran**, Kolar, Orsang (right). **Purna** is **not** a Narmada tributary.
[37:6:3] - Projects: **Sardar Sarovar** (Gujarat), **Indira Sagar** (Khandwa, MP – **largest reservoir in India by volume**; Nagarjuna Sagar 2nd), **Omkareshwar** (Khandwa), **Bargi**, Maheshwar. The Narmada Valley plan has **30 major dams** – **29 major projects in MP** plus Sardar Sarovar in Gujarat.
[37:6:4] - Riverine islands: **Aliabet** (largest), **Sarfuddin, Dashan, Mehgam, Vegni**.
[37:6:5] - Basin: MP, Gujarat, Maharashtra and **Chhattisgarh** (Kabirdham/**Rajnandgaon** area of the Maikal).
[37:6:6] # Tapi (Tapti)
[37:6:7] - **Multai, Betul (MP)** → MP, Maharashtra, Gujarat → Arabian Sea at **Suvali near Surat**; **724 km**, second-longest west-flowing; "twin / handmaid of the Narmada"; **Purna** (largest tributary), Girna; **Ukai** dam.
[37:6:8] # Other west-flowing rivers
[37:6:9] TABLE head: River | Fact
  [37:6:9.0] Mahi | Minda, Vindhyas (Dhar, MP) → Banswara (Rajasthan) → Gujarat → Gulf of Khambhat; crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice
  [37:6:9.1] Sabarmati | Aravallis (Udaipur) → Ahmedabad → Gulf of Khambhat; shortest and smallest of the major (>20,000 sq km) basins
  [37:6:9.2] Vaitarna | Trimbak hills (Nashik) → Arabian Sea north of Mumbai
  [37:6:9.3] Mithi | Rises at Vihar Lake, Mumbai; Powai Lake water joins; Mahim Bay
  [37:6:9.4] Periyar | Longest river of Kerala; Mullaperiyar dam; Idukki/Cheruthoni dam on a Periyar tributary
  [37:6:9.5] Sharavati / Kali / Netravati / Mandovi | Jog falls / Diggi, Karwar / Mangaluru / Dudhsagar, Goa
[37:6:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.1-2; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49-58; Rocket Indian Geography p.5-8; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.13; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narmada_Valley_Development_Authority; app notes 4:37 (sub 6)
[37:6:11] - **Gandhi Sagar** is on the **Chambal** (Mandsaur, MP), not the Narmada.
## SUB 7 | Length and Basin Ranking
[37:7:0] TABLE head: River | Length (km) | Basin (sq km)
  [37:7:0.0] Ganga | 2,525 – longest flowing in India | ~8.6 lakh
  [37:7:0.1] Godavari | 1,465 – longest Peninsular | 3,12,812
  [37:7:0.2] Krishna | ~1,400 | 2,58,948
  [37:7:0.3] Narmada | 1,312 – longest west-flowing | 98,796
  [37:7:0.4] Mahanadi | 851 | 1,41,589
  [37:7:0.5] Kaveri | ~800 | 81,155
  [37:7:0.6] Tapi | 724 | 65,145
[37:7:1] - Length order: **Godavari > Narmada > Mahanadi > Tapi**; Godavari > Krishna > Narmada > Mahanadi > Tapi.
[37:7:2] - Catchment: **Godavari > Krishna > Mahanadi > Narmada > Kaveri > Tapi**; Narmada and Kaveri basins are about the same size.
[37:7:3] - Basins **within India**: **Ganga > Indus (3,21,289) > Godavari > Krishna > Brahmaputra (~1.94 lakh)**.
[37:7:4] - Among Kaveri, Pennar, Mahi, Sabarmati: **Sabarmati** is the shortest (~371 km) with the smallest basin (~21,700 sq km).
[37:7:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.56; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.5, p.12-13; NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.13; app notes 4:37 (sub 3)
## SUB 8 | Luni and Inland Drainage
[37:8:0] - **Luni** – rises in the Aravallis south-west of **Ajmer** (near Pushkar; called **Sagarmati**), flows west then south-west after **Telwara**, and is **lost in the marshy Rann of Kutch** – does not reach the sea (not the Gulf of Khambhat or Kutch); **endorheic / land-bound**; largest river of the Thar; ~495–511 km.
[37:8:1] - Its water is **fresh in the upper course and saline in the lower course** (salt-bearing desert soils).
[37:8:2] - Left-bank tributaries **Jawai, Sukri**, Guhiya, Bandi; right bank Jojari.
[37:8:3] - Inland drainage: **Luni, Ghaggar**. **Ghaggar** water is **not** used by the Indira Gandhi Canal (which draws on the Sutlej–Beas at Harike).
[37:8:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.18, p.55; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.13-14; Rocket Indian Geography p.6; app notes 4:37 (sub 1)
[37:8:5] - **Sahibi** – rises in the Aravallis and flows **north/north-east** (to Haryana–Delhi), not south.
## SUB 9 | River Linking, Water Disputes and Watershed
[37:9:0] - After bifurcation (2014), **Telangana and AP** fight over the **Krishna and Godavari** waters (KRMB, GRMB; Polavaram–Banakacherla / Nallamala Sagar link opposed by **Telangana**).
[37:9:1] - **River linking:** first proposed by **Sir Arthur Cotton** (19th c.); **National Perspective Plan 1980** (NWDA) – **30 links = 14 Himalayan + 16 Peninsular**. First link completed: **Godavari–Krishna (Pattiseema), 2015**. **Ken-Betwa** (MP–UP; Daudhan dam in **Panna Tiger Reserve**) is the flagship link; **Par-Tapi-Narmada** – Gujarat and Maharashtra; **Tapti Basin Mega Recharge** – MP–Maharashtra MoU (May 2025). AP priorities: Vamsadhara-Penna intra-linking, Godavari-Krishna.
[37:9:2] - **Disputes:** **Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956** under **Article 262**; water = **Entry 17, State List**, subject to **Entry 56, Union List**.
[37:9:3] TABLE head: Dispute | Tribunal / outcome
  [37:9:3.0] Krishna (MH, KA, AP/Telangana) | KWDT-I Bachawat (1969/1973); KWDT-II Brijesh Kumar (2004)
  [37:9:3.1] Kaveri (KA, TN, Kerala, Puducherry) | CWDT 2007; SC 2018: TN 404.25, KA 284.75 tmcft
  [37:9:3.2] Mahadayi/Mandovi | Goa, Karnataka, Maharashtra (award 2018)
[37:9:4] - **Watershed** = small catchment (basin = large); **PMKSY-WDC** run by the **Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development**.
[37:9:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.16; app notes 4:37 (sub 10-11)
[37:9:6] - **Vamsadhara** dispute (AP–Odisha): tribunal 2010, award **2017**; the Cauvery tribunal's final award was **2007** (not 2018).
[37:9:7] - **Water-deficit basins:** Sabarmati, Tapi (CWC storage shortfall), and in NWDA terms Krishna, Kaveri, Pennar, Vaigai; **surplus:** Mahanadi, Godavari, Brahmaputra.
## SUB 10 | Waterfalls on Peninsular Rivers
[37:10:0] TABLE head: Falls | River | Note
  [37:10:0.0] Kunchikal | Varahi | Karnataka – highest (height)
  [37:10:0.1] Jog (Gersoppa) | Sharavati | Shivamogga – noted for width
  [37:10:0.2] Shivasamudram | Kaveri | Karnataka – volume; Hogenakkal, Chunchanakatte also on the Kaveri
  [37:10:0.3] Dudhsagar | Mandovi | Goa
  [37:10:0.4] Dhuandhar / Kapildhara | Narmada | Jabalpur / near Amarkantak
  [37:10:0.5] Chitrakote | Indravati | Bastar
  [37:10:0.6] Hundru / Jonha / Dasam | Subarnarekha / Rarhu / Kanchi | Jharkhand
  [37:10:0.7] Lodh (Budha Ghagh) | Burha | Latehar – highest in Jharkhand
  [37:10:0.8] Amritdhara | Hasdeo | Chhattisgarh (not Jharkhand)
  [37:10:0.9] Bhalkund (Rahatgarh) | Bina | MP
  [37:10:0.10] Duduma | Machkund | AP–Odisha
[37:10:1] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Geography p.8, p.15; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.48; app notes 4:37 (sub 8)
[37:10:2] - **Chitrakote** (Indravati, Bastar) – the **'Niagara of India'**, India's **widest** waterfall (horseshoe, ~300 m wide in the monsoon).
[37:10:3] - **Gokak falls** – on the **Ghataprabha** (Krishna tributary), Belagavi, Karnataka.
## SUB 11 | Lakes, Lagoons and River Islands
[37:11:0] TABLE head: Lake | State | Fact
  [37:11:0.0] Chilika | Odisha | Asia's largest brackish lagoon; India's first Ramsar site (1981) – not freshwater
  [37:11:0.1] Pulicat | AP–Tamil Nadu border | Brackish lagoon (not Odisha)
  [37:11:0.2] Kolleru | AP | Freshwater, between the Krishna and Godavari deltas; fed by Budameru, Tammileru
  [37:11:0.3] Vembanad | Kerala | Longest lake; Periyar, Pamba drain into it
  [37:11:0.4] Sambhar | Rajasthan | Largest inland saline lake
  [37:11:0.5] Lonar | Maharashtra | Meteorite-impact crater, saline-alkaline
  [37:11:0.6] Loktak | Manipur | Freshwater, phumdis
  [37:11:0.7] Nakki / Surajkund | Rajasthan (Mount Abu) / Haryana | –
[37:11:1] - River islands: **Srirangam** (Kaveri + **Kollidam**, Tiruchirappalli), **Aliabet** (Narmada), **Majuli** (Brahmaputra).
[37:11:2] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.14; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.39; app notes 4:37 (sub 9)
[37:11:3] - **Centripetal drainage:** streams converge into a central lake – **Loktak** (Manipur).
[37:11:4] - **Rajasthan saline lakes:** **Sambhar, Didwana, Kuchaman, Sargol, Khatu, Degana, Pachpadra** (UPSC 2021).
[37:11:5] - **Not a lagoon:** **Periyar lake** (Thekkady) – an artificial freshwater reservoir of the Mullaperiyar dam; **Ashtamudi**, Chilika, Pulicat are lagoons.
[37:11:6] - **Roopkund** ('skeleton lake') – Chamoli, **Uttarakhand**; **Bhimtal** – Nainital, Uttarakhand.

=== NOTES 4:38 | Indian Climate – Monsoon Mechanism, Theories and Seasons
## SUB 0 | Winter Season, Retreating and North-East Monsoon, Western Disturbances
[38:0:0] # Retreating monsoon (October–November/December)
[38:0:1] - Caused by the **southward movement of the Sun's vertical rays**; the NW low disappears, the **subtropical westerly jet returns south of the Himalayas**, the TEJ disappears.
[38:0:2] - Withdrawal is gradual (about three months): from the extreme **north-west first** – NextGen/NCERT: from the beginning of **October**; PMF/IMD: from **mid-September** – out of the peninsula by October and from the south-east tip by **December**.
[38:0:3] - **Fine weather and clear skies**; land temperature rises again → hot, humid "**October heat**".
[38:0:4] - **Tropical cyclones** are the hallmark: they form mostly in the **Bay of Bengal** (rarely the Arabian Sea), and their frequency peaks in **October–November**; they bring heavy rain to the east coast → **bimodal** rainfall in the south.
[38:0:5] - The retreating winds blow from land **towards the Bay of Bengal**, pick up moisture there and rain on the Coromandel coast.
[38:0:6] - About **13%** of annual rainfall comes in this season.
[38:0:7] > "Declining monsoon is indicated by clear sky, pressure change over the Bay of Bengal and rising temperature on land" – all three (BPSC).
[38:0:8] # North-east monsoon and Tamil Nadu
[38:0:9] - The winter high over NW India sends winds NW → SE down the plains; over the Bay of Bengal they become the **north-east monsoon** and pick up moisture.
[38:0:10] - **Tamil Nadu / Coromandel coast** gets its **main rain in October–December (Nov–Dec)** from the NE monsoon; South Arcot and Ramanathapuram get **over 50%** of their rain then. Also **Rayalaseema, Nellore, south coastal AP, SE Karnataka, SE Kerala**; **not the Gujarat coast**.
[38:0:11] - **Why Tamil Nadu is dry in the SW monsoon:** it lies in the **rain shadow** of the Western Ghats for the Arabian Sea branch, and the Bay branch blows **parallel to the coast**. So **Chennai** gets the least SW-monsoon rain among Kolkata, Mangalore, Chennai, Delhi.
[38:0:12] - States **not** fed mainly by the June–September monsoon: **Tamil Nadu** (NE monsoon) and **Jammu & Kashmir** (western disturbances).
[38:0:13] # Western disturbances
[38:0:14] - **Temperate (extra-tropical) cyclones from the Mediterranean**, carried east by the westerlies through Iran–Afghanistan–Pakistan into **north-west India**.
[38:0:15] - Give **10–15 cm** of winter rain to the **north-western plains** – **beneficial for rabi crops (wheat)** – and **snowfall** in J&K, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand.
[38:0:16] - Winter rain in the NW plains **decreases from west to east** (and from north to south).
[38:0:17] - **Northern plains' winter rain = western disturbances**, not the NE monsoon (which is active in winter but is not the cause) and not the retreating monsoon.
[38:0:18] - They are **not** part of the monsoon system (CDS: "not associated with monsoon climate" = western disturbances).
[38:0:19] # Winter season (December/January–February)
[38:0:20] - **High pressure over NW India** (NCERT: the **1019 mb** isobar passes through north-west India, **1013 mb** in the far south) → **anticyclonic**, dry, outblowing winds; cold northern plains, cold waves, fog; **no loo or thunderstorms**.
[38:0:21] - **Anticyclonic conditions** form because the land is **cold and the air dense** – not because of winter rain (UPSC 2001: A true, R false).
[38:0:22] - Winter is the **driest season (~2%)**: most of India is dry under the **north-east trade winds**, which blow from land to sea.
[38:0:23] - **Dry winters** (Koeppen Cwg, "monsoon with dry winter"): **Bengal / Ganga plain**; J&K and Punjab–Haryana get western-disturbance rain, Tamil Nadu gets NE-monsoon rain.
[38:0:24] - **South India:** maritime – **low diurnal and annual range**, high temperature all year, **no extremes**; the 20 °C January isotherm runs from the Tapi mouth to the Mahanadi delta.
[38:0:25] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.2-4 (book p.86-88); NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.10 (book p.80); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.22, p.32-33; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 05 p.5-6; app notes 4:38 (sub 7)
## SUB 1 | Monsoon – Meaning, Characteristics and Controls of Indian Climate
[38:1:0] # Meaning and characteristics
[38:1:1] - India has a **tropical monsoon** climate; "monsoon" from Arabic **Mausim** = season; **Al Masudi** (Arab geographer) described the seasonal rhythm of winds.
[38:1:2] - Monsoons are **seasonal (secondary/periodic) winds** that **reverse direction** with the season – **not primary (planetary) winds**.
[38:1:3] - They are confined to the tropics, roughly **20°N–20°S** (textbook statement).
[38:1:4] - The distribution of SW-monsoon rain is governed mainly by **relief**.
[38:1:5] - Monsoon rain is **not steady**, **unevenly (not equally) distributed**, has **breaks** and is **uncertain/variable**.
[38:1:6] - India is a "**thirsty land**" despite abundant rain: rain is **concentrated in a few months**, **runs off rapidly** and **evaporates quickly** – all three.
[38:1:7] - Main cause of the monsoon: the **temperature (pressure) contrast between the land and the Indian Ocean**.
[38:1:8] - **Early maritime links** of India with South-East Asia across the Bay of Bengal were helped by the **monsoon winds** (UPSC 2011).
[38:1:9] # Controls (factors) of Indian climate
[38:1:10] - **Latitude** – the **Tropic of Cancer** crosses the middle of India; the south is tropical, the north sub-tropical. India lies about **8°4'–37°6'N**, so it is **not wholly between the tropics** (Jharkhand PCS: A true, R false).
[38:1:11] - **Himalayas** – block cold Central Asian winds, trap the monsoon and give India its **climatic distinctiveness**.
[38:1:12] - **Distance from the sea (continentality)**, **altitude**, **relief**, **pressure and winds**, **upper-air circulation (jet streams)**, **ocean currents**, **cyclones/western disturbances**.
[38:1:13] - CDS 2015: **location, thermal contrast, upper-air circulation and the Himalayas** are all major factors.
[38:1:14] - **Amritsar and Shimla** lie on nearly the same latitude; Shimla is cooler because of **altitude** (~2,200 m vs ~230 m). Likewise **Ooty vs Coimbatore**, **Agra (16 °C) vs Darjiling (4 °C)** in January.
[38:1:15] - At a similar latitude **Mumbai** is moderate while **Nagpur** is extreme – **distance from the sea**. In **Kerala and the Andaman Islands** the day–night range is only about **7–8 °C**.
[38:1:16] > A–R (NDA 2011): "Monsoon winds are driven by the size of the Asian landmass" and "upper-air circulation is associated with the monsoon" – both true, R not the explanation of A.
[38:1:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.8-9, p.13 (book p.78-79, 83); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.18-19; app notes 4:38 (sub 0)
## SUB 2 | Onset, Advance, Branches and Breaks of the South-West Monsoon
[38:2:0] # Onset and advance
[38:2:1] - Season: **June–September** (IMD); also stated as **mid-June to mid-September**; gives **~75%** of annual rain.
[38:2:2] - Sudden onset = "**burst**" in the first week of June; rain in Kerala called **Varsha**.
[38:2:3] TABLE head: Stage | Normal date
  [38:2:3.0] Andaman & Nicobar Islands (first Indian territory) | ~25 May
  [38:2:3.1] Kerala (first state, Malabar coast) | 1 June (2026: 4 June)
  [38:2:3.2] Bhopal / Delhi | ~15 June / ~25 June
  [38:2:3.3] Whole country | 8 July (IMD revised normal)
[38:2:4] - IMD declares the Kerala onset after **10 May** when **60% of 14 stations** get **2.5 mm** on two consecutive days (5-day **pentads** used).
[38:2:5] - Order of onset: **Kerala → West Bengal → Uttar Pradesh → Rajasthan** (CDS 2010).
[38:2:6] - Duration: **> 120 days** in the SW peninsula, **< 75 days** in west Rajasthan; the monsoon reaches **west Rajasthan last**.
[38:2:7] # Arabian Sea branch
[38:2:8] - Strikes the **Western Ghats** and Malabar first; heaviest rain at **Agumbe, Hulikal** on the crest; the **windward west coast** gets very heavy **orographic** rain because the **Western Ghats** lie across the winds.
[38:2:9] - **Mumbai** (windward) gets far more than **Pune** (leeward); the eastern side of the Ghats is a **rain-shadow** area.
[38:2:10] - Enters central India via the **Narmada–Tapi** valleys; one arm runs **parallel to the Aravallis** → scanty rain in Rajasthan.
[38:2:11] - The **Chhattisgarh Basin** is **not much affected** by the Arabian Sea branch (it gets Bay branch rain).
[38:2:12] - The **Palghat Gap** lets only part of the Arabian Sea branch through to Tamil Nadu – the **majority** of monsoon winds do **not** enter through it.
[38:2:13] # Bay of Bengal branch
[38:2:14] - Strikes Myanmar and the **funnel-shaped Garo–Khasi–Jaintia hills** → orographic rain in **Meghalaya** (Mawsynram, Cherrapunji).
[38:2:15] - Deflected **westward by the Himalayas** along the Ganga plain → rain **decreases east to west**; **Jharkhand** and the east get their rain from the **SW monsoon**.
[38:2:16] > APPSC FRO: "Kerala is the first state to get the SW monsoon in early June" and "the Bay branch causes heavy rain in Meghalaya" – **both correct**.
[38:2:17] # Breaks
[38:2:18] - A **break** occurs when the **monsoon trough (ITCZ) shifts north to the Himalayan foothills**: the plains stay dry, the hills get heavy rain, and temperature rises.
[38:2:19] - One or two breaks a season; most often in the **second week of August**.
[38:2:20] - Rajasthan **does** get some SW monsoon rain (little), so "Rajasthan gets no SW monsoon rain" is false.
[38:2:21] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.12 (book p.82); NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.1-2 (book p.85-86); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.5, p.29-32; app notes 4:38 (sub 4, 5)
[38:2:22] - The **west coast** gets more rain (narrow plain, high Ghats), but the **east coast** produces more **rice** (wide deltas, alluvial soil).
## SUB 3 | Hot Weather Season, Local Storms and the Six Traditional Seasons
[38:3:0] # Hot weather (pre-monsoon) season – March to May
[38:3:1] - Northward march of the Sun; over **42.5 °C** in the north and NW; **Ganganagar** recorded about **50 °C** (1935).
[38:3:2] - **Heat waves** in north India: **March to June** (peak May–June); IMD plains threshold **40 °C**.
[38:3:3] - **Dust storms (Andhi)** – commonest in **May**, in Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, Delhi, western UP.
[38:3:4] - Pre-monsoon rain (~**10%** of annual) is **convectional**: strong heating → rising air **cools adiabatically** → thunderstorms (CDS 2009 A–R: both true, R explains A).
[38:3:5] TABLE head: Local storm / wind | Region | Note
  [38:3:5.0] Mango showers | Kerala and coastal Karnataka (PMF adds Tamil Nadu, AP) | Help mangoes ripen
  [38:3:5.1] Blossom / cherry blossom showers | Karnataka, Kerala coffee areas | Coffee flowering
  [38:3:5.2] Kaal Baisakhi / Nor'westers | West Bengal, Assam, Odisha, NE | Violent evening storms; useful for tea, jute, rice
  [38:3:5.3] Bardoli Chheerha | Assam | Assam's name for the Nor'westers
  [38:3:5.4] Loo | N and NW plains (Punjab to Bihar) | Hot, dry wind – not rain
  [38:3:5.5] Karaburan | Central Asia | Hot dusty wind – not Indian
[38:3:6] - Tornadoes and hailstorms peak in **March–May**; hailstorms are rare in the monsoon; most hail-prone: **Vidarbha and Marathwada**. Deadliest tornado: **Belda, 24 March 1998**.
[38:3:7] # Seasons
[38:3:8] TABLE head: IMD season | Months
  [38:3:8.0] Winter | January–February
  [38:3:8.1] Pre-monsoon / hot weather | March–May
  [38:3:8.2] South-west monsoon | June–September
  [38:3:8.3] Post-monsoon (NE monsoon) | October–December
[38:3:9] # Six traditional seasons
[38:3:10] TABLE head: Traditional season | Months
  [38:3:10.0] Vasanta (Spring) | Chaitra–Vaishakha (March–April)
  [38:3:10.1] Grishma (Summer) | Jyeshtha–Ashadha (May–June)
  [38:3:10.2] Varsha (Rainy) | Shravana–Bhadra (July–August)
  [38:3:10.3] Sharad (Autumn) | Ashvina–Kartika (September–October)
  [38:3:10.4] Hemanta (pre-winter) | Margashirsha–Pushya (November–December)
  [38:3:10.5] Shishira (winter) | Magha–Phalguna (January–February)
[38:3:11] - Order by the Hindu calendar: **Spring → Summer → Rainy → Autumn**. "Pravaha" is not a season. **Nautapa** = nine-day peak of summer heat before the monsoon.
[38:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.11-12 (book p.81-82); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.24-25; app notes 4:38 (sub 2, 3)
## SUB 4 | Theories of the Monsoon Mechanism, ENSO and Monsoon Research
[38:4:0] TABLE head: Theory / driver | Core idea
  [38:4:0.0] Thermal (differential heating) – Edmund Halley, 1686 | Land heats faster than sea → summer low over land draws moist sea winds; reversed in winter
  [38:4:0.1] Dynamic / ITCZ shift (1950s) | ITCZ moves north over the Ganga plain as the monsoon trough; SE trades cross the equator and turn south-westerly
  [38:4:0.2] Jet streams | STJ shifts north of the Himalayas → onset; returns south → withdrawal. TEJ (South China Sea → East Africa) coincides with the SW monsoon; Somali jet + Somalia Current strengthen it
  [38:4:0.3] Tibetan Plateau (~5,000 m) | Summer heat island → upper-air anticyclone, stronger TEJ; heavy snow cover weakens it
  [38:4:0.4] ENSO / IOD / MJO | El Nino weakens (delayed, weak monsoon, drought); La Nina strengthens; positive IOD can offset El Nino; MJO repeats every 30–60 days
[38:4:1] - **Mascarene High** (near **Madagascar**) drives the cross-equatorial flow; **dust aerosols** over the Indo-Gangetic Plain help pull the monsoon inland.
[38:4:2] - **Gilbert Walker** (1920s) described the **Southern Oscillation**: low pressure over the Indian Ocean (Darwin) + high over the Pacific (Tahiti) = good monsoon.
[38:4:3] - **MONEX** (Monsoon Experiment) **1979** under the **WMO** confirmed the role of the shifting ITCZ (an earlier Indo-Soviet experiment was held in 1973).
[38:4:4] - **El Nino**: a warm current off **Peru** every **3–7 years** replacing the cold Peruvian current; it **causes drought-like conditions in parts of India**.
[38:4:5] # Research and forecasting
[38:4:6] - **IMD** works under the **Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES)**.
[38:4:7] TABLE head: Mission | Facts
  [38:4:7.0] National Monsoon Mission | 2012, MoES, through IITM Pune + IMD; dynamic coupled model (MMCFS)
  [38:4:7.1] Mission Mausam | 14 Jan 2025 with IMD Vision 2047; Rs 2,000 crore; Bharat Forecast System (6 km, 10-day rain)
[38:4:8] - **LPA** of SW-monsoon rain (1971–2020) = **868.6 mm**. **Ocean Mean Temperature (OMT)** – upper ocean down to the **26 °C isotherm** – predicts better than **SST**.
[38:4:9] - **2026 (as of Sep 2026):** April forecast 92% of LPA, revised to 90%; June deficit **43%** → contingency plans; El Nino building.

=== NOTES 4:39 | Rainfall Distribution, Variability, El Nino, Drought and Flood-prone Areas
## SUB 0 | Wettest and Driest Places, Rainfall Zones
[39:0:0] # Extremes
[39:0:1] TABLE head: Extreme | Place
  [39:0:1.0] Wettest in India / world | Mawsynram (Mausimram), Khasi Hills, Meghalaya – NextGen ~1,187 cm (≈ 467.4 inches); PMF 1,221 cm
  [39:0:1.1] Second wettest | Cherrapunji (Sohra), East Khasi Hills, Meghalaya (~1,102 cm)
  [39:0:1.2] Wettest state | Meghalaya
  [39:0:1.3] "Cherrapunji of the South" | Agumbe, Shivamogga, Karnataka (highest rainfall in Karnataka)
  [39:0:1.4] Least rainfall | Leh / Ladakh (cold desert behind the Great Himalaya; under 50 cm), then Jaisalmer, Bikaner (Thar)
  [39:0:1.5] Driest state | Rajasthan
[39:0:2] - Mawsynram and Cherrapunji lie on the **southern (windward) slopes of the Khasi hills**; the **funnel** of hills forces the Bay branch up → orographic rain. Mawsynram (Mawjymbuin cave) is also known for **stalagmites and stalactites**.
[39:0:3] - **Highest rainfall regions:** **Western Ghats (windward), Himalayan region / NE and Meghalaya**.
[39:0:4] - Among Arunachal, Sikkim, Kerala and J&K, older IMD normals rank **Kerala** highest (~3,055 mm); newer normals (factodata/IMD) give Sikkim 2,972, Arunachal 2,934, Kerala 2,924 mm.
[39:0:5] - Same latitude, very different rainfall: **Ajmer (dry) vs Shillong (very wet)**.
[39:0:6] # Rainfall zones
[39:0:7] TABLE head: Zone | Rainfall | Areas
  [39:0:7.0] Heavy | > 200–250 cm | Windward Western Ghats, Purvachal/NE, Meghalaya, sub-Himalayan West Bengal
  [39:0:7.1] Moderate | 100–200 cm | Most of the northern plains, Odisha, MP, eastern slopes of the Ghats
  [39:0:7.2] Low | 50–100 cm | E Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat, rain-shadow Deccan
  [39:0:7.3] Very low | < 50 cm | W Rajasthan, Kachchh, Ladakh
[39:0:8] # Andhra Pradesh angle
[39:0:9] - AP gets about **two-thirds** of its rain (avg ~966 mm) from the **SW monsoon** (mid-June–September); **July** is its rainiest month; **Rayalaseema** depends more on the **NE monsoon**.
[39:0:10] - Wettest: **Sileru–Sabari valleys** (140–152 cm); driest: **Hagari valley** (< 51 cm), **Anantapur** district. Hottest **Rentachintala**, coolest **Lambasingi**.
[39:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.2, p.5 (book p.86, 89); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.11, p.14, p.32, p.34; NextGen AP Geography 02 p.6; Rocket AP Geography p.28-29; factodata.com (IMD normals); app notes 4:39 (sub 0)
## SUB 1 | Seasonal Share and Regional Gradients of Rainfall
[39:1:0] TABLE head: Season | Share of annual rain
  [39:1:0.0] South-west monsoon (June–Sept) | ~75% – the main source for almost all India
  [39:1:0.1] Retreating / NE monsoon | ~13%
  [39:1:0.2] Summer (pre-monsoon) | ~10%
  [39:1:0.3] Winter | ~2% (driest season)
[39:1:1] - **Northern plains:** rain **decreases from east to west** (the Bay stream loses moisture): Kolkata > Patna > Prayagraj > Delhi > Bikaner. In the **Ganga basin** it also falls **away from the Himalayan foothills**, i.e. **north to south**.
[39:1:2] - **Duration of the monsoon decreases from south to north** (UPSC 2012: both statements true).
[39:1:3] - **Peninsula:** rain **decreases from west to east** – away from the **Western Ghats**, not away from the Eastern Ghats.
[39:1:4] - **Rain-shadow** (leeward) areas: **east of the Western Ghats** – **Pune, Bengaluru**, interior Maharashtra (Vidarbha), Karnataka, Telangana, Rayalaseema; **Leh** behind the Himalaya. **Mangaluru, Mumbai** are **windward**.
[39:1:5] - The **western coastal plains** get more rain than the plateau because they lie on the **windward side of the SW monsoon** (orographic rain on the Western Ghats).
[39:1:6] - **Tropical deserts** lie in the **trade-wind belt on the western sides of continents**; the **Eastern Himalaya** gets most rain from the **SW (Bay) monsoon**, not from north-east winds.
[39:1:7] > A–R (IAS 1994): "monsoon rain decreases westward in the Ganga plain" is true; the reason given in the key ("winds go higher") differs from the textbook cause – progressive **loss of moisture**.
[39:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.1-2, p.4-5 (book p.85-86, 88-89); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.7, p.32; app notes 4:39 (sub 1, 2)
## SUB 2 | Drought – Types, Extent and Management
[39:2:0] TABLE head: Type | Based on
  [39:2:0.0] Meteorological | Rainfall deficit (lack of rain)
  [39:2:0.1] Agricultural | Soil moisture
  [39:2:0.2] Hydrological | Reduced streamflow, reservoirs, groundwater
  [39:2:0.3] Socio-economic | Demand exceeds supply
  [39:2:0.4] Flash drought | Sudden heat + no rain
[39:2:1] # Extent
[39:2:2] TABLE head: Category | Rainfall | Share
  [39:2:2.0] Drought-prone in all | – | ~68% of cultivable/agricultural land (nearest option: 70%)
  [39:2:2.1] Chronically drought-prone | < 750 mm | ~33%
  [39:2:2.2] Drought-prone | 750–1,125 mm | ~35%
[39:2:3] - Most frequent drought: **western India – Rajasthan, Gujarat, parts of Maharashtra**; also Marathwada, Rayalaseema, south Prakasam, north Karnataka.
[39:2:4] - **IMD:** an **all-India drought year** when the season's rainfall is **more than 10%** below normal (and over 20% of the area is affected).
[39:2:5] - **West Bengal plateau** (Purulia, Bankura): occasional drought with low, erratic rain on porous **lateritic** soil.
[39:2:6] - **Manual for Drought Management 2016** (Ministry of Agriculture; revised 2020) – multi-indicator declaration (rainfall deficit, vegetation, soil moisture, water).
[39:2:7] - **Disaster Management Act = 2005** (not 2006). DPAP 1973–74; the Green Revolution reduced famine relief. Kautilya's Arthashastra prescribes famine measures.
[39:2:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.22-23; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.64; app notes 4:39 (sub 7)
## SUB 3 | Rainfall Variability, El Nino and IMD Rainfall Categories
[39:3:0] # Variability
[39:3:1] - **CV = (standard deviation / mean) × 100**; **low-rainfall areas have the highest variability**.
[39:3:2] TABLE head: CV | Regions
  [39:3:2.0] < 25% | West coast, Western Ghats, NE, Meghalaya, Kerala, West Bengal
  [39:3:2.1] > 50% (over 60% in parts) | W Rajasthan, Kachchh/Gujarat, Ladakh
[39:3:3] # El Nino linkage
[39:3:4] TABLE head: Term | Effect
  [39:3:4.0] El Nino | Central/east Pacific ≥ 0.5 °C warmer for five overlapping 3-month periods; weakens the monsoon
  [39:3:4.1] La Nina | Generally strengthens the monsoon
  [39:3:4.2] Positive IOD | Can offset El Nino
[39:3:5] - Deficient years: **2015** – 86% of LPA; 2023 (El Nino).
[39:3:6] # IMD categories
[39:3:7] TABLE head: All-India season | % of LPA
  [39:3:7.0] Deficient | < 90
  [39:3:7.1] Below normal | 90–95
  [39:3:7.2] Normal | 96–104
  [39:3:7.3] Above normal | 105–110
  [39:3:7.4] Excess | > 110
[39:3:8] # State / district
[39:3:9] TABLE head: State / district | Departure from normal
  [39:3:9.0] Large excess | +60% or more
  [39:3:9.1] Excess | +20% to +59%
  [39:3:9.2] Normal | −19% to +19%
  [39:3:9.3] Deficient (scanty) | −20% to −59% – deficiency of more than 19%
  [39:3:9.4] Large deficient | −60% to −99%
[39:3:10] - **Rainy day** (IMD) = **2.5 mm or more** in 24 hours.
[39:3:11] - **2026** (by 16 Sep): Meghalaya −59% (worst), Manipur −43%, **AP −42%**.
[39:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.10, p.14 (book p.80, 84); app notes 4:39 (sub 4, 5, 6)
## SUB 4 | Flood-prone Areas
[39:4:0] - Largest floods: the **Ganga and Brahmaputra** basins (heavy monsoon rain, silt).
[39:4:1] - About **40 million ha ≈ 12%** of India's land is prone to **floods and river erosion** (Rashtriya Barh Ayog; NDMA; NIDM Annual Report 2023–24).
[39:4:2] - **Brahmaputra** = "sorrow of Assam" (not Bihar – that is the Kosi); cloudburst flash floods rising in the Himalaya and NE; ~37,760 sq km flood-prone area protected in West Bengal.
[39:4:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.57; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 05 p.25; app notes 4:39 (sub 8)

  x: Western Rajasthan, Kutch and Ladakh generally have a high rainfall coefficient of variation above 50 percent. The west coast, Western Ghats, north-east and eastern peninsula generally have low variability below 25 percent.

=== NOTES 4:40 | Natural Vegetation of India and Forest Cover (india State of Forest Report)

[40:0:2] - Percent order (2021): Kerala 55 > Odisha 34 > Karnataka 20 > AP 18; **Chhattisgarh 41 > Odisha 34 > MP 25 > Maharashtra 17** (ascending: Maharashtra–MP–Odisha–Chhattisgarh); **Manipur 74 > Odisha 34 > Maharashtra 17 > Haryana 4**.
[40:0:3] - **Nagaland is not** the most forested State (Mizoram is).

[40:0:5] - Teak: largest area in **Madhya Pradesh**; largest bamboo area: MP.
[40:0:6] - District facts: **West (Paschim) Champaran** has Bihar's largest dense deciduous forest (Valmiki); **Jodhpur** has the least very dense forest in Rajasthan.

[40:0:8] - **Madhya Pradesh** (on the Tropic of Cancer): its forests were classed as "sub-tropical" in the RAS 2003 key.
[40:0:9] - **Tree cover by physiographic zone** (older SFRs): maximum in the **East Deccan**.
## SUB 1 | Deciduous, Thorn and Dry Evergreen Forests – Key Trees
[40:1:0] # Moist deciduous (100–200 cm)
[40:1:1] - Eastern slopes of the Western Ghats, **Bhabar–Terai/Siwalik strip**, Chota Nagpur, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, NE, A&N.
[40:1:2] - **Teak is the dominant species** (UPSC 2015); also **sal**, sandalwood, arjun, laurel, rosewood, bamboo, mahua. Teak and sal = products of the **tropical deciduous** forests.
[40:1:3] # Dry deciduous (70–100 cm)
[40:1:4] - Interior peninsula, central India, UP–Bihar plains; teak, **sandalwood (south)**, axlewood, red sanders, **tendu, palas, khair**, bamboo.
[40:1:5] - Most prone to **forest fires**; the dry deciduous forests of the **central Deccan** hold large protected habitats for the **tiger**.
[40:1:6] # Thorn forests (< 70 cm)
[40:1:7] - **Open stunted forests with long roots and sharp thorns** – Rajasthan, SW Punjab, W Haryana, Kutch–Saurashtra and the leeward Deccan, i.e. **Western Andhra Pradesh (Rayalaseema)** – not eastern Odisha, NE Tamil Nadu or the Terai.
[40:1:8] - Species: **acacia/babul**, ber, wild date, euphorbia, cacti, neem, **khejri**.
[40:1:9] # Tropical dry evergreen
[40:1:10] - **Coast of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh** (NE-monsoon rain, ~100 cm); jamun, tamarind, neem.
[40:1:11] # Tree → forest / region / use
[40:1:12] TABLE head: Tree | Fact
  [40:1:12.0] Teak (Tectona grandis) | Deciduous; central India (largest teak area Madhya Pradesh) and western peninsula; not evergreen forests
  [40:1:12.1] Sal (Shorea robusta) | Moist deciduous; sub-Himalaya, NE peninsula; Sitanadi (Udanti–Sitanadi, Chhattisgarh) = sal forests
  [40:1:12.2] Mahua (Madhuca indica) | Deciduous; flowers distilled into country liquor (AP tribal areas)
  [40:1:12.3] Jackfruit | Evergreen (W Ghats native) – so of jackfruit, mahua, teak only two are deciduous
  [40:1:12.4] Palash (Butea monosperma, dhak) | "Flame of the forest"
  [40:1:12.5] Khejri (Prosopis cineraria) | Rajasthan – moisture-retaining, fodder, fuel; multipurpose social-forestry tree, "king of the desert"
  [40:1:12.6] Khair (Acacia catechu) | Yields katha; dry deciduous / sub-tropical Siwalik belt
  [40:1:12.7] Tendu (Diospyros melanoxylon) | Leaves used as bidi wrappers
  [40:1:12.8] Dalbergia | Rosewood (sheesham) genus
  [40:1:12.9] Dendrocalamus strictus | Solid bamboo – commonest bamboo of central India / Chhattisgarh
  [40:1:12.10] Sundari (Heritiera fomes) | Mangrove of the Sundarbans
  [40:1:12.11] Deodar | Western Himalaya – not Nilgiris, not MP
  [40:1:12.12] Cinchona | Himalayan foothill/Terai and southern hills (match: Teak–Central India, Deodar–high Himalaya, Sundari–Sundarbans, Cinchona–Terai)
[40:1:13] - Bamboo flowers gregariously after long cycles (about **40–50 years**; 48 years among the options).
[40:1:14] ~~ Sources: PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.44-50; NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.8-10 (book p.106-108); OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.11; Rocket Indian Geography p.78, p.124-125; PMF Environment 03 p.83 (Udanti-Sitanadi TR); app notes 4:40 (sub 2)
## SUB 2 | Tropical Evergreen (Rain) Forests and Biodiversity
[40:2:0] - Tall trees (**> 45 m**, 45–60 m), **multi-layered continuous canopy**, little undergrowth; **lianas, epiphytes**, orchids, canes, bamboo; **leaf litter decomposes fastest** – soil surface almost bare (UPSC 2021).
[40:2:1] - **Maximum plant diversity and biomass**: "greatest variety of animal and plant species" = **tropical moist (rain) forests** – not temperate deciduous, taiga, savanna, grassland, tundra, mangrove or desert.
[40:2:2] - In India, maximum tree diversity in the wet evergreen/semi-evergreen forests of the **Western Ghats**, then the **North-East** (ISFR).
[40:2:3] - Near the **equator** (about 10°N–10°S): no dry season, so the trees do not shed leaves together.
[40:2:4] - **Where in India:** western slopes of the **Western Ghats** (Kerala, Karnataka), **Assam**, Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura, Nagaland, **Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram**, **Andaman & Nicobar** – so "rain forest in India" = **Assam and Kerala**; **not Himachal Pradesh**, UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha.
[40:2:5] - **Species:** **rosewood, ebony**, mahogany, gurjan, ironwood, jamun, aini, champa, mesua, white cedar, canes; dominant species asked = **ebony** (not sandalwood, juniper, acacia).
[40:2:6] - **Cinchona** is an evergreen tropical (hill) plant – grown in WB (Darjeeling), Assam, Kerala/TN hills, **not Chhattisgarh**.
[40:2:7] - **Semi-evergreen:** 200–250 cm; buttressed trunks; laurel, rosewood, mesua, thorny bamboo.
[40:2:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.8 (book p.106); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.41-44; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.10; app notes 4:40 (sub 1)
## SUB 3 | Mangrove, Littoral and Tidal Forests
[40:3:0] - Also called **tidal / littoral** forests: intertidal zone of sheltered coasts, mudflats, mix of salt and fresh water; **stilt and knee roots**; Rhizophora, Avicennia, Sonneratia, **Sundari**.
[40:3:1] - On both coasts – deltas of the **Ganga (Sundarbans), Mahanadi, Godavari (Coringa), Krishna, Cauvery** – and the **Andaman & Nicobar Islands** (A&N = mangrove + evergreen + deciduous together). Mangroves are reported from **every coastal State** – not **Assam** (landlocked).
[40:3:2] - **Sundarbans** (Hooghly–Ganga delta, West Bengal) = mangroves; Sundari tree; littoral/tidal type.
[40:3:3] - India holds about **3%** of the world's mangroves.
[40:3:4] TABLE head: Mangrove site | State
  [40:3:4.0] Bhitarkanika (Brahmani–Baitarani delta, Kendrapara), Devi, Dhamra | Odisha – not West Bengal, not Vamsadhara–Subarnarekha
  [40:3:4.1] Coringa, Korangi (Kakinada, Godavari delta) | Andhra Pradesh
  [40:3:4.2] Pichavaram, Muthupet | Tamil Nadu
  [40:3:4.3] Vembanad | Kerala
  [40:3:4.4] Coondapur, Honnavar | Karnataka
  [40:3:4.5] Achra–Ratnagiri | Maharashtra
  [40:3:4.6] Chorao Island (Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary) – protected mangroves | Goa
  [40:3:4.7] Gulf of Kachchh | Gujarat
