[40:3:7] - **MISHTI** (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes): launched **5 June 2023** (not 2019) to **restore mangroves** (54,000 ha by 2028); extended to 2029.
[40:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.9-10 (book p.107-108); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.45-46, p.71-72; Rocket Indian Geography p.123; gktoday.in State of Forests Report 2015 (3% of world mangroves); Rocket CA 2026-01 p.30 (MISHTI); app notes 4:40 (sub 4)
## SUB 4 | ISFR – National Figures, Canopy Classes and Global Ranking
[40:4:0] - **Forest Survey of India** (1981, **Dehradun**, MoEFCC) publishes the **biennial ISFR** (first 1987; satellite: IRS Resourcesat LISS III).
[40:4:1] TABLE head: Class | Canopy density
  [40:4:1.0] Very Dense Forest | ≥ 70%
  [40:4:1.1] Moderately Dense | 40–70%
  [40:4:1.2] Open | 10–40%
  [40:4:1.3] Scrub | < 10% – not forest cover
[40:4:2] - **Forest cover** = land **> 1 ha** with canopy **≥ 10%**, irrespective of ownership; **tree cover** = tree patches < 1 ha outside recorded forest.
[40:4:3] TABLE head: Report | Forest cover | Forest + tree cover
  [40:4:3.0] SFR 1999–2003 (satellite) | ~19–20.6% (about 19–22% among options) | –
  [40:4:3.1] Tenth Plan estimate (2001) | 20.50% | –
  [40:4:3.2] ISFR 2015 | 21.34% | ~24.16%
  [40:4:3.3] ISFR 2017 | 21.54% | 24.39%
  [40:4:3.4] ISFR 2019 | 21.67% | 24.56%
  [40:4:3.5] ISFR 2021 | 21.71% | 24.62%
  [40:4:3.6] ISFR 2023 | 21.76% (7,15,343 sq km) | 25.17% (8,27,357 sq km); tree cover 3.41%
[40:4:4] - Dense (VDF + MDF) = about **57%** of forest cover – not 40% (UPSC 2005: only statement 2 true).
[40:4:5] - ISFR 2023 net gain 1,445.81 sq km over 2021 (only ~156 sq km forest cover, the rest tree cover); **Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam** campaign claims ~140 crore saplings.
[40:4:6] - **Forest fires:** about **36%** of forest cover is prone to frequent fires (ISFR; ~35.5% in ISFR 2021); **dry deciduous** forests most vulnerable; AP had the largest fire-affected area in 2023–24.
[40:4:7] - **FAO GFRA 2020:** India **3rd** in annual net forest gain 2010–20 (China, Australia, India); India ~2% of world forest. GFRA 2025: India 3rd in net gain, 9th in total area.
[40:4:8] - **Bhutan's constitution** mandates **60%** of its area under forest.
[40:4:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.59-64; mongabay.com (ISFR 2017, Feb 2018); gktoday.in (SFR 2015); Praveen CA360 Jul 2026 p.18 (ISFR 2023); app notes 4:40 (sub 6, 7)
[40:4:10] - **Population and forest cover:** forest loss is usually linked to population pressure (an A–R key treats it as the demographic-transition effect), but ISFR shows forest cover **rising** from ~19% (1999–2003) to **21.76% (2023)** while population grew.
## SUB 5 | Himalayan, Montane and Temperate Forests; Sholas
[40:5:0] TABLE head: Zone (bottom → top) | Altitude | Species
  [40:5:0.0] Tropical moist deciduous (foothills) | < 1,000 m | Sal
  [40:5:0.1] Sub-tropical pine | 1,000–1,800 m | Chir pine, khair
  [40:5:0.2] Montane wet / Himalayan moist temperate | 1,500–3,000 m (1,800–3,000 m wet temperate) | Oak, deodar, fir, chestnut, maple, rhododendron
  [40:5:0.3] Himalayan dry temperate (Ladakh, Kinnaur, Lahul) | inner ranges | Chilgoza, deodar, oak, juniper
  [40:5:0.4] Sub-alpine | 2,900–3,500 m | Fir, spruce, birch, rhododendron
  [40:5:0.5] Moist alpine scrub / alpine meadows | 3,000 m to snowline (~4,750 m) | Rhododendron, birch; meadows (bugyals, margs)
  [40:5:0.6] Dry alpine scrub | > 3,500–4,000 m | Juniper, honeysuckle, artemisia
[40:5:1] - **Deodar** is the tree of the **highest elevation** among deodar, pine, sal, teak; abundant in the temperate **Western Himalaya**; covers **1,800–2,600 m** (not sal, chir).
[40:5:2] - Uttarakhand **oak–rhododendron** (banj oak, burans) = **temperate** forest. Oak and rhododendron grow naturally in the Himalaya; **sandalwood does not**.
[40:5:3] - **Mahogany** is a tropical (American) tree – **not** Himalayan; juniper, silver fir, spruce are.
[40:5:4] - **Himalayan Yew (Taxus wallachiana)** – source of **taxol**, the biggest-selling anti-cancer drug.
[40:5:5] - **Southern slopes** carry denser forest (more rain and sun); northern slopes are thinner (A false, R true).
[40:5:6] - **Coniferous forests** = **temperate/cold** regions (taiga 50°–60°N: Canada, Scandinavia, Finland, Siberia) – **not Amazonia**. Alpine forests are not on the Western Ghats.
[40:5:7] - **Sholas**: temperate (montane wet temperate) forests of the **Nilgiri, Anaimalai and Palani hills**.
[40:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.10-11 (book p.108-109); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.50-53; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.13; OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 09 p.13 (Himalayan Yew); app notes 4:40 (sub 3)
[40:5:9] - **Ginkgo biloba** (maidenhair tree) – gymnosperm called a **living fossil** (sole survivor of Ginkgophyta; cycads are also called living fossils) – not Pinus, Cedrus deodara or Ephedra.
[40:5:10] - **Lichens** (alga + fungus) – pioneers on bare rock, alpine and tundra surfaces; the **litmus** dye is extracted from **lichens** – not from palash ('flame of the forest') flowers or indigo leaves.
## SUB 6 | Forest Types – Classification, Rainfall and Area Ranking
[40:6:0] # Classification
[40:6:1] - **H.G. Champion (1935)**, refined with **S.K. Seth (1968)**: **5 major groups, 16 type groups** – Moist Tropical, Dry Tropical, Montane Sub-tropical, Montane Temperate, Alpine.
[40:6:2] TABLE head: Type | Rainfall | Leaf habit
  [40:6:2.0] Tropical wet evergreen (rain forest) | > 250 cm (NCERT: > 200 cm), temp > 22–25 °C | Evergreen – no leaf-shedding season
  [40:6:2.1] Tropical semi-evergreen | 200–250 cm | Mixed evergreen + deciduous
  [40:6:2.2] Tropical moist deciduous | 100–200 cm | Shed leaves in the dry season
  [40:6:2.3] Tropical dry deciduous | 70–100 cm | Leafless in the long dry season
  [40:6:2.4] Tropical thorn | < 70 cm (NCERT < 50 cm) | Open, stunted, xerophytic
  [40:6:2.5] Desert vegetation | < 25 cm | Xerophytes
[40:6:3] - **Deciduous** = sheds leaves before winter or in the dry spell (adaptation to moisture shortage); evergreen = no common leaf fall.
[40:6:4] - Forests of **> 200 cm rain and > 22 °C** = tropical **evergreen and semi-evergreen** forests.
[40:6:5] # Which type is largest?
[40:6:6] TABLE head: Measure | Answer
  [40:6:6.0] Most widespread group | Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests – 65.6% of forest area (NextGen)
  [40:6:6.1] Largest single type (ISFR 2021) | Tropical dry deciduous 2,80,547 sq km (39.30%)
  [40:6:6.2] Second (ISFR 2021) | Tropical moist deciduous 1,31,805 sq km (18.47%)
  [40:6:6.3] Then | Plantation/TOF 10.54%, semi-evergreen 9.69%, sub-tropical broad-leaved hill 4.35%
  [40:6:6.4] Wet evergreen / montane wet temperate | 2.74% / 2.83%; sub-tropical dry evergreen only 0.02%
[40:6:7] - NextGen/NCERT (older figures): **moist deciduous ~37%** is "most widely distributed", dry deciduous 28.6% second, **wet evergreen ~8% third** (semi-evergreen 4.1%). ISFR forest-type mapping now ranks **dry deciduous first** – key "dry deciduous" when both are offered; when dry deciduous is **not** an option (UPSC 2010), the answer is **moist deciduous**.
[40:6:8] - **World:** FAO FRA 2020 ranks climatic domains **Tropical > Boreal > Temperate > Subtropical**; most books and the UPSC 2003 key give **temperate coniferous (taiga)** as the largest forest type of the world.
[40:6:9] - **Highest deforestation** in the world: the **tropical** zone (FAO).
[40:6:10] > Forest-type angle (8 PYQs): "most widespread" = tropical deciduous; "largest single type" = dry deciduous; options without dry deciduous → moist deciduous.
[40:6:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.7-9 (book p.105-107); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.40-41, p.64 (ISFR 2021 table, FRA 2020); OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.11
## SUB 7 | Forest Policy, Law, Silviculture, Social Forestry and Grasslands
[40:7:0] # National Forest Policy 1988
[40:7:1] - Principal aim: **ecological balance** / environmental stability; target **one-third (33%)** of India's area under forest/tree cover (**two-thirds in the hills** – not two-thirds of the country); social forestry, massive afforestation, people's movement incl. women, JFM.
[40:7:2] - **National Forestry Action Programme** – also aims at one-third under tree/forest cover.
[40:7:3] # Law
[40:7:4] TABLE head: Act / body | Provision
  [40:7:4.0] Indian Forest Act 1927 | Reserved (barred unless permitted), Protected (allowed unless prohibited), Village forests
  [40:7:4.1] Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 | Central approval to divert forest land
  [40:7:4.2] CAMPA | Manages compensatory afforestation funds
  [40:7:4.3] WPA (Amendment) 2002 | Conservation and community reserves (not the 1927 Act)
[40:7:5] # Terms
[40:7:6] - **Silviculture** = the art and science of cultivating (raising and tending) forest crops.
[40:7:7] - **Coppice** = regrowth from stool shoots, short rotation; **high forest** = raised from seed, long rotation; **selection system** = trees removed singly or in groups, uneven-aged forest.
[40:7:8] - **Afforestation** = planting on land never forested; **reforestation** = re-establishing depleted forest.
[40:7:9] - **Social forestry** (NCERT) = management and protection of forests and afforestation on barren/public land for community benefit – urban, rural (agro/community) and farm forestry; community forestry = trees on public/community land.
[40:7:10] - **Van Mahotsav** – started **1950** by **K.M. Munshi** (Union Agriculture Minister).
[40:7:11] # Grassland types
[40:7:12] TABLE head: Grass type | Habitat
  [40:7:12.0] Sehima–Dichanthium | Black soils
  [40:7:12.1] Phragmites–Saccharum | Marshy localities
  [40:7:12.2] Deschampsia–Deyeuxia | Alpine region
  [40:7:12.3] Bothriochloa | High-rainfall paddy tracts
[40:7:13] - **Banni** (Kutch) tropical grassland; **bugyals** (Uttarakhand), **margs** (Kashmir); **sabai grass** – rope and paper.

[ff143d045b266] sub7
  In the selection system of silviculture, mature trees are removed:
  All at once by clear felling | Only to raise stool shoots on a short rotation | Only after the crop is raised from seed on a short rotation | *Singly or in groups, keeping the forest uneven-aged
  x: In the selection system mature trees are removed singly or in groups, so the forest stays uneven-aged; stool shoots on a short rotation describe coppice.

[41:4:0] - **First / oldest NP of India (and mainland Asia):** **Jim Corbett**, 1936 as **Hailey NP**; Project Tiger launched there 1973.

[41:4:2] - **Most national parks:** **Madhya Pradesh (11)**; then A&N (6 or 9, depending on whether the three Button Island NPs are counted), **Assam (8 since 2025)**, Kerala/Maharashtra/Uttarakhand/WB 6.
[41:4:3] - **Most wildlife sanctuaries:** **A&N Islands (~97)**; among States **Maharashtra (~48)** > Karnataka (~35) > Tamil Nadu (~33) > MP (~24).

## SUB 7 | Protected-area Law, Zoos and Parks
[41:7:0] TABLE head: Category (WPA 1972) | Declared by / on | Rights
  [41:7:0.0] National Park | State (or Centre); boundaries fixed | Highest protection; no grazing, no private rights
  [41:7:0.1] Wildlife Sanctuary | State | Some rights and grazing regulated but allowed
  [41:7:0.2] Conservation Reserve (Sec 36A) | State, on government land adjoining/linking PAs, after consulting locals | Local rights unaffected
  [41:7:0.3] Community Reserve (Sec 36C) | State, on private/community land volunteered | Rights unaffected; not inside NP/WLS/CR
[41:7:1] - WPA got Presidential assent **9 September 1972**; reserves added by the 2002 amendment. Protection: **NP > WLS > Reserved > Protected forests**.
[41:7:2] - **ESZ:** ordinary buffer **1 km** around NPs/WLS (SC, June 2022); SC extended a **10-km mining buffer** to wetland conservation reserves.
[41:7:3] - **Zoos:** **Nandankanan** (Bhubaneswar, **Odisha**); Bannerghatta Biological Park (Bengaluru); Indira Gandhi Zoological Park (Visakhapatnam).
[41:7:4] - Other firsts: ISA – first treaty-based IGO in India (Secretariat **Gurugram**); Montreal Protocol in force **1989**.
[41:7:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment - APPSC Exams 05 p.11-14; NextGen Environment - APPSC Exams 06 p.4-5; Rocket Environment p.19, p.25-26; PMF Species and PAN 02 p.77 (Nandankanan); app notes 4:41 (sub 0)

=== NOTES 4:42 | India – Tiger Reserves, Elephant Reserves, Ramsar Sites, Important Bird Areas
## SUB 0 | Tiger Reserves – Project Tiger, NTCA and Reserve → State
[42:0:0] # Project Tiger and NTCA
[42:0:1] - **Project Tiger** launched **1 April 1973** with **9 reserves**; formally launched at **Corbett** (Uttarakhand) – **India's first tiger reserve**.
[42:0:2] - **NTCA** (National Tiger Conservation Authority): **statutory body** set up in **2006** under the amended **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972**; chaired by the Environment Minister.
[42:0:3] - **Count:** **58 tiger reserves** (as of Sep 2026; 47 a decade ago): 56th **Guru Ghasidas–Tamor Pingla** (Chhattisgarh, Nov 2024), 57th **Ratapani** (MP, Dec 2024), 58th **Madhav** (MP, Mar 2025). **Rajaji** (Uttarakhand) became the **48th** in 2015, then **Orang** (Assam) the 49th.
[42:0:4] - **Most tiger reserves:** **Madhya Pradesh (9)**. **Largest:** **Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam (NSTR, Andhra Pradesh)**, then Manas, then Guru Ghasidas–Tamor Pingla. NSTR is AP's only tiger reserve; its Telangana part is **Amrabad TR**.
[42:0:5] - **M-STrIPES**: app-based patrolling and monitoring tool used in tiger reserves.
[42:0:6] # Tiger numbers
[42:0:7] - **All India Tiger Estimation 2022:** average **3,682** (upper limit 3,925); **over 70% of the world's wild tigers**; 2006 baseline 1,411. A growing share live **outside** notified reserves → more human–tiger conflict.
[42:0:8] - **Most tigers by State:** **Madhya Pradesh 785** (2022) > Karnataka 563 > Uttarakhand 560 > Maharashtra 444. In the **2014** estimate **Karnataka (406)** led.
[42:0:9] # Reserve → State

## SUB 2 | Ramsar Convention, Montreux Record and Wetland Programmes
[42:2:0] - **Ramsar Convention (Convention on Wetlands):** adopted **2 Feb 1971** at **Ramsar, Iran**; in force 1975; **India joined 1 Feb 1982**; Secretariat **Gland, Switzerland**. Aim: **conservation and wise use of wetlands** – not oceans, deserts, arid lands, hills or ozone.
[42:2:1] - **World Wetlands Day: 2 February**.
[42:2:2] - Other days (distractors): **22 March World Water Day**; **22 April Earth Day**; 5 June World Environment Day.
[42:2:3] - **Wetland definition:** marsh, fen, peatland or water; **natural or artificial**; fresh, brackish or salt; includes **marine water up to 6 m deep at low tide**.
[42:2:4] - **Montreux Record:** register of Ramsar sites where **changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring or are likely to occur** because of technology, pollution or other human interference – not a WHS status, not a 5-km ban.
[42:2:5]   - India's entries: **Keoladeo** (1990) and **Loktak** (1993). **Chilika** was added in 1993 and **removed in 2002**.
[42:2:6] - **Supreme Court:** no mining within **10 km** of a Ramsar site without approval of **NBWL** and **MoEFCC**.
[42:2:7] - **National Wetland Conservation Programme (NWCP, 1985-86):** **115 wetlands** identified for urgent conservation; merged with NLCP into **NPCA** (2013).
[42:2:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment - APPSC Exams 02 p.10; Rocket Environment p.7; PMF Environment 03 p.9-10 (Montreux, UPSC 2014); PMF Species and PAN 03 p.63; Shankar Environment 05 p.6 (NWCP 115 wetlands); daily EM CA 20 Oct 2026 p.6; app notes 4:42 (sub 0)
## SUB 3 | Migratory Birds and Flyways
[42:3:0] TABLE head: Bird | Migration fact
  [42:3:0.0] Bar-headed goose | Breeds on high Central Asian lakes; crosses the Himalaya – world's highest-flying bird
  [42:3:0.1] Amur falcon | Longest raptor migration; SE Siberia/N China → stopover in Nagaland / NE India (Doyang, Pangti; Oct–Nov) → winters in southern Africa
  [42:3:0.2] Siberian crane | Winter visitor from Siberia; its favourite Indian wintering site was Keoladeo NP, Bharatpur (no longer comes)
  [42:3:0.3] Demoiselle crane | From Mongolia/Central Asia to Rajasthan (Khichan) and Gujarat
  [42:3:0.4] Arctic tern | Longest migration of any bird – Arctic to Antarctic every year
  [42:3:0.5] Black-necked crane (*Grus nigricollis*) | Breeds in Ladakh; Ladakh's State bird (2021)
[42:3:1] - Common raven = *Corvus corax*; golden eagle = *Aquila chrysaetos* (*Aquila clanga* is the greater spotted eagle).
[42:3:2] - **Chilika Lake** (Odisha) is the **largest wintering ground for migratory waterfowl** in the Indian subcontinent.
[42:3:3] - **Central Asian Flyway**: Arctic/Siberia → Indian Ocean; India hosted **CMS COP13** at **Gandhinagar (2020)**.
[42:3:4] - **National bird of India:** **Indian peafowl (peacock)**, *Pavo cristatus* (1963).

## SUB 6 | Elephant Reserves and Elephant Census
[42:6:0] - **Project Elephant:** launched **February 1992** (centrally sponsored); **33 elephant reserves in 14 States**; ERs **overlap** tiger reserves, sanctuaries and reserved forests.
[42:6:1] - **Most ERs: Assam and Tamil Nadu (5 each)**; Odisha 3 (Mayurbhanj – Similipal, Mahanadi, Sambalpur).
[42:6:2] - **Largest elephant population: Karnataka** – 6,000+ (2017) and **6,013** in the DNA-based **SAIEE 2021-25** (Oct 2025), then Assam 4,159, Tamil Nadu 3,136, Kerala 2,785. **Kerala is not first.**
[42:6:3] - India: **22,446** wild elephants (2025; 27,312 in 2017) – about 60% of the world's Asian elephants.
[42:6:4] - **Andhra Pradesh:** 1 ER (**Rayala**, incl. Koundinya WLS), 1 TR (NSTR), 1 BR (**Seshachalam**, 2010), Ramsar: Kolleru only.
[42:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment - APPSC Exams 07 p.1; Rocket Environment p.26; PMF Species and PAN 01 p.54; PMF Species and PAN 03 p.42-43; PMF Environment 03 p.95-96; Praveen CA360 Sep 2026 p.33; app notes 4:42 (sub 3, 8)

=== NOTES 4:43 | India – Soil Types, Characteristics and Distribution; Soil Erosion and Conservation
## SUB 0 | Soil Conservation – Methods and Practices
[43:0:0] # Meaning
[43:0:1] - **Soil conservation:** protecting soil from harm – **controlling erosion and keeping fertility high** (NCERT); it prevents **soil erosion**, not fertility or farming.
[43:0:2] - **Best single method to prevent erosion:** **afforestation**; deforestation, overgrazing and heavy rain cause erosion.
[43:0:3] # Methods
[43:0:4] TABLE head: Method | How it works / where
  [43:0:4.0] Contour ploughing / contour bunding | Ploughing and bunds along contour lines on hilly, sloping, rainfed land slow runoff – reduces erosion by water flow (not up-and-down ploughing)
  [43:0:4.1] Terrace cultivation | Steps on steep slopes and mountain areas – the best check on steep slopes; a conservation measure, not a cause of erosion
  [43:0:4.2] Shelter belts | Rows of trees that cut wind speed and protect soil (arid W India, coasts); CAZRI dune fixing in Rajasthan
  [43:0:4.3] Check dams, gully plugging | Trap sediment and stop gully growth
  [43:0:4.4] Strip cropping | Alternate erosion-resistant strips (grass) with row-crop strips
  [43:0:4.5] Mulching | Cover of residue/straw on the soil – retains soil moisture, reduces erosion
  [43:0:4.6] Crop rotation | Different crops in sequence on the same land – increases soil fertility, cuts pests, prevents degradation; an example of sustainable agriculture
  [43:0:4.7] Afforestation, regulated forestry, controlled grazing, cover cropping, mixed farming | NCERT remedial measures
[43:0:5] - **Government-promoted measures to prevent erosion:** **contour bunding and afforestation** (SI 2017).
[43:0:6] - **Soil fertility is improved by** crop rotation, mixed cropping, multiple cropping, manuring, green manuring – **seed modification does not** improve fertility.
[43:0:7] - **Contour bunding is NOT for** desert margins (wind), low flat flood plains or weedy scrublands – so "none of the above" (UPSC 2013).
[43:0:8] # Conservation agriculture (FAO)
[43:0:9] - Three principles: **minimum / zero tillage**, **permanent soil cover with crop residues**, **crop rotation / diversification** – so 2, 4 and 5 (UPSC 2018); "avoiding monoculture" and "avoiding plantation crops" are not its defined components.
[43:0:10] - **Zero tillage:** new crop sown into the previous crop's residue without seed-bed preparation – raises soil organic matter, cuts runoff; of contour bunding, relay cropping and zero tillage, **only zero tillage** is counted as storing carbon in the soil (UPSC 2012).
[43:0:11] - **Relay cropping:** next crop sown into the standing crop just before its harvest (e.g. paddy–lucerne).
[43:0:12] - Other: agroforestry, biochar (raises water holding, cuts soil N2O), China's **straw checkerboards** (stabilise dunes).
[43:0:13] - **Kurnool (Jul 2026):** Pre-Monsoon Dry Sowing with **Jeevamrutham** to conserve soil moisture (target 92,000 acres).
[43:0:14] # Schemes
[43:0:15] - **Soil Health Card:** launched **19 Feb 2015** at **Suratgarh, Rajasthan**; slogan "**Swasth Dharaa, Khet Haraa**"; card **every two years**; **12 parameters** – N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, pH, EC, organic carbon (micronutrients: **Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B**); **25.79 crore** cards by Feb 2026, most in **Uttar Pradesh**.
[43:0:16] - Most Indian soils are deficient in **nitrogen, phosphorus and humus** – the reason for soil testing.
[43:0:17] - **IWMP** (2009-10) merged in **2015-16** into the Watershed Development Component of **PMKSY**.
[43:0:18] > Problem → remedy pairs: deforestation → afforestation; soil erosion → soil stabilisation; habitat destruction → restoration.
[43:0:19] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.6-8 (book p.71-73); Shankar Environment 20 (zero tillage, relay cropping); getmarks.app UPSC 2012 PYQ page; app notes 4:43 (sub 7, 9)
## SUB 1 | Alluvial Soil, Khadar–Bhangar and the Soil-Type Ranking
[43:1:0] # Ranking by area
[43:1:1] TABLE head: Soil | Area | Note
  [43:1:1.0] Alluvial | 15 lakh sq km, 45.6% (NCERT: ~40%) | Largest / most widespread and most productive group
  [43:1:1.1] Black (regur) | 5.46–5.47 lakh sq km, 16.6% | Deccan Plateau
  [43:1:1.2] Red (and yellow) | 5.18 lakh sq km (NextGen); 3.5 lakh sq km, 10.6% (PMF) | Often called the "second largest" group – see the dispute below
  [43:1:1.3] Laterite | 2.48 lakh sq km | Ghats summits
  [43:1:1.4] Forest / mountain | 2.85 lakh sq km, 8.67% | Himalaya, Ghats
  [43:1:1.5] Arid / desert | 1.42 lakh sq km, ~4.3% | W Rajasthan
[43:1:2] - **Eight** major soil types (ICAR): alluvial, black, red and yellow, laterite, arid, saline and alkaline, peaty and marshy, forest and mountain.
[43:1:3] - **Residual (in situ)** soils dominate **Peninsular India**; **drifted (ex situ)** soils dominate **North India**.
[43:1:4] # Alluvial soil
[43:1:5] - **Deposited by rivers** (transported/azonal); Indo-Gangetic–Brahmaputra plains, river valleys, **deltas** of Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery, Narmada–Tapi valleys, coasts.
[43:1:6] - **Sand content decreases from west to east**; becomes more loamy and clayey towards the Brahmaputra valley.
[43:1:7] - NCERT: **rich in potash but poor in phosphorus**; poor in **nitrogen** and humus (PMF: potash, phosphate and lime adequate) – so alluvial soils are **deficient in nitrogen**.
[43:1:8] - Most fertile / **most productive** soil; needs the **least chemical fertiliser**; crops rice, wheat, sugarcane, jute, cotton, oilseeds.
[43:1:9] - **Very little alluvium:** **Madhya Pradesh** (Deccan Trap black soil) – not Bihar, Punjab or Tamil Nadu (deltas).
[43:1:10] - **Depth:** average **1,000–2,000 m** in the plains, maximum **about 6,100 m** – exams answer "about 6,000 m".
[43:1:11] - **Alluvial sand** has the **minimum water retention**; **clay** retains the most (tiny pores).
[43:1:12] # Khadar, Bhangar, Bhabar, Tarai
[43:1:13] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [43:1:13.0] Khadar | New alluvium, renewed by flood silt every year; lighter, sandy; fertile, ideal for intensive agriculture
  [43:1:13.1] Bhangar | Old alluvium on higher ground beyond flood reach; kankar (calcareous concretions); "old Kachhari clay"; pale reddish brown
  [43:1:13.2] Bhabar | Coarse, pebbly piedmont belt below the Shiwaliks; streams disappear
  [43:1:13.3] Tarai | Marshy lowland south of Bhabar; now largely reclaimed
[43:1:14] - Khadar and Bhangar are both **alluvial** soils – not regur, kankar or Bhabar.
[43:1:15] - **⚠ Trap:** "Khadar contains kankar" is **false** – kankar belongs to Bhangar (NCERT notes kankar can occur in both, but the exam reason is false).
[43:1:16] # Karewa soils
[43:1:17] - **Lacustrine (old lake-bed) deposits** of glacial clay and moraines on plateaus above the Jhelum in the **Kashmir Himalayas** (and Bhadarwah).
[43:1:18] - Famous for **saffron (zafran)** at Pampore, also almonds and walnuts.
[43:1:19] > Dispute: by area in PMF and NextGen, black soil (5.46–5.47 lakh sq km) is larger than red soil, but most books and keys call red (and yellow) soil the second-largest group.
[43:1:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.3-4 (book p.101-102); OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.3 (book p.68); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.82-84, p.86; PMF Indian Physical Geography 01 p.73 (alluvium depth); Rocket Indian Geography p.56-58; app notes 4:43 (sub 1, 2)
## SUB 2 | Black (Regur) Soil
[43:2:0] # Formation and properties
[43:2:1] - Formed by weathering of **Deccan Trap basalt** – **fissure volcanic rock** (lava); in Tamil Nadu from gneiss and schist. Also called **regur**, **black cotton soil**, tropical chernozem; Krebs called regur essentially a mature soil.
[43:2:2] - **Clay above 62%**: **highest moisture retention** – **needs little irrigation**, suits dry farming.
[43:2:3] - **Sticky when wet**, shrinks with **deep cracks** when dry – "**self-ploughing**" soil.
[43:2:4] - Colour from **titaniferous magnetite / iron** and dark parent rock – **not from humus**.
[43:2:5] - **Rich in** lime, iron, magnesia, alumina, potash (calcium, potassium, magnesium); **poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus** – so "rich in humus / nitrogen and organic matter" is a **false reason**.
[43:2:6] - Neutral to alkaline; in USDA terms = **Vertisols** (= Grumusols; semi-arid; crack in summer; **not humus-rich**).
[43:2:7] # Distribution
[43:2:8] - **5.46 lakh sq km (16.6%)** – Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh (**Malwa Plateau**), western AP, north Karnataka, Telangana, Tamil Nadu.
[43:2:9] - **Largest area / most widespread: Maharashtra** – not Assam, Bihar, Punjab, Tamil Nadu or Jharkhand. **Not** found in the Himalayan region.
[43:2:10] - **Very deep black soils:** **north-western Deccan Plateau** and upper Godavari–Krishna valleys.
[43:2:11] # Crops
[43:2:12] - **Cotton** (most suitable soil), jowar, wheat, linseed, tobacco, chillies, oilseeds, sunflower.
[43:2:13] TABLE head: AP black-soil areas (Rocket) | Crops
  [43:2:13.0] Deep black – Adoni, Aluru; unclassified black – West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, mid-Kurnool | Maize, bajra, tobacco, turmeric, chillies
[43:2:14] > Key note: the app's old notes record an APPSC Group-I 2002 key of **Assam** for the largest black-soil State; the verified answer is **Maharashtra**.
[43:2:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.6 (book p.104); OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.3-4 (book p.68-69); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.84-85 (UPSC 2021 PYQ); Rocket Indian Geography p.58-59; Rocket AP Geography p.44; app notes 4:43 (sub 1, 4)
## SUB 3 | Laterite and Red Soils
[43:3:0] # Laterite
[43:3:1] - Latin **"later" = brick**; formed by **intense leaching** under **high temperature and heavy rainfall (> 200 cm)** with alternate wet and dry seasons; lime and silica leached, **iron and aluminium oxides** left.
[43:3:2] - **Red** in colour (iron oxide); **acidic**, **low fertility** – **excess iron** makes it infertile; **poor in nitrogen, phosphate, calcium (lime)**, organic matter; NCERT: iron oxide and **potash** in excess (PMF: poor in potash).
[43:3:3] - **Not** moisture-retentive with a large clay factor – it is porous and well drained (that describes black soil).
[43:3:4] - **Building material:** cut into bricks that harden in air.
[43:3:5] - Crops with manure: **tea, coffee, rubber, cashew, tapioca**, coconut, arecanut.
[43:3:6] - **Where:** summits of Western and Eastern Ghats, **Malabar coast (Kerala)**, Vindhya–Satpura, Rajmahal hills, Malwa, south **Maharashtra**, Karnataka, Odisha, Assam, Meghalaya; **Gangani (West Medinipur, West Bengal)**; **not** Rajasthan, UP, HP or Punjab.
[43:3:7] # Red (and yellow) soil
[43:3:8] - From **ancient crystalline granite, gneiss and schist** under low rainfall; red colour from **ferric oxide** (wide diffusion of iron), **yellow when hydrated**.
[43:3:9] - Porous, light, **low moisture retention**; poor in lime, humus, nitrogen, phosphates; fairly rich in potash.
[43:3:10] - **Where:** Peninsular India – almost all of **Tamil Nadu**, **Andhra Pradesh**, Karnataka, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Chota Nagpur; Kanyakumari–Jhansi and Kutch–Rajmahal; surrounds the black soil on the south, east and north.
[43:3:11] - Crops: ragi, groundnut, tobacco, millets, pulses.
[43:3:12] # Andhra Pradesh
[43:3:13] - Cultivated area: **red ~60%**, black ~25%, deltaic alluvium 5–6%, laterite ~1%; 22 soil categories; **six agro-climatic zones**.
[43:3:14] - Red soils (Rayalaseema): red gram, green gram, horse gram, groundnut, castor; AP laterite is poor in nitrogen.
[43:3:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.7 (book p.105); OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.4 (book p.69); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.85-88 (UPSC 2010, 2013 PYQs); Rocket Indian Geography p.59-60; Rocket AP Geography p.43-44; app notes 4:43 (sub 1, 3, 9)
[43:3:16] - **Coffee** is grown on the red and laterite soils of the Western Ghats, not on alluvium.
[43:3:17] - **Tea** needs slightly acidic soil without calcium and cannot bear standing water – so it is grown on hill slopes.
## SUB 4 | Soil Erosion – Types, Agents and Causes
[43:4:0] # Types
[43:4:1] TABLE head: Type | Process | Example
  [43:4:1.0] Splash | Raindrop impact breaks crumbs – first stage | Bare soil
  [43:4:1.1] Sheet | Thin uniform topsoil layer removed by overland flow; widespread, least noticed | Gentle slopes
  [43:4:1.2] Rill | Small, shallow channels on the soil surface | Bare fields
  [43:4:1.3] Gully | Deep trenches; badlands and ravines; final stage | Chambal ravines
  [43:4:1.4] Wind | Deflation, saltation, creep | Thar Desert
  [43:4:1.5] Mass (landslide) | Gravity on slopes | Himalayan monsoon slopes
  [43:4:1.6] Tunnel | Subsurface removal | Parts of Australia, Africa
[43:4:2] - **Increasing soil loss:** **splash → sheet → rill → gully** (II, IV, III, I).
[43:4:3] - **Ravines:** Chambal–Yamuna basin on the **periphery of the Gangetic plain** (MP, Rajasthan, UP); also Tamil Nadu, West Bengal; India loses ~8,000 ha a year to gullies.
[43:4:4] # Causes and rate
[43:4:5] - **Deforestation** is the main human cause (removes root binding and humus); also overgrazing, shifting cultivation, faulty farming. **Terrace cultivation is a remedy**, and tropical climate is not counted a cause – "only deforestation" (UPSC 2014).
[43:4:6] - **Deforestation generally decreases rainfall** (and increases erosion, drought, warming).
[43:4:7] - Erosion rate depends on **all** of: rainfall intensity and duration, slope, vegetation cover, soil texture, land use.
[43:4:8] - **Rainfall intensity matters more than total annual rainfall**; higher intensity → more runoff → **effective rainfall reduces**.
[43:4:9] - Wind erosion worst on **bare, dry, fine-textured soil** with strong winds; **water is the most powerful agent**.
[43:4:10] - Widely spaced row crops leave soil bare between rows – **sorghum** is the exam answer for fastest erosion (dense clover and wheat protect the soil).
[43:4:11] - **RUSLE** model predicts long-term water erosion on slopes (ICAR C- and P-factor maps).
[43:4:12] - Intense bursts exceed **infiltration capacity** → runoff, so soils can end up drier (2026 studies).
[43:4:13] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.6-7 (book p.71-72); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.81 (Chambal ravines); gktoday.in UPSC 2014 PYQ page; app notes 4:43 (sub 6)
## SUB 5 | Problem Soils – Salinity, Alkalinity, Acidity and Degradation
[43:5:0] # Saline and alkaline soils
[43:5:1] - Local names **reh, kallar, usar**, thur, rakar, chopan; caused by **unscientific irrigation and poor drainage**; capillary rise leaves salts on top.
[43:5:2] - **Salinisation** of irrigated land: salts left by evaporating water **make some soils impermeable** – it does not raise yields.
[43:5:3] - **Largest saline area: Gujarat** (Rann of Kutch, Gulf of Khambhat); **maximum alkali area: Uttar Pradesh**.
[43:5:4] - Affected: Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, UP, Bihar; Green Revolution canal areas of Punjab–Haryana.
[43:5:5] # Amendments
[43:5:6] TABLE head: Problem | Remedy
  [43:5:6.0] Alkaline / sodic (and saline-alkali) | Gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) – replaces sodium with calcium; long-term solution, with leaching water
  [43:5:6.1] Excess soluble salts | Leaching – removing salts by applying water
  [43:5:6.2] Alkalinity | Acid-forming chemicals (sulphur etc.) neutralise it
  [43:5:6.3] Acidic | Lime – decreases soil acidity
  [43:5:6.4] Poor fertility | Green manuring – boosts microbes and fertility
[43:5:7] # Degradation
[43:5:8] - **Soil impoverishment** = soil becoming very deficient in plant nutrients.
[43:5:9] - **Green Revolution reduced soil fertility**: chemical fertilisers without manure, over-irrigation, salinity.
[43:5:10] TABLE head: Cause | States
  [43:5:10.0] Overgrazing | Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Maharashtra
  [43:5:10.1] Over-irrigation | Punjab, Haryana, western UP
  [43:5:10.2] Mining | Jharkhand, Odisha, MP, Chhattisgarh
[43:5:11] - **Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas** (ISRO **SAC, Ahmedabad**, June 2021): **97.85 mha (29.7%)** degraded in 2018-19 (28.76% in 2003-05); rose in **28 of 31** States/UTs; **water erosion** the largest driver.
[43:5:12] - **FAO Status of the World's Soil Resources 2026:** soil-biodiversity loss **4th of 7** threats (after erosion, SOC loss, nutrient mismanagement).
[43:5:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.5 (book p.103); OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.5, p.7 (book p.70, 72); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.89-90; Rocket Indian Geography p.61; app notes 4:43 (sub 8)
## SUB 6 | Other Soils, Rain-Forest Soils and the ICAR/USDA Orders
[43:6:0] # Desert, peaty, forest soils
[43:6:1] - **Arid / desert:** sandy, saline; poor in nitrogen and humus, **phosphate normal/high**; **calcium increases downward** (kankar) – **western Rajasthan soils are rich in calcium**.
[43:6:2] - **Peaty / marshy:** areas of **heavy rainfall and high humidity with good vegetation**; organic matter 40–50%; black, heavy, highly acidic (NCERT: alkaline in places); Kottayam–Alappuzha, Sundarbans, coastal Odisha–TN, north Bihar, Almora. "Semi-arid with salinity" = saline soil.
[43:6:3] - **Forest / mountain:** humus-rich in forests and lower valleys (NextGen, PMF), but **acidic with low humus** on snow-clad upper slopes (NCERT); poor in potash and phosphorus.
[43:6:4] - **Podzol:** acidic leached soil of **coniferous (taiga)** forests (about 60°N).
[43:6:5] # Tropical rain-forest soils
[43:6:6] - **Poor in nutrients**: heat and moisture **decompose organic matter quickly** (true), but nutrients go straight into vegetation or are **leached** (UPSC 2023: I false, II true).
[43:6:7] - Cleared rain forest **cannot** support intensive farming for years without fertilisers, though its **primary productivity is very high** (UPSC 2003: A false, R true).
[43:6:8] # ICAR / USDA soil orders
[43:6:9] TABLE head: Order | Share of India
  [43:6:9.0] Inceptisols (largest) | 39.74%
  [43:6:9.1] Entisols | 28.08%
  [43:6:9.2] Alfisols | 13.55%
  [43:6:9.3] Vertisols (black soils) | 8.52%
  [43:6:9.4] Aridisols | 4.28%
  [43:6:9.5] Ultisols | 2.51%
  [43:6:9.6] Mollisols (smallest) | 0.40%
[43:6:10] - Decreasing order asked: **Entisols > Alfisols > Aridisols > Ultisols**.
[43:6:11] - **Histosols** = organic (peat/bog) soils with very high organic matter; **Gelisols** frozen; **Spodosols** acidic leached (podzols); **Vertisols** cracking clays.
[43:6:12] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.2, p.5-6 (book p.67, 70-71); NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.4-5 (book p.102-103); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.88-90; app notes 4:43 (sub 4, 5)
[43:6:13] - **Acidic soils:** laterite, peaty and forest soils; black and saline-alkaline soils are neutral to alkaline.
## SUB 7 | Soil Formation, Profile, Water and Nutrients
[43:7:0] # Formation
[43:7:1] - Five factors: **parent material, climate, relief, organisms, time** (soil colour is a property, not a factor); limestone → calcium-rich soil.
[43:7:2] - **Tors:** rounded granite boulders left by weathering and erosion of granite – common in Andhra Pradesh (e.g. Rayalaseema).
[43:7:3] # Profile
[43:7:4] - **Soil profile** = the **vertical arrangement of horizons** down to the parent rock (a single layer is a horizon).
[43:7:5] TABLE head: Horizon | Meaning
  [43:7:5.0] O | Organic litter
  [43:7:5.1] A | Topsoil, humus-rich
  [43:7:5.2] E | Leached layer
  [43:7:5.3] B | Subsoil – minerals washed down accumulate
  [43:7:5.4] C | Weathered parent material
  [43:7:5.5] R | Bedrock
[43:7:6] - Order from the surface: **O → A → B → C → R**.
[43:7:7] # Composition and water
[43:7:8] - Good soil by volume: **mineral 45%, organic matter 5%, water 25%, air 25%**.
[43:7:9] - **Soil organic carbon** binds particles into aggregates, raises infiltration, feeds microbes; India's average SOC reportedly fell from **1% to 0.3%** in 70 years.
[43:7:10] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [43:7:10.0] Infiltration | Entry of water at the surface
  [43:7:10.1] Percolation | Movement down through the soil column
  [43:7:10.2] Permeability | Ease of water movement
  [43:7:10.3] Saturated flow | All soil pores filled with water
[43:7:11] - **Clay** retains the most water because of its many **small** pores (not large ones).
[43:7:12] # Nutrients
[43:7:13] TABLE head: Nutrient | Main source in soil
  [43:7:13.0] Nitrogen | Organic matter
  [43:7:13.1] Iron | Pyrites
  [43:7:13.2] Calcium | Gypsum
  [43:7:13.3] Boron | Tourmaline
[43:7:14] - **Zinc** is the micronutrient most widely deficient in Indian soils.
[43:7:15] - Crops remove large amounts of **potassium** – among Ca, K, Zn and P the most depleted after harvest.
[43:7:16] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.1 (book p.66); PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.79-82; app notes 4:43 (sub 0)

=== NOTES 4:44 | India – Rocks and Mineral Belts; Distribution of Metallic and Non-metallic Minerals
## SUB 0 | Ores, Alloys and Classification of Minerals
[44:0:0] TABLE head: Metal | Ores asked
  [44:0:0.0] Aluminium | Bauxite (Al₂O₃·xH₂O, chief ore), cryolite (Na₃AlF₆), corundum (anhydrous Al₂O₃), diaspore
  [44:0:0.1] Iron | Haematite Fe₂O₃, magnetite Fe₃O₄ (magnetic, "black ore"), limonite FeO(OH)·nH₂O (brown), siderite FeCO₃, pyrites FeS₂ (used for sulphur, not for iron)
  [44:0:0.2] Copper | Chalcopyrite CuFeS₂, chalcocite Cu₂S, cuprite, malachite Cu₂(CO₃)(OH)₂, azurite
  [44:0:0.3] Lead / Zinc | Galena PbS / zinc blende (sphalerite) ZnS, calamine, smithsonite ZnCO₃
  [44:0:0.4] Mercury / Tin | Cinnabar HgS / cassiterite SnO₂
  [44:0:0.5] Silver | Argentite Ag₂S, horn silver (AgCl), ruby silver; lunar caustic = AgNO₃
  [44:0:0.6] Manganese | Pyrolusite MnO₂, psilomelane, manganite, hausmannite, braunite
  [44:0:0.7] Titanium | Ilmenite FeTiO₃, rutile TiO₂ (coastal beach sands)
  [44:0:0.8] Thorium / Uranium | Monazite (thorium + rare earths) / pitchblende (uranium, not copper)
  [44:0:0.9] Tungsten | Wolframite (China leads), scheelite
  [44:0:0.10] Na / K / Mg / Ca | Rock salt NaCl / sylvine, carnallite KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O / magnesite MgCO₃, dolomite CaMg(CO₃)₂ / limestone CaCO₃, gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O (calcium sulphate dihydrate), fluorspar CaF₂
[44:0:1] - **Iron content:** **magnetite** highest (about 70–72%; "superior grade") > **haematite** (60–70%) > limonite (40–60%) > **siderite** (lowest). **Haematite** = most widely used and India's **largest reserve** type.
[44:0:2] - **Magnetite:** black ore, up to ~70% iron, magnetic – all three statements true.
[44:0:3] - **Not an ore:** **pig iron** (a smelted product); bauxite, malachite and zinc blende are ores.
[44:0:4] - **Native (free) state:** **gold** (best-known), silver, platinum, copper – a single type of atom = **native elements**. **Never free:** K, Na, Ca, Mg, **Al** (top of the reactivity series).
[44:0:5] - **Alloys:** **German silver** = copper + zinc + nickel (Cu 60, Ni 20, Zn 20) – **contains no silver**; **brass** = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin. Horn silver, ruby silver and lunar caustic all contain silver.
[44:0:6] - **Ferrous minerals** (contain iron): iron ore, manganese, chromite, nickel, cobalt (NCERT). **Non-ferrous:** copper, bauxite (aluminium), lead, zinc, tin (NCERT); precious: gold, silver, platinum.
[44:0:7] - **⚠ Tungsten:** exam keys treat it as **non-ferrous**, but NextGen lists it among ferrous (ferro-alloy) minerals with cobalt and nickel.
[44:0:8] - **Non-ferrous group:** **nickel, zinc, copper, aluminium** (not iron ore, pig iron or steel).
[44:0:9] - **Non-metallic:** **marble**, **gypsum**, mica, limestone, salt, potash, graphite (not haematite, bauxite, limonite, manganese, silver, lead).
[44:0:10] TABLE head: Deposit type | How formed | Minerals
  [44:0:10.0] Placer | Heavy minerals in alluvial / beach sands | Gold, tin, platinum
  [44:0:10.1] Veins / lodes | Cracks in igneous and metamorphic rocks | Tin, copper, zinc, lead
  [44:0:10.2] Sedimentary beds | Layers | Coal, gypsum, salt, potash
  [44:0:10.3] Residual weathering | Decomposed rock (laterite) | Bauxite
[44:0:11] - **Kimberlite** pipes (ultrabasic) = host rock of **diamond**.
[44:0:12] - **Talc:** softest mineral; a magnesium silicate (softness comes from its weakly bonded layers, not from being Mg silicate).
[44:0:13] - **Plaster of Paris** is made by heating **gypsum** (CaSO₄·½H₂O, written 2CaSO₄·H₂O); anhydrite = CaSO₄.
[44:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 09 p.1 (iron ore grades; ferrous/non-ferrous lists); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 09 p.18, p.22-23 (classification; magnetite ~70%); NextGen Indian Geography 10 (zinc blende, diamonds in kimberlite); PMF H&E Geography 04 p.23 (wolframite); app notes 4:44 (sub 2, 3)
## SUB 1 | Non-ferrous, Precious and Atomic Minerals
[44:1:0] TABLE head: Mineral | Places asked
  [44:1:0.0] Copper | Khetri (Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan), Malanjkhand (Balaghat, MP – largest producing mine), Mosabani/Singhbhum (Jharkhand), Alwar
  [44:1:0.1] Bauxite | Odisha – Koraput, Kalahandi, Rayagada, Lanjigarh; Gujarat – Jamnagar, Bhavnagar, Junagadh; Jharkhand – Lohardaga, Palamu, Gumla; Chhattisgarh – Bastar (Kondagaon), Bilaspur, Surguja (Mainpat), Amarkantak
  [44:1:0.2] Lead-zinc | Zawar (Udaipur), Rampura-Agucha (Bhilwara), Rajpura-Dariba – Rajasthan
  [44:1:0.3] Gold | Kolar (closed 2001) and Hutti (Raichur; main working mine) – Karnataka; Ramagiri (AP); Subarnarekha placers
  [44:1:0.4] Silver | By-product of lead-zinc (Zawar, Rajasthan); also Jharkhand, AP, Karnataka, Odisha – not Gujarat
  [44:1:0.5] Tin | Chhattisgarh (Dantewada) – only producing State
  [44:1:0.6] Diamond | Panna – Majhgawan mine (MP), the only working, mechanised diamond mine
  [44:1:0.7] Uranium | Jaduguda (first commercial mine; first found 1951), Turamdih, Bhatin, Narwapahar (Singhbhum, Jharkhand); Tummalapalle (Kadapa, AP)
  [44:1:0.8] Nickel / Tungsten | Nickel ~92–93% in Odisha (Sukinda); tungsten mainly Karnataka (~42%), not Kerala
[44:1:1] - **Copper ranks:** reserves – **Rajasthan ~52–54%** (largest), Jharkhand, MP; production – **MP first** (Malanjkhand). Jharkhand is not the 90% source.
[44:1:2] - **Bauxite ranks:** reserves – **Odisha ~50%**, Chhattisgarh, **AP ~12–18%**, Jharkhand; production 2021-22 – **Odisha 73%**, **Gujarat 9% (2nd)**, Jharkhand 8%, Chhattisgarh 4%. Odisha + AP hold >90% of metallurgical-grade bauxite.
[44:1:3] - **Rajasthan:** sole producer of **lead-zinc ores, wollastonite and selenite** – near monopoly in **zinc**; not the sole copper producer.
[44:1:4] - **Tin resources:** Haryana ~64% and Chhattisgarh ~36% (IMYB 2024), but only Chhattisgarh produces.
[44:1:5] - **Thorium:** from **monazite**; largest monazite concentration on the **Kerala** coast (Chavara; IREL Udyogamandal) – Kerala = leading thorium answer; monazite also on TN, AP and Odisha coasts. India is **self-sufficient in thorium**; uranium = main nuclear fuel.
[44:1:6] - **Beach sands (seven heavy minerals):** ilmenite, rutile, zircon, sillimanite, garnet, monazite, leucoxene – Kerala (Neendakara–Kayamkulam), TN, Odisha, AP (Srikakulam, Visakhapatnam). Ilmenite and rutile = **titanium**.
[44:1:7] - **Uranium oxide to metal:** U₃O₈ is ~84.8% uranium, so 1.22 lakh t U₃O₈ ≈ **1.04 lakh t** uranium.
[44:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 09 p.7-14 (bauxite, chromite, gold, copper), 10 (lead-zinc, diamond, mica); PMF H&E Geography 04 p.5 (bauxite reserves/production), p.9-13 (lead-zinc), p.17-19 (gold, silver), p.24-26 (tungsten, copper), p.30-31 (nickel), p.52 (uranium, monazite on Kerala coast); Rocket Indian Geography p.27-28; app notes 4:44 (sub 5)
[44:1:9] - **Gold – AP and Jharkhand:** AP – Ramagiri, Chigargunta–Bisanatham; Jharkhand – Lawa, Parasi. Non-coal mineral blocks are **auctioned by State Governments** (MMDR 2015).
## SUB 2 | Iron Ore, Manganese and Chromite – Places and Ranks
[44:2:0] TABLE head: Belt / State | Iron ore places asked
  [44:2:0.0] Odisha | Barbil–Koira (Barabil) valley – richest haematite, most mines; Keonjhar (Kendujhar), Mayurbhanj (Badampahar, Gurumahisani), Sundargarh, Bonai
  [44:2:0.1] Chhattisgarh | Bailadila (Dantewada/Bastar – high-grade haematite; largest mechanised mine; feeds Visakhapatnam Steel Plant; ore exported to Japan via Vizag), Dalli-Rajhara (Durg)
  [44:2:0.2] Jharkhand | Singhbhum – Noamundi, Gua, Chiria (West Singhbhum)
  [44:2:0.3] Karnataka | Kudremukh (Chikkamagaluru), Kemmangundi (Bababudan hills), Bellary–Hospet–Sandur, Chitradurga
  [44:2:0.4] Others | Goa (Bicholim), Maharashtra (Chandrapur, Ratnagiri), Rajasthan – Nathara-ki-Pal (Udaipur), AP – Anantapur
[44:2:1] - **Trap pairs:** **Bailadila – Chhattisgarh, not MP**; **Zawar** = lead-zinc, not iron; **Guntur** = not iron ore; Jharia = coal; Kemmangundi – Karnataka ✓; Punjab has no iron ore.
[44:2:2] - **Steel plant supply:** **Rourkela** (Sundargarh, Odisha; German Krupps–Demag, 1959) gets ore from **Keonjhar** and Sundargarh (Barsua); Mayurbhanj ore historically fed Jamshedpur. Bhilai ← Dalli-Rajhara; Vizag ← Bailadila.
[44:2:3] - **Reserves:** haematite – **Odisha ~34–39%**, Jharkhand ~20–23%, Chhattisgarh ~19–22%, Karnataka ~11%; magnetite – **Karnataka ~72%**, AP ~13%. Odisha + Jharkhand ≈ 58% of haematite – **not 80%**. Total iron ore (haematite + magnetite) – **Karnataka first** (IMYB, as on 1.4.2020).
[44:2:4] - **Production:** **Odisha** first (~50% of output; 104.6 Mt of 204.5 Mt in **2020-21**; first again in 2023-24), then Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Jharkhand.
[44:2:5] - **World:** India **4th** in iron ore production (2020, 2022: Australia, China, Brazil, India) – not 2nd. India is **self-sufficient and a net exporter** of iron ore (it imports petroleum, machinery, gold).
[44:2:6] - **Old "two richest iron-ore States":** **Bihar (now Jharkhand) and Odisha** – the Singhbhum–Keonjhar belt.
[44:2:7] TABLE head: Manganese | Facts
  [44:2:7.0] Reserves | Odisha largest (~34–44%), Karnataka 2nd, MP, Maharashtra
  [44:2:7.1] Production 2020-21 | MP 34% > Maharashtra 24% > Odisha 18% > Karnataka 12% > AP 8%; Rajasthan minor
  [44:2:7.2] Places | MP – Balaghat (Asia's deepest Mn mine), Chhindwara; Maharashtra – Bhandara, Nagpur; Odisha – Kendujhar, Sundargarh, Koraput; Karnataka – Shimoga, Ballari, Chikkamagaluru, Chitradurga; AP – Srikakulam, Vizianagaram
[44:2:8] - **⚠ Manganese leader:** MP leads production in most recent years; **Odisha** led in some years (UPPSC 2012 key) and has the largest reserves. Srikakulam is in **AP**, not Karnataka.
[44:2:9] - **Chromite:** **Odisha** – largest producer (~99%) and >96% of resources – **Sukinda Valley** (Jajpur), Kendujhar, Dhenkanal; also Karnataka (Hassan), Manipur.

## SUB 3 | Non-metallic Minerals – Mica, Gypsum, Marble and Others
[44:3:0] # Mica
[44:3:1] - **Occurrence:** pegmatite veins in Archaean/Dharwar granite, gneiss, schist; varieties **muscovite** (white), **phlogopite** (amber/Mg) and biotite – **phlogopite and pegmatite → mica**.
[44:3:2] - **Use:** an **insulator** in electrical and electronic industries; India historically monopolised **sheet mica** (led world output when asked in 1992, 2001).
[44:3:3] - **Belts:** **Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh–Munger** ("Capital of Mica", ruby mica, Jharkhand–Bihar) – the largest belt; **Nellore** (AP); **Ajmer–Bhilwara** (Rajasthan).
[44:3:4] - **Reserves:** **AP 41%**, **Rajasthan 28%**, Odisha 17%, Maharashtra 13% (2015) – Rajasthan, AP, Bihar and **Jharkhand** are the classic reserve States.
[44:3:5] - **Producers:** AP long the **largest producer** (Nellore); IMYB 2020-21: **Rajasthan 17.7 thousand t, AP 16.7 thousand t**. Jharkhand, Rajasthan, AP produce mica; **Madhya Pradesh does not**.
[44:3:6] # Gypsum, marble and others
[44:3:7] TABLE head: Mineral | Use | Areas
  [44:3:7.0] Gypsum | Cement (setting regulator), fertiliser (soil fertility), Plaster of Paris | Rajasthan ~99% (Churu–Bikaner–Sri Ganganagar belt); also TN
  [44:3:7.1] Marble | Building | Makrana (Rajasthan) – finest; Taj Mahal, Victoria Memorial
  [44:3:7.2] Limestone | Cement, steel flux | MP, Rajasthan, AP (Kurnool), Gujarat, Chhattisgarh; Kaimur–Rohtas
  [44:3:7.3] Dolomite | Steel flux, refractories | Chhattisgarh, Odisha, AP
  [44:3:7.4] Asbestos | Fire-proofing | Resources Rajasthan 59%, Karnataka 36%; chrysotile – AP (Kadapa) ~96%
  [44:3:7.5] Barytes | Oil-well drilling mud | Mangampet (Kadapa, AP) – AP ~92% of resources
  [44:3:7.6] Kyanite / sillimanite | Refractories | Lapsa Buru (Jharkhand) / Sona Pahar (Meghalaya), Odisha
  [44:3:7.7] Salt | — | Didwana (Rajasthan), Gujarat
[44:3:8] - **Asbestos production:** only AP (Kadapa chrysotile) reported output until 2013-14; **no production in India since 2014-15**. Old keys name Rajasthan the largest producer.
[44:3:9] - **Graphite:** Bellary area (Karnataka) in the UPSC 1998 match; graphite also at Rampa (AP Eastern Ghats).
[44:3:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 10 (mica reserves and producers); PMF H&E Geography 04 p.44-46 (mica; 2020-21 production), p.47 (asbestos), p.49 (gypsum 99% Rajasthan); IBM Indian Minerals Yearbook 2022 – Asbestos (state-wise chrysotile resources); app notes 4:44 (sub 6)
[44:3:11] - **Sonbhadra (UP):** **andalusite** (~91% of India's resources, Salaidih–Harwariya), **pyrite**, **dolomite** (Bari); keys leave out uranium (Lalitpur), though AMD reports low-grade uranium at Naktu–Kundabhati.
## SUB 4 | State Rankings, Value of Production and Trade
[44:4:0] TABLE head: State | Value share 2021-22
  [44:4:0.0] Odisha | 44.11% (first)
  [44:4:0.1] Karnataka | 17.34%
  [44:4:0.2] Jharkhand | 4.36%
  [44:4:0.3] Madhya Pradesh | 2.96%
[44:4:1] - **2024-25:** Odisha first (**43.49%**) > Rajasthan > Chhattisgarh > Karnataka > Maharashtra > Jharkhand; 8 States give ~97.7%. India produces **95 minerals** (4 fuel, 10 metallic, 23 non-metallic, 3 atomic, 55 minor).
[44:4:2] - **Mineral-rich regions:** the **peninsular plateau** – Chota Nagpur, Odisha and Dandakaranya plateaus (the "heart" of Indian minerals, keyed "South East"); the Gangetic plains are poor in minerals.
[44:4:3] - **Old "richest" answers:** most mineral-rich State – **Bihar** (undivided, before 2000); "maximum prosperity" among Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, TN – **Karnataka**. Today **Odisha** ("State of minerals").
[44:4:4] - **India's world rank 2020:** iron ore **4th**, manganese ore **5th**, bauxite **6th**, aluminium (primary) **3rd**. Iron ore output 2020-21 ≈ **204 Mt**.
[44:4:5] - **Self-sufficiency:** iron ore (net exporter), thorium, near self-sufficient in bauxite and coal reserves; about 75% of lead imported; copper, nickel, gold largely imported.
[44:4:6] - **Trade 2004 (India's share of world exports):** **rice 18.0%**, iron ore 17.8%, tea 10.3%, woven cotton fabrics 3.0%.

## SUB 5 | Rock Systems and Mineral Belts
[44:5:0] TABLE head: Rock system | Where | Minerals
  [44:5:0.0] Archaean (>2,500 Ma; fossil-free, formed before life) | Peninsular shield | Metallic minerals; storehouse of mineral wealth
  [44:5:0.1] Dharwar (oldest schist belts; economically most important) | Karnataka, Aravallis, Singhbhum | Iron ore, manganese, copper, lead, gold, mica – ferrous and non-ferrous
  [44:5:0.2] Cuddapah (Purana; shale, slate, quartzite, limestone) | Kadapa basin, AP | Barytes, asbestos, copper, iron, lead, diamond, uranium – no coal
  [44:5:0.3] Vindhyan (Purana; Semri lower; Kaimur, Rewa, Bhander upper) | Central India | Limestone, sandstone, Panna diamonds
  [44:5:0.4] Dravidian (Palaeozoic) | Himalaya, Kashmir | Abundant marine fossils
  [44:5:0.5] Gondwana (Carboniferous–Jurassic) | Damodar, Son, Mahanadi, Godavari valleys | Coal – about 98% (99.54% as on 1.4.2022); not natural gas
  [44:5:0.6] Deccan Trap (end-Cretaceous fissure basalt) | Maharashtra, Malwa | Black cotton (regur) soil
  [44:5:0.7] Tertiary (youngest) | Assam, Gujarat, Rajasthan, offshore | Petroleum, natural gas; Neyveli lignite
[44:5:1] - **Gondwana coal** is younger and lower in carbon than Carboniferous coal. A–R: Gondwana ~95%+ coal ✓ and Dharwar ferrous/non-ferrous ✓, but R does not explain A.
[44:5:2] - **Madhya Pradesh geology:** part of the old **Gondwana land** (peninsular block) and holds Vindhyan, Gondwana and Deccan Trap rocks.
[44:5:3] - **AP rocks:** Dharwar – Anantapur, Chittoor, Kadapa (iron ore, gold); Kurnool group – cement limestone; Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt (khondalite, charnockite) – bauxite, manganese, graphite.
[44:5:4] TABLE head: Belt | Area | Minerals
  [44:5:4.0] North-Eastern Plateau ("Golden Triangle") | Chota Nagpur, Odisha plateau, WB, parts of Chhattisgarh | Coal, iron ore, manganese, mica, bauxite, copper, uranium
  [44:5:4.1] Central | Chhattisgarh, MP, Maharashtra, Telangana | Iron ore (Bailadila), manganese (Balaghat), coal, limestone, bauxite
  [44:5:4.2] South-Western / Southern | Karnataka, Goa, TN uplands, Kerala, AP | High-grade iron ore, manganese, gold (Kolar), chromite, Neyveli lignite, Kerala monazite
  [44:5:4.3] North-Western | Aravalli (Rajasthan), Gujarat | Non-ferrous copper, lead-zinc, gypsum, salt, marble; Gujarat petroleum
  [44:5:4.4] North-Eastern | Assam, Meghalaya | Crude oil (Digboi), Meghalaya coal and limestone
[44:5:5] - **Chota Nagpur industrial region** grew on the discovery of **coal** in the Damodar valley; Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih, Raniganj, Karanpura = coalfields.
[44:5:6] - **Statement keys:** natural gas – marine sedimentary basins, not Gondwana; mica – Koderma ✓; Dharwars – not petroleum; Cuddapah – barytes/asbestos, not "famous for diamonds".
[44:5:7] - **Geological firsts:** GSI set up 1851; "Archaean" coined by J.D. Dana (1872); Indian rock grouping by T.H. Holland. Fossil parks: Siwalik Fossil Park, Saketi (HP); Marine Gondwana Fossil Park, Manendragarh (Chhattisgarh); Akal Wood Fossil Park (Jaisalmer); Lonar = meteorite crater lake.
[44:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.12-14 (rock systems, mineral belts); NextGen Indian Geography 09 p.1 (regions); Rocket Indian Geography p.24-27, p.114 (rock–mineral pairs, coalfields); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 09 p.21-22 (belts); PMF H&E Geography 04 p.46 (UPSC 2013 statements); app notes 4:44 (sub 0, 1)
[44:5:9] - **Match pairs:** coal – Giridih; copper – Alwar (Kho-Dariba); manganese – **Dharwar**; lignite – **Jayamkondam** (Ariyalur, TN).
## SUB 6 | Critical Minerals and Rare Earths
[44:6:0] - **Critical minerals list:** Ministry of Mines, **June 2023 – 30 minerals**; rare earth elements (17 elements) are **included**.
[44:6:1] - **National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM):** approved **January 2025**; 1,200 exploration projects by 2030-31; **50 overseas assets**; encourages PSUs and private firms to buy assets abroad; national stockpile. **Critical Mineral Recycling Incentive Scheme** – Central Sector, Rs 1,500 crore (Sep 2025).
[44:6:2] - **Rare earths:** China ~70% of mining (>85% processing) – **India is not second**; uses in AI, robotics, EVs, space. Budget 2026-27 rare-earth corridors: Odisha, Kerala, **AP**, TN.
[44:6:3] - **Lithium:** GSI inferred **5.9 Mt** at **Salal-Haimana, Reasi (J&K)** (Feb 2023); AMD 1,600 t at **Marlagalla, Mandya** (Karnataka).
[44:6:4] TABLE head: Partner | Deal
  [44:6:4.0] KABIL (NALCO + HCL + MECL) | Lithium blocks, Catamarca, Argentina (agreement Feb 2025)
  [44:6:4.1] Australia | 2022 – lithium, cobalt
  [44:6:4.2] Chile | Largest copper supplier
[44:6:5] - **Others:** coking coal notified Critical and Strategic (Jharia >90% of coking-coal reserves); GSI "Uncover India" with **Geoscience Australia**.
[44:6:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:44 (sub 8); UPSC CSE 2026 PYQ explanation (PMF)
[44:6:7] - **Minerals Security Partnership:** India joined in **June 2023**. **MMDR Amendment 2023:** only the **Centre** auctions mining leases / composite licences for the **24 critical and strategic minerals** (Part D, First Schedule); India is import-dependent for many of the 30 critical minerals.
## SUB 7 | Mining Law and Policy
[44:7:0] - **MMDR Act 1957:** Ministry of Mines; excludes petroleum, gas, atomic minerals; major minerals – Centre; **minor minerals – States (Section 15)**.
[44:7:1] TABLE head: Amendment | Change
  [44:7:1.0] 2015 | Auction-only allotment; DMF and NMET created; PMKKKY uses DMF funds (yearly audit)
  [44:7:1.1] 2021 | NMET autonomous; captive mines may sell output
  [44:7:1.2] 2025 | New minerals added to leases (States approve in 30 days); captive-sale limit removed
  [44:7:1.3] 2026 Bill (Aug) | Limits States' power to tax mineral rights and mineral-bearing land
[44:7:2] - **MADA v. SAIL (2024):** royalty is **not a tax**; States may tax mineral-bearing land. SC (Jul 2026) upheld royalty on an Average Sale Price including royalty, DMF and NMET.
[44:7:3] - **Offshore:** **Art. 297** vests offshore minerals in the Union; OAMDR Amendment 2023 – auction-only leases. **National Mineral Policy 2019** replaced the 2008 policy.
[44:7:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:44 (sub 9)
[44:7:5] - **District Mineral Foundation:** non-profit trust in mining-affected districts (MMDR 2015, Sec 9B), funded by miners, for **persons and areas affected by mining** – not exploration (NMET) or licensing.
[44:7:6] - **Major vs minor:** the Centre notifies minor minerals (**Sec 3(e)**); **bentonite** was declared **minor** (10 Feb 2015); chromite, kyanite and sillimanite are **major**.
[44:7:7] - **Minor-mineral rules:** **States** make concession rules for minor minerals (**Sec 15**); the **Centre** can notify any mineral as minor (**Sec 3(e)**).

=== NOTES 4:45 | India – Earthquake Zones, Landslide-prone Areas, Cyclone-prone Coasts; Seismic Zoning Map
## SUB 0 | Tsunami – Warning Centres, 2004 Tsunami and International Centres
[45:0:0] # Tsunami basics
[45:0:1] - **Tsunami:** large waves from a sudden movement of the **ocean floor** – mostly an **undersea earthquake** (also submarine landslides, volcanic eruptions); Japanese "harbour wave". A **natural** disaster, not man-made.
[45:0:2] - **26 December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami** (Sumatra–Andaman earthquake): hit Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Kerala and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands; **Indira Point** (southern tip of Great Nicobar) went **under the sea**.
[45:0:3] - Most exposed: the **east coast** and the **Andaman & Nicobar Islands**.
[45:0:4] # Indian warning system
[45:0:5] TABLE head: Question | Answer
  [45:0:5.0] Tsunami Warning Centre of India / ITEWC | Hyderabad, at INCOIS
  [45:0:5.1] INCOIS | Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, Hyderabad; autonomous body (1999) under the Ministry of Earth Sciences (ESSO unit)
  [45:0:5.2] ITEWC set up | After the 2004 tsunami; inaugurated 15 Oct 2007, working 24x7 since 2007
  [45:0:5.3] Detection | Tsunamigenic earthquakes detected within ~10 minutes; seismic network, buoys, tide gauges
  [45:0:5.4] Other INCOIS tools | Real-time coastal risk / wave-height / vulnerable-building forecast (first in the world), SAMUDRA app, storm-surge and high-wave warnings
[45:0:6] - **Not** IMD Delhi, **not** NIO Goa, **not** NIOT Chennai – the tsunami warning system is run by **INCOIS, Hyderabad**.
[45:0:7] - The **IOC (UNESCO)-coordinated Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System** was set up after 2004; India (ITEWC) is one of its regional tsunami service providers (with Australia, Indonesia).
[45:0:8] - **Mock drills:** IOC-UNESCO's **IOWave 18** (Sept 2018, India + 23 Indian Ocean nations); later IOWave-23, IOWave-25.
[45:0:9] # International and regional centres
[45:0:10] TABLE head: Centre | Location
  [45:0:10.0] ITIC (International Tsunami Information Centre, UNESCO-IOC with NOAA) | Honolulu, Hawaii (not Jakarta, Tokyo, Goa)
  [45:0:10.1] PTWC (Pacific Tsunami Warning Center) | Honolulu
  [45:0:10.2] UNESCO-IOC | Paris
  [45:0:10.3] UNDRR (Sendai Framework focal point) | Geneva
  [45:0:10.4] ADPC (Asian Disaster Preparedness Center) | Bangkok – Asia-Pacific focal point for disaster awareness and local capability
  [45:0:10.5] ADRC (Asian Disaster Reduction Center) | Kobe, Japan
[45:0:11] - World Tsunami Awareness Day: **5 November**.
[45:0:12] > Asked again and again: ITEWC/INCOIS = Hyderabad; ITIC = Honolulu; tsunami year = 2004.
[45:0:13] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Mgmt p.10-13, p.51-52, p.64; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.54-55; NCERT (OnlyIAS Physical Geography 08) p.1 (Indira Point); INCOIS press clipping via web search (inaugurated 15 Oct 2007); app notes 4:45 (subs 6-7)
## SUB 1 | Landslides and Avalanches – Causes, Prone Areas, Zonation, Mitigation
[45:1:0] # Where and why
[45:1:1] - **About 12.6% of India's area (~0.42 million sq km)** is landslide-prone (GSI 12.6–15%): **Himalayas, North-East, Western Ghats (incl. Nilgiris)**; parts of the Eastern Ghats.
[45:1:2] - Landslides occur **mostly in hilly terrain** on **steep slopes of rocky mountains** – not in mud valleys, seashores or plateaus.
[45:1:3] - **Natural causes:** heavy rain and cloudbursts, earthquakes, fragile young fold mountains, steep slopes.
[45:1:4] - **Man-made causes:** **deforestation**, **road building**, **shifting cultivation**, mining and quarrying, changes in **land-use pattern**, hill cutting. **Increased forestation is NOT a cause** – it is a remedy.
[45:1:5] - India's vulnerability = **deforestation + heavy rainfall in mountains** (India has little volcanic activity).
[45:1:6] - **Himalayas:** landslide frequency has **increased**, with large-scale **mining**, roads and dams (A and R both true, R explains A in the keys).
[45:1:7] - Western Ghats/Nilgiris: steep escarpments and orographic rain (not permafrost).
[45:1:8] # Major events
[45:1:9] TABLE head: Event | Type | Year
  [45:1:9.0] Malpa (Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand) | Landslide – Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrims killed | 18 Aug 1998
  [45:1:9.1] Wayanad (Kerala) | Landslides after very heavy rain | July 2024
  [45:1:9.2] Badrinath (Mana), Chamoli | Snow avalanche hit a BRO labour camp | 28 Feb 2025
  [45:1:9.3] Kedarnath | Cloudburst + flash flood | June 2013
  [45:1:9.4] Chamoli | Glacier (rock-ice) flood | 2021
[45:1:10] - **Avalanches** = rapid flow of snow and ice down steep (30°–45°) slopes – mainly in **high Himalayan hilly terrain**; nodal ministry: Defence (DGRE).
[45:1:11] - Hanging-glacier collapse in high seismic zones can trigger **GLOFs**.
[45:1:12] # Landslide hazard zonation
[45:1:13] - **Landslide (hazard) zoning:** division of hill areas into **homogeneous spatial units** by degree of **actual or potential** landslide susceptibility, hazard or risk; maps are **probabilistic** (likelihood, not exact time/place).
[45:1:14] - Preparing a full zonation map needs **huge data** on many variables over large slope areas, and **aerial photographs, satellite images and remote sensing** help collect it (both conclusions follow).
[45:1:15] TABLE head: Rock falls (number/annum/km of cliff or rock cut) | Frequency zone
  [45:1:15.0] > 10 | Very high
  [45:1:15.1] 1 to 10 | High
  [45:1:15.2] 0.1 to 1.0 | Moderate
  [45:1:15.3] 0.01 to 0.1 | Low
  [45:1:15.4] < 0.01 | Very low
[45:1:16] - NDMA's **National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019)**; GSI national susceptibility mapping; GSI **LANDSLIP** regional early warning system.
[45:1:17] # Mitigation
[45:1:18] - **Cheapest and most effective:** **increasing vegetative cover** (afforestation); walls and engineered works cost more.
[45:1:19] - **NCERT list:** **area-specific measures**, **limiting agriculture to valleys and moderate slopes**, **large-scale afforestation and bunds** to reduce water flow (all three).
[45:1:20] - **Structural:** retaining walls, rock bolting, wire mesh, drainage, slope grading. **Non-structural:** hazard zonation mapping, early warning, land-use regulation. **Regulatory:** restrict construction in high-risk zones.
[45:1:21] ~~ Sources: PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.61-63; Rocket Disaster Mgmt p.30-31, p.64, p.66; AGS 2007 Guideline Table 5 (rock-fall hazard descriptors; landslide-risk-html.pages.dev pdf, the classes the NDMA compendium uses); app notes 4:45 (subs 4, 8)
## SUB 2 | India's Hazard Profile – the Number Game
[45:2:0] TABLE head: Hazard | Exposure (most-asked figure)
  [45:2:0.0] Earthquake | ~59% (58.6%) of landmass prone to moderate-to-very-high intensity (MoES in Lok Sabha, July 2021 and Dec 2022)
  [45:2:0.1] Flood | ~40 million ha ≈ 12% of land (Rashtriya Barh Ayog); Rocket also gives "about 10%"
  [45:2:0.2] Cyclone and tsunami | ~5,700 km of the 7,516 km coastline (NDMA)
  [45:2:0.3] Drought | ~68% of cultivable area
  [45:2:0.4] Landslide | ~12.6% of area (0.42 million sq km)
  [45:2:0.5] Share of world tropical cyclones | ~10% affect the Indian coasts (most books and keys); PMF: North Indian Ocean has 6–7% of global tropical cyclones
[45:2:1] - **Disaster risk = Hazard x Vulnerability.**
[45:2:2] - Man-made disasters: war, hazardous-material exposure, transport accidents; **tsunami, cyclone, earthquake = natural**.
[45:2:3] - **DM Act 2005** shifted focus from post-disaster **relief → prevention, mitigation, preparedness**.
[45:2:4] - **APSDMA** is chaired by the **Chief Minister** (AP Disaster Management Rules, 2007). **NDMA–MoPR community DRR project:** Rs 507.37 crore, through **panchayats** in 81 districts of 20 States.
[45:2:5] - **Vulnerability Atlas of India** (housing and infrastructure): published by **BMTPC** (Building Materials and Technology Promotion Council).
[45:2:6] > The 5,700 km figure uses the old 7,516.6 km coastline (now 11,098.81 km after the 2025 re-measurement).
[45:2:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.45, p.55; PMF Physical Geography 02 p.100; Down To Earth "As told to Parliament (22 Dec 2022)" (59%); Rocket Disaster Mgmt p.27-28; app notes 4:45 (subs 0, 2, 9)
## SUB 3 | Seismic Zoning Map of India
[45:3:0] - Prepared by **BIS** (**IS 1893**); **four zones – II, III, IV, V** (Zone V = very high damage risk, MSK IX+).
[45:3:1] - **Killari (Latur) 1993** quake hit a "low-risk" area → **2002** revision merged **Zone I into Zone II**.
[45:3:2] TABLE head: Zone | Share of area | Places
  [45:3:2.0] V | ~11% | Entire North-East (e.g. Meghalaya), J&K, Ladakh, HP, Uttarakhand, Kutch, North Bihar, Andaman & Nicobar; Guwahati, Aizawl
  [45:3:2.1] IV | ~18% | Delhi, parts of J&K/HP; Srinagar (IV–V)
  [45:3:2.2] III | ~30% | Indo-Gangetic plains, coasts, Kerala, Goa; Amaravati region
  [45:3:2.3] II | ~41% (largest single zone) | Most of the stable peninsula – Hyderabad (least prone)
[45:3:3] - Karnataka, Maharashtra and Kerala are **not** Zone V. **Andhra Pradesh: Zones II and III only** (no Zone V).
[45:3:4] - **Withdrawn revision:** a BIS probabilistic (PSHA) map adding a **Zone VI** was **rolled back in March 2026** – the four-zone map still applies.
[45:3:5] - Codes: **IS 1893** = seismic design criteria; **IS 13920** = ductile detailing. GSI tracks crustal strain through **34 GNSS stations**.
[45:3:6] TABLE head: Earthquake | Type / year
  [45:3:6.0] Koyna (Maharashtra) | Reservoir-induced, 1967
  [45:3:6.1] Killari (Latur) | Intraplate, 1993
  [45:3:6.2] Bhuj (Kutch) | 26 Jan 2001 → DM Act 2005
[45:3:7] - AP: reservoir-induced tremors not ruled out near **Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam, Polavaram**. **Liquefaction** hazard: Indo-Gangetic plain.
[45:3:8] > "Majority of India's area" – official key Zone III; by the MoES shares Zone II (~41%) is the largest single zone.
[45:3:9] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Mgmt p.25-26; PMF Physical Geography 02 p.99-100; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.53; Down To Earth "As told to Parliament (22 Dec 2022)" (11/18/30% and the rest Zone II); app notes 4:45 (subs 1-3)
## SUB 4 | Cyclone-prone Coasts
[45:4:0] - **Cyclone = low-pressure area**; Indian cyclones start from low-pressure areas in the **Bay of Bengal near the Andaman Sea / Andaman & Nicobar Islands** (8–14°N).
[45:4:1] - Bay of Bengal : Arabian Sea ≈ **4 : 1** → the **east coast** is hit far more (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu).
[45:4:2] - **Most cyclone-prone coast:** **Odisha (Orissa) coast** in most books (most landfalls over a century); **Andhra Pradesh** was hit most in 1995–2020 (NDMI tally) and is the APPSC GS 2025 key's "most cyclone-prone State".
[45:4:3] - **West coast:** **Gujarat** is the most vulnerable (Kandla 1998, Tauktae 2021, Biparjoy 2023).
[45:4:4] - **Mangroves** shield coasts; their clearing in the **Mahanadi delta** added to Odisha's cyclone risk.
[45:4:5] - Exposure: **13 coastal States/UTs**, **84 coastal districts**. AP's most vulnerable stretch: **Ongole–Machilipatnam**; deadliest AP cyclone: **1977** cyclone.
[45:4:6] - IMD cyclone warning centres (7): Chennai, Mumbai, Kolkata, Ahmedabad, Thiruvananthapuram, **Visakhapatnam**, Bhubaneswar – **not Hyderabad**. ISRO runs **NDEM**; GIS and remote sensing map coastal vulnerability.
[45:4:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Mgmt p.30, p.34-36; PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.55; Down To Earth (cyclones account for nearly half of climate-disaster deaths; AP hit most 1995-2020); app notes 4:45 (sub 5)

  x: Landslide Hazard Zonation divides hill areas into homogeneous units by susceptibility, hazard or risk; such maps are probabilistic, not exact forecasts. Tsunami and flood mapping are different exercises, and landslide zonation is done mostly for hilly areas.

## SUB 3 | Area and Rank
[46:3:0] - **Area: 1,62,970 sq km** (often printed 1,62,975) = **4.96%** of India; 1,60,205 sq km = area left in 2014 before the 7 mandals were added; undivided AP ~2,75,000 sq km.
[46:3:1] - **Rank by area:** **8th** in NextGen, Rocket, the AP Socio-Economic Survey and most keys (counting J&K as a State, as in 2014); strictly **7th** among today's States since J&K became a UT (31 Oct 2019) – after Rajasthan, MP, Maharashtra, UP, Gujarat, Karnataka.
[46:3:2] - Coastal Andhra ~95.47 thousand sq km; Rayalaseema ~67.29 thousand sq km.

## SUB 4 | Regions, Physiography and Rocks
[46:4:0] TABLE head: Region (2022 set of 26) | Districts
  [46:4:0.0] Uttarandhra ("Kalinga Andhra", 6) | ASR, Anakapalli, Parvathipuram Manyam, Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Srikakulam
  [46:4:0.1] Rest of Coastal Andhra (12) | Kakinada, Konaseema, East and West Godavari, Eluru, NTR, Krishna, Guntur, Palnadu, Bapatla, Prakasam, SPSR Nellore
  [46:4:0.2] Rayalaseema (8) – inland south/south-west | Kurnool, Nandyal, Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, YSR Kadapa, Annamayya, Tirupati, Chittoor
[46:4:1] - Coastal Andhra: deltas, most farm output, highest population density. Rayalaseema: Deccan plateau, drought-prone, very low density; borders TN, Karnataka, Telangana. Palnadu, Bapatla and NTR are coastal.
[46:4:2] - **Physiographic divisions:** coastal plains (~950 km long, "Rice Bowl"), Eastern Ghats hill region, western (Rayalaseema) plateau.
[46:4:3] - Western (Rayalaseema) plateau lies mostly at **150–600 m**; Mahendragiri belongs to the Eastern Ghats hill region (Srikakulam), not this plateau.
[46:4:4] - **Rayalaseema plateau** is made of **gneissic** (granite-gneiss) Archaean rock; red soils.
[46:4:5] - **Oldest rocks:** Archaean **Dharwar** rocks (>2,500 million years) of Anantapur, Chittoor, Kadapa – e.g. the schist belt round **Kuppam**.
[46:4:6] TABLE head: Landmark | Fact
  [46:4:6.0] Borra Caves | Ananthagiri hills, ASR; limestone karst; Gosthani river; found by William King, 1807
  [46:4:6.1] Belum Caves | Nandyal (earlier Kurnool); 2nd-longest cave of the subcontinent
  [46:4:6.2] Billa Surgam | Kurnool, near Betamcherla; prehistoric
  [46:4:6.3] Gandikota | YSR Kadapa – Penna gorge, "Grand Canyon of India"
[46:4:7] - AP called the **"Kohinoor of India"** (Kohinoor diamond from Kollur, Krishna valley). Firsts: first linguistic State; Asia's first rubber dam (**Janjavathi**, Nagavali tributary); first private gold mine **Jonnagiri** (Kurnool).
[46:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 01 p.13-14; Rocket AP Geography p.2, p.53-54; NextGen AP History 07 p.10 (Kohinoor, Kollur); app notes 4:46 (subs 3, 4, 6, 9)
