=== NOTES 4:47 | Andhra Pradesh – Coastline, Deltas, Hill Ranges (eastern Ghats, Nallamala, Seshachalam)
## SUB 0 | Eastern Ghats – Character, Sections, Rocks and Limits
[47:0:0] # Character
[47:0:1] - Lie between the **western side of the Coastal Plain** and the **eastern side of the Deccan Plateau** – the **major hill system of AP**; AP = eastern part of the **Deccan plateau** + a large part of the **Eastern Ghats**.
[47:0:2] - **Discontinuous, eroded, residual hills** – not a continuous range, not young fold or volcanic mountains, no snow; cut by the **Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri**; **older and lower** than the Western Ghats (the Sahyadri are the Western Ghats).
[47:0:3] - In AP the **Godavari and Krishna** split the Ghats into two sections:
[47:0:4] TABLE head: Section | Name
  [47:0:4.0] North AP | Eastern Ranges
  [47:0:4.1] South AP | Kadapa Ranges
[47:0:5] - Geologically the old residual hills form the **Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt**.
[47:0:6] - Rocks: **khondalite and charnockite** (Archaean); **khondalite hills = highest bauxite-bearing mountains** → AP's **bauxite** lies in the **Eastern Ghats** (erstwhile Visakhapatnam and East Godavari: Ananthagiri, Araku, Galikonda, Chintapalli belt).
[47:0:7] - Rivers rising in the Eastern Ghats: **Vamsadhara** (biggest), **Nagavali**, Sabari, Machkund (UPSC 2021: Nagavali and Vamsadhara – not Brahmani or Subarnarekha).
[47:0:8] # Limits beyond AP
[47:0:9] - The Eastern Ghats run from the **Mahanadi valley** (Odisha) **to the Nilgiris**, where they **join the Western Ghats**; Mahendragiri is only the northern start in AP.
[47:0:10] - Eastern Ghats hills outside AP: **Garhjat** (Odisha), **Javadi** (Vellore–Tiruvannamalai, TN), **Shevaroy** (Yercaud, **Salem, Tamil Nadu**), **Kalvarayan** (TN), Kolli Malai (TN), Biligirirangan (Karnataka). **Tirumala** hills are also Eastern Ghats.
[47:0:11] - **North → south:** **Nallamalai – Javadi – Nilgiri – Anaimalai** (UPSC 2005); Kaimur – Nallamalai – Seshachalam – Biligirirangan.
[47:0:12] - **Salher** (Maharashtra) is a **Western Ghats** peak, not Eastern Ghats.
[47:0:13] > Most asked: "discontinuous and eroded"; Eastern Ranges (north) / Kadapa Ranges (south); Mahanadi to Nilgiris.
[47:0:14] ~~ Sources: Rocket AP Geography p.19, p.21-22, p.24-25; NextGen AP Geography 02 p.1-2; NextGen Indian Geography 05 p.13-14; app notes 4:47 (sub 6)
## SUB 1 | Eastern Ghats Ranges in AP – Seshachalam, Nallamala, Velikonda, Mahendragiri
[47:1:0] TABLE head: Range (local name) | District(s) | Key feature
  [47:1:0.0] Mahendragiri (Mahendra Girulu) | Srikakulam, into Odisha | Local name of the Ghats in Srikakulam
  [47:1:0.1] Papikondalu | Godavari districts (not Krishna) | Godavari gorge; average height 915 m; Papikonda NP (WLS 1978, NP 2008)
  [47:1:0.2] Nallamala | Kurnool, Nandyal, Prakasam, Palnadu (also Telangana) | Between the Krishna and the Penna; biggest forest of AP; Srisailam; Chenchus; NSTR
  [47:1:0.3] Erramala | Kurnool–Nandyal | Water divide: Krishna (north) / Penna (south)
  [47:1:0.4] Seshachalam | YSR Kadapa and Chittoor/Tirupati | Tirumala–Tirupati hills; Red Sanders (red sandalwood) endemic – smuggled for export; Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve (2010)
  [47:1:0.5] Palakonda | YSR Kadapa–Tirupati | Southern extent
  [47:1:0.6] Velikonda (Veliconda) | SPSR Nellore–Prakasam | South-eastern AP; easternmost southern range
  [47:1:0.7] Simhachalam, Yarada | Visakhapatnam | Northern extent; coastal hills
  [47:1:0.8] Anantagiri | ASR | Source of the Gosthani; Borra Caves
[47:1:1] - **Tirupati / the Venkateswara temple** lie on the **Seshachalam** range (Eastern Ghats) – not Nallamala, Palakonda or Velikonda in the books; some keys (UPPCS 2018) give "Nallamala".
[47:1:2] - **Seshachalam = Eastern Ghats**, not the Nilgiri, Cardamom, Annamalai or Palani hills (Western Ghats).
[47:1:3] - **Long mountain pass (>300 km)** from the Seshachalam north to the Nallamala: Venkatagiri–Badvel–Porumamilla–Giddalur–Markapur; **Ganjikunta pass** links the two.
[47:1:4] - **Horsley Hills** (Annamayya, Madanapalle; ~1,265 m) = locally **Enugu Mallamma Konda (Enugula Mallamma hills)**.
[47:1:5] - Velikonda, Nallamala, Seshachalam, Palakonda are AP ranges; **Javadi, Sirumalai, Karanthamalai** are in Tamil Nadu.
[47:1:6] # Wildlife and tribes
[47:1:7] - **NSTR** (Nallamala; est. 1983, ~3,728 sq km; Telangana part = Amrabad TR) – India's largest tiger reserve; **gaur** to be moved from Central India to NSTR/Nallamala from Sep 2026.
[47:1:8] TABLE head: Tribe | Belt
  [47:1:8.0] Chenchu (PVTG) | Nallamala (ITDA Srisailam)
  [47:1:8.1] Koya, Konda Reddi | Godavari hills
  [47:1:8.2] Savara, Jatapu | Srikakulam–Vizianagaram
  [47:1:8.3] Bagata, Gadaba, Porja | Araku / ASR
[47:1:9] ~~ Sources: Rocket AP Geography p.15-16, p.21-25, p.30, p.41-42; NextGen AP Geography 02 p.1, p.6, p.12; NextGen Indian Geography 05 p.14; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 06 p.1 (Seshachalam BR 2010); app notes 4:47 (sub 7)
## SUB 2 | Coastline – Length, Rank and End Points
[47:2:0] # Length and rank (revised)
[47:2:1] - **India's coastline revised: 7,516.6 km → 11,098.81 km** (PIB, 4 Dec 2025; GIS retracing at 1:250,000 scale, not physical change).
[47:2:2] TABLE head: State | Revised coastline
  [47:2:2.0] Gujarat | 2,340.62 km (1st)
  [47:2:2.1] Tamil Nadu | 1,068.69 km (2nd)
  [47:2:2.2] Andhra Pradesh | 1,053.07 km (3rd) – Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways recalculation, 2025
[47:2:3] - **Old figure:** **974 km, 2nd longest** after Gujarat – the key in every paper before 2025.
[47:2:4] - AP is still the longest coast **on the east coast** in older questions; in the revised figures Tamil Nadu edges it.
[47:2:5] # End points and districts
[47:2:6] - AP coast runs along the Bay of Bengal (**eastern boundary**) from **Ichchapuram (Srikakulam)** in the north to **Tada** (Tirupati; earlier Nellore district) at Pulicat in the south – i.e. **Srikakulam to Nellore** in the 13-district map.
[47:2:7] - Longest district coast: **Srikakulam (~193 km)**; shortest: West Godavari (~23 km); 12 districts touch the coast (2022).
[47:2:8] - Beaches: **Yarada – Visakhapatnam**, **Manginapudi – Krishna (Machilipatnam)**, **Suryalanka – Bapatla**, **Mypadu – Nellore**.
[47:2:9] - Erosion (NCCR, Aug 2026): 38% of the east coast eroding; **Uppada (Kakinada)** worst.
[47:2:10] ~~ Sources: Rocket AP Geography p.26-27 (3rd, 1,053.07 km); NextGen AP Geography 01 p.7, p.15 (974 km, 2nd); PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.19 (7,516.6 → 11,098.81 km); app notes 4:47 (sub 1)
## SUB 3 | Highest Peaks of AP and the Eastern Ghats
[47:3:0] TABLE head: Peak | Height | Location
  [47:3:0.0] Jindhagada | 1,690 m (NextGen/Rocket; 1,681 m in NextGen Indian Geography) | Araku, ASR
  [47:3:0.1] Arma Konda (Aroma / Aroya / Sitamma Konda) | 1,680 m | Chintapalli, ASR
  [47:3:0.2] Galikonda | ~1,643 m | Northern Ghats, ASR
  [47:3:0.3] Sinkram (Sintram) Gutta | ~1,620 m | Northern Ghats
  [47:3:0.4] Deomali | ~1,672 m | Koraput, Odisha
  [47:3:0.5] Mahendragiri | 1,501 m | Ganjam/Gajapati, Odisha
  [47:3:0.6] Dolphin's Nose | 335 m | Visakhapatnam – lowest hills
[47:3:1] - **Arma Konda** is the answer most books and keys give for the **highest peak of AP / of the Eastern Ghats / of the Godavari basin**; NextGen and Rocket list **Jindhagada (1,690 m)** above it.
[47:3:2] - Maximum height of the Eastern Ghats in AP: **Chintapalli (Paderu)**. Arma Konda, Galikonda, Sinkram Gutta = **Eastern Ghats** peaks.
[47:3:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 02 p.2; Rocket AP Geography p.24, p.50; NextGen Indian Geography 05 p.13; app notes 4:47 (sub 8)
## SUB 4 | Pulicat, Kolleru and Sriharikota
[47:4:0] TABLE head: Feature | Pulicat | Kolleru
  [47:4:0.0] Type | Brackish (saltwater) lagoon – India's 2nd largest after Chilika | Freshwater lake – AP's largest
  [47:4:0.1] Place | Southern tip of AP (Tirupati; earlier Nellore), shared with Tamil Nadu; on the Coromandel Coast – not north-eastern AP | Between the Godavari and Krishna deltas (Eluru, Krishna)
  [47:4:0.2] Links | Cut off from the Bay by Sriharikota island; Buckingham Canal; Arani river | Fed by Tammileru, Budameru; drains to the sea through Upputeru
  [47:4:0.3] Birds | Greater flamingos | Painted storks, grey pelicans; Ramsar site 2002
[47:4:1] - **Sriharikota:** barrier island **near Pulicat Lake**, in **Andhra Pradesh** (Nellore district when asked, now Tirupati), partly in **Sullurpeta** and partly in **Tada** mandal; **separates Pulicat from the Bay**; SDSC-SHAR – chosen 1969, operational 1971.
[47:4:2] - Coastal bird sites: Nelapattu (Tirupati), Uppalapadu (Guntur), Coringa WLS (Kakinada, Godavari mangroves), Krishna WLS, Kondakarla Ava, Rollapadu (Nandyal, dry grassland).
[47:4:3] - Threats: aquaculture encroachment (Kolleru); ISRO launches, thermal plants, sand mining (Pulicat) – not Himalayan glacial erosion. **Uppalapadu** (Guntur): spot-billed storks/pelicans, black-headed ibises; **Rollapadu**: Great Indian Bustard, **lesser florican**; Kondakarla Ava: freshwater lake near Anakapalle.
[47:4:4] - Waddepally and Laknavaram are Telangana lakes; Sur Sagar is in Gujarat.
[47:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.3-6; NextGen AP Geography 01 p.24, p.27; Rocket AP Geography p.3, p.27, p.30-31; Rocket Indian Geography p.98-99; Wikipedia "Sriharikota" (fetched: Tirupati district, Sullurpeta and Tada mandals); app notes 4:47 (sub 5)
## SUB 5 | Coastal Plains and Deltas
[47:5:0] - **Coastal plain:** from **Mahendragiri/Srikakulam to Pulicat/Nellore**, ~950 km long, ~60 km wide (narrow in the far north and south), up to 150 m; part of the **emergent Eastern Coastal Plains**.
[47:5:1] - AP falls in the **Eastern Ghats and Coastal region** physiographic division; order east → west: coastal plains – Eastern Ghats – western plateau.
[47:5:2] TABLE head: Coast | Where
  [47:5:2.0] Northern Circars | AP coast north of the Krishna (Odisha to Krishna) – the AP coastal plain in most keys
  [47:5:2.1] Coromandel | South of the Krishna to Kanyakumari – mainly Tamil Nadu, but includes the southern AP coast
[47:5:3] - **Deltas:** **Godavari** (Konaseema; central delta ~150 km wide) and **Krishna** form the fertile alluvial **"Rice Bowl"** (Krishna–Godavari delta), on the **Eastern Coastal Plains**; the **Penna** forms a small delta in Nellore.
[47:5:4] - Yarada hills / **Dolphin's Nose** (335 m): a rocky headland with **sea cliffs** on the Visakhapatnam coast, shielding Visakhapatnam Port.
[47:5:5] - **Krishna delta:** Krishna, Guntur, Bapatla; **Godavari delta (Konaseema):** Konaseema, East/West Godavari, Kakinada – **coconut and banana**. The **Penna** meets the sea at **Utukuru (Vutukuru)**, Nellore – not at Pulicat.
[47:5:6] - **Yanam** (Puducherry, ~30 sq km) is an enclave in the Godavari delta.
[47:5:7] - Mangroves: Coringa (Godavari estuary), **Krishna WLS (Krishna estuary)**; India's 2nd largest mangrove cover is **Gujarat** (ISFR 2023), not AP.
[47:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 01 p.23-27; Rocket AP Geography p.26-27; NextGen Indian Geography 06 p.2; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.8; Rocket Indian Geography p.122 (Coromandel: Krishna delta–Kanyakumari); app notes 4:47 (subs 2-4)

[48:0:0] TABLE head: Project | River | Place / key fact
  [48:0:0.0] Sir Arthur Cotton (Dowleswaram) Barrage | Godavari | Dowleswaram, Rajamahendravaram (East Godavari bank, spans to West Godavari); anicut built 1847–1852 by Sir Arthur Cotton; feeds Eastern, Central and Western delta canals, 10.30 lakh acres; ICID World Heritage Irrigation Structure (Oct 2022)
  [48:0:0.1] Prakasam Barrage | Krishna | Vijayawada; links Krishna (now NTR) and Guntur districts; first anicut 1852–55 (idea of 1798 by Captain Buckle, revised by Best and Lake 1839–41, approved 1850 after Cotton's endorsement); present barrage 1954–57
  [48:0:0.2] Nagarjuna Sagar | Krishna | Nandikonda; on the Palnadu (AP) – Nalgonda (TS) border; masonry dam; Right Main Canal = Jawahar Canal (Guntur, Prakasam)
  [48:0:0.3] Srisailam | Krishna | Nandyal (erstwhile Kurnool) – Nagarkurnool (TS) border; masonry gravity dam; hydropower; source of Telugu Ganga, Handri-Neeva and Veligonda
  [48:0:0.4] Pulichintala | Krishna | Palnadu (erstwhile Guntur)

  [48:0:0.6] Jurala | Krishna | Telangana (Jogulamba Gadwal)

  [48:0:0.10] Kandaleru | Penna basin | Nellore; Telugu Ganga balancing reservoir – not a Godavari project

  [48:0:0.16] Brahmamsagar | Pennar basin (Telugu Ganga) | YSR Kadapa

[48:0:2] - **Sir Arthur Cotton** = **pioneer of irrigation works in South India** (Godavari and Krishna anicuts).

## SUB 1 | Basins, Rankings and Inter-state Rivers
[48:1:0] - **Count:** AP has **about 40 major, medium and minor rivers**, of which **15 are inter-state** (Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25); records also speak of **40 river basins**.
[48:1:1] - **Big three:** about **75%** of AP lies in the **Godavari, Krishna and Pennar** basins.
[48:1:2] - **Sharing:** **Krishna and Godavari** by **tribunal awards**; **Bahuda, Vamsadhara, Nagavali, Pennar, Palar, Ponniar** by **inter-state agreements**.
[48:1:3] TABLE head: Shared with | Inter-state rivers (SES Table 7.1)
  [48:1:3.0] Odisha | Bahuda, Mahendra Tanaya, Poondi minor drainages, Vamsadhara, Nagavali
  [48:1:3.1] Telangana | Budameru, Errakalava, Tammileru (Pennar never touches Telangana)
  [48:1:3.2] Karnataka | Pennar (Karnataka + AP only)
  [48:1:3.3] Tamil Nadu | Araniar, Kortaliar
  [48:1:3.4] Karnataka + Tamil Nadu | Palar, Ponniar (Palar is not an Odisha river)
  [48:1:3.5] Krishna basin | Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, AP – largest share in Karnataka
  [48:1:3.6] Godavari basin | Maharashtra, Telangana, AP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, MP, Karnataka, Puducherry (Yanam) – no Jharkhand, no Gujarat
[48:1:4] - **Longest river flowing in AP = Godavari** (1,465 km; "longest and broadest river of South India", AP's lifeline); **longest course inside AP = Penna** (536 km).
[48:1:5] - **Largest basin in AP:** keys answer **Godavari**; strictly, by area inside present AP the **Pennar** is largest (**48,276 sq km** of its 55,213 sq km) – the Godavari's AP share is only ~4.5% of 312,812 sq km, most having gone to Telangana in 2014.
[48:1:6] - **Undivided AP's Godavari basin:** **73,201 sq km** (about 23% of the basin) – a pre-2014 figure.
[48:1:7] - **Godavari = longest river of Peninsular India** and, in books and keys, the **2nd-largest basin of India after the Ganga** (~9.5–10% of India); strictly the Indian part of the **Indus** basin (321,289 sq km) is a little larger.
[48:1:8] - **Peninsular order:** basin Godavari > Krishna > Mahanadi; length **Godavari 1,465 > Krishna ~1,400 > Narmada ~1,312 > Cauvery ~800**; Penna 597 > Vamsadhara 254.
[48:1:9] - **India's basins:** **20 = 12 major** (over 20,000 sq km) **+ 8 composite**; the **Kaveri** basin has the highest water utilisation (CWC), mostly for irrigation in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
[48:1:10] - **Irrigation lifeline:** the **Krishna** is the classic answer for "major irrigation source of Maharashtra, Telangana and AP" (the Godavari also crosses all three).
[48:1:11] - **Penna districts:** Anantapur → YSR Kadapa → SPSR Nellore (**not Chittoor**).
[48:1:12] > Read the stem: "longest river flowing in AP" = Godavari; "longest course within AP" = Penna; "largest basin" = Godavari in keys.

[48:1:14] - **Godavari's national code:** **'E'** in the printed APPSC FRO 2023 key (not verified from a basin-code table).
## SUB 2 | Polavaram, Lift Schemes, Canals and River Links
[48:2:0] # Polavaram
[48:2:1] - **Site:** multipurpose **earth-cum-rockfill** dam on the **Godavari** at **Polavaram** village (erstwhile **West Godavari**, now Eluru), **42 km upstream of the Cotton Barrage**; contemplated 1941, begun 2005 (Jalayagnam).
[48:2:2] - **Name:** first planned as **Ramapada Sagar** by **Dr. K.L. Rao**.
[48:2:3] - **Status:** **National Project** under **Section 90**, AP Reorganisation Act 2014; **seven Khammam mandals** transferred to AP to facilitate it.
[48:2:4] - **Design:** gross storage **194.6 TMC** (FRL 45.72 m); **live storage ~75.2 TMC ≈ 2,130 Mm³**; **7.20 lakh acres**; **960 MW**; **80 TMC Godavari → Krishna** (the Godavari–Krishna link of the ILR, not Krishna → Godavari); 23.44 TMC for Visakhapatnam; reservoir spreads into **Odisha and Chhattisgarh**.
[48:2:5] - **Left Main Canal** → **North Coastal Andhra and Visakhapatnam** (5 TMC to Kanithi, Sep 2026); **Right Main Canal** → Krishna at Vijayawada.
[48:2:6] - **Progress:** 53.47% overall, works 77% (Dec 2024, SES); 89% (2026); to be dedicated by **March 2027**, before the **Godavari Pushkaralu 2027**.
[48:2:7] # Lift schemes and canals
[48:2:8] TABLE head: Scheme | Source → route | Serves / fact
  [48:2:8.0] Pattiseema LIS | Godavari → Polavaram Right Main Canal → Krishna above Prakasam Barrage | India's first river link (Godavari–Krishna, UPSC 2016); finished within a year → Limca Book of Records 2017; 17.52 tmc ft by 10 Aug 2026
  [48:2:8.1] Purushothapatnam LIS | Godavari → Polavaram Left Main Canal → Yeleru | Visakhapatnam, North Andhra
  [48:2:8.2] Thota Venkatachalam Pushkara LIS | Godavari | East Godavari uplands
  [48:2:8.3] Chintalapudi LIS | Godavari | West Godavari and Krishna uplands
  [48:2:8.4] Handri-Neeva | Srisailam backwaters | Kurnool, Anantapur, Kadapa, Chittoor
  [48:2:8.5] Galeru-Nagari | Krishna floodwaters | Kadapa, Chittoor, Nellore
  [48:2:8.6] Gandikota LIS | Gandikota reservoir (Penna) | water to the Pulivendula Branch Canal, Jan 2017
  [48:2:8.7] Veligonda (Poola Subbaiah) | Srisailam → twin Nallamala tunnels → Nallamala Sagar (Gundlakamma basin) | Prakasam, Nellore, Kadapa; 4.47 lakh acres; Phase-I 31 Aug 2026
  [48:2:8.8] Rayalaseema LIS | Srisailam reservoir | disputed by Telangana
  [48:2:8.9] KC (Kurnool–Cuddapah) Canal | Sunkesula on the Tungabhadra | Kurnool, Kadapa; built by the Madras Irrigation and Canal Company, 1863–1870 (some books: 1871)
[48:2:9] # Telugu Ganga
[48:2:10] - **Route:** Krishna water from **Srisailam** → **Pothireddypadu head regulator** at the start of the **Srisailam Right Main Canal** → Somasila (Penna) → **Kandaleru** → **Poondi (TN)**: a **Krishna–Pennar** link.
[48:2:11] - **Purpose:** **drinking water to Chennai (Madras)**, plus irrigation in **Kurnool, Kadapa, Nellore and Chittoor** (Rayalaseema and Nellore, not Nellore alone); 10 tmc ft for Chennai (2026).
[48:2:12] - **Partners:** conceived by **N.T. Rama Rao**; agreement of **Tamil Nadu** with the Krishna States **AP, Maharashtra, Karnataka** (**5 tmc each = 15 tmc**) – an example of **AP–Tamil Nadu** cooperation.
[48:2:13] # River links and waterway
[48:2:14] TABLE head: Link | Fact
  [48:2:14.0] Godavari–Krishna (Pattiseema) | working; called India's first river-linking initiative
  [48:2:14.1] Ken–Betwa | first national (NPP) link under implementation
  [48:2:14.2] NWDA Godavari–Cauvery | Inchampalli → Nagarjunasagar → Somasila → Grand Anicut
  [48:2:14.3] Godavari–Penna Phase-I | 73 TMC, 5-stage lift
  [48:2:14.4] Polavaram–Nallamala Sagar (earlier Banakacherla) | Godavari floodwater to Rayalaseema via Bollapalli
  [48:2:14.5] Vamsadhara–Nagavali; Nagavali–Suvarnamukhi | ~73% (target June 2027); 19.32%
[48:2:15] - **National Waterway-4:** **Kakinada – Puducherry**, on Godavari and Krishna stretches with canals (Kakinada, Eluru, Commamur, **Buckingham**); the Buckingham Canal passes through Pulicat Lake.
[48:2:16] - **Drought-free plan:** surplus Godavari water is to make AP drought free.

## SUB 3 | Origin, Length, Mouth and Other Names
[48:3:0] TABLE head: River | Origin | Length (total / in AP) | Mouth
  [48:3:0.0] Godavari | Trimbakeshwar, Nashik | 1,465 km (Water Resource Information System) / ~250 km | Gautami → Yanam; Vasishta → Antarvedi
  [48:3:0.1] Krishna | Mahabaleshwar, Western Ghats (Maharashtra) | ~1,400 km / 485 km (APPSC key; NextGen: 720 km in TS + AP) | Hamsaladeevi
  [48:3:0.2] Penna | Nandidurga (Nandi) hills – Chenna Kesava hill, Chikkaballapur, Karnataka | 597 km = 61 km Karnataka + 536 km AP | Utukuru, SPSR Nellore (Bay of Bengal)

## SUB 4 | Tributaries of AP's Rivers
[48:4:0] # Godavari
[48:4:1] - **Left bank:** Purna, **Pranhita** (largest tributary = Wainganga + Wardha + Penganga; Maharashtra–Telangana boundary, joins at Kaleshwaram in Telangana – **not an AP river**), **Indravati**, **Sabari**.
[48:4:2] - **Right bank:** Pravara, **Manjira**, Manair; **Kinnerasani** joins in the Bhadrachalam reach.
[48:4:3] - **Sabari** (Kolab), from the Sinkaram hills, Odisha, is the main tributary inside AP; its tributary **Sileru** (upper reach = Machkund) joins at the AP–Chhattisgarh–Odisha tri-junction.
[48:4:4] > UPSC 2015: of Vamsadhara, Indravati, Pranhita, Pennar, only **Indravati and Pranhita** are Godavari tributaries.
[48:4:5] # Krishna
[48:4:6] - **Right bank:** Koyna, **Panchganga**, **Ghataprabha, Malaprabha**, **Tungabhadra** – the **largest by drainage area** ("biggest and most important").
[48:4:7] - **Left bank:** **Bhima** (longest), Dindi, **Musi**, **Paleru, Munneru** – Paleru and Munneru are the Krishna tributaries inside AP.
[48:4:8] - **Tungabhadra:** joins the Krishna at **Sangameswaram (Kurnool)**; Karnataka–AP boundary for **58 km**; biggest tributary **Hagari = Vedavathi** (joins near Siruguppa).
[48:4:9] - Not Krishna tributaries: Wardha (Godavari), Chitravathi and Jayamangali (Penna).
[48:4:10] # Penna (Uttara Pinakini)
[48:4:11] TABLE head: Tributary | Fact
  [48:4:11.0] Major six | Jayamangali, Kunderu, Sagileru, Chitravati, Papagni, Cheyyeru (no Penganga, Indravati or Pranhita)
  [48:4:11.1] Cheyyeru | Bahuda + Pincha (Pancha) join at Rayavaram; joins Penna at Gundlamada (Kadapa)
  [48:4:11.2] Chitravathi | from the Nandi hills (Chikkaballapur, Karnataka); Puttaparthi on its bank; joins at Gandikota
  [48:4:11.3] Kundu (Kunderu) | rises at Uppalapadu (Kurnool); "Sorrow of Nandyal"; valley = Renadu; joins at Adinimmayapalli
  [48:4:11.4] Papagni | right bank; Nandi hills (Chikkaballapur); joins near Kamalapuram
  [48:4:11.5] Sagileru | joins near Kamalapuram
[48:4:12] # North-coastal and minor rivers
[48:4:13] TABLE head: River | Tributary / fact
  [48:4:13.0] Vamsadhara | Mahendratanaya (flows in Odisha and AP); biggest river born in the Eastern Ghats; enters AP at Pathapatnam; between the Rushikulya and Godavari basins
  [48:4:13.1] Nagavali | Janjavathi – Asia's first rubber dam
  [48:4:13.2] Swarnamukhi | Kalyani (Kalyani dam)
  [48:4:13.3] Champavathi | Eduvampula, Chitti, Pothula, Gadi Gedda
  [48:4:13.4] Tammileru | Eluru (erstwhile West Godavari) – Krishna boundary; drains into Kolleru Lake; Tammileru dam
  [48:4:13.5] Gosthani | basin on Khondalites; 3% of Visakhapatnam district
[48:4:14] > Combination trap: **Langulya** is the Nagavali itself, not a Vamsadhara tributary; Godavari – **Kinnerasani** is the right pair.
[48:4:15] ~~ Sources: Rocket AP Geography p.3-4, p.6-13; NextGen AP Geography 02 p.16-27; NextGen AP Geography 03 p.1-6; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.35-36; app notes 4:48 (sub 2-5)
## SUB 5 | Places, Deltas and Islands on the Rivers
[48:5:0] - **Godavari delta:** below Rajahmundry the river splits at **Dowleswaram** into **2** main distributaries, **Gautami** (east) and **Vasishta** (west); **7 mouths** in all (Gautami–Yanam, Vasishta–Antarvedi, Vainateya–Komarigiripatnam, Tulya and Bharadwaja–Bendamurlanka, Kausika, Atreya); 2.7 km wide at Rajahmundry.
[48:5:1] - **Konaseema** = delta between Gautami and Vasishta; **lankas** = silt islands.
[48:5:2] - **Krishna delta:** splits at **Puligadda**, 64 km below Vijayawada; **Diviseema** lies between the two branches.
[48:5:3] - **Bhavani Island:** in the **Krishna at Vijayawada**, near Prakasam Barrage – one of India's largest river islands.
[48:5:4] TABLE head: Place | River
  [48:5:4.0] Vijayawada; Amaravati; proposed cable-stayed Iconic Bridge (Amaravati–Vijayawada) | Krishna
  [48:5:4.1] Srimukhalingam | Vamsadhara
  [48:5:4.2] Srikalahasti, Tirumala | Swarnamukhi
  [48:5:4.3] Gandikota fort and canyon | Penna
  [48:5:4.4] Puttaparthi | Chitravathi
  [48:5:4.5] Pattiseema | Godavari
  [48:5:4.6] Panchavati (Nashik), Rama's exile home | Godavari
  [48:5:4.7] Visakhapatnam district | Sarada and Tandava (also Varaha, Gosthani)
  [48:5:4.8] Nandyal floods | Kundu
  [48:5:4.9] Sangameswaram (Kurnool) | Krishna–Tungabhadra confluence; Raichur Doab lies between the two
[48:5:5] - **Kolleru Lake** is fed by the **Budameru and Tammileru**, not directly by the Krishna; UPSC 2023: Jhelum–Wular ✓, Gandak meander–Kanwar ✓, Krishna–Kolleru ✗ → **only two correct**.
[48:5:6] - **Pollution (2025):** the Godavari stretch near **Rajamahendravaram** was named among India's most polluted (untreated industrial and sewage waste).
[48:5:7] - **Godavari floods, Jul–Aug 2026:** 3rd warning level crossed at **Bhadrachalam**; 5.2 lakh cusecs at Dowleswaram; ~521 tmc ft to the sea by 10 Aug 2026.
[48:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 02 p.14-19; Rocket AP Geography p.5, p.10; NextGen AP Geography 03 p.4; app notes 4:48 (sub 2, 6)
## SUB 6 | Boards, Tribunals and Disputes
[48:6:0] - **APRA 2014, Part IX (Sections 84-91):** **Apex Council** = Union **Water Resources Minister** (chair) + CMs of AP and Telangana; **s.85: GRMB HQ in Telangana, KRMB HQ in AP** (not Chittoor or New Delhi); both boards are **autonomous** bodies regulating Godavari and Krishna water for the two successor States.
[48:6:1] - **Schedule 11:** drinking water > irrigation > power.
[48:6:2] - **Srisailam water allocation** under APRA = **Krishna River Management Board**; El Niño (25 Aug 2026): KRMB committee limited Srisailam and Nagarjunasagar to **drinking water only**.
[48:6:3] - **Control after 2014:** AP – **Srisailam, Pulichintala, Prakasam Barrage**; Telangana – **Nagarjuna Sagar and Jurala** (since 3 Dec 2023 Nagarjuna Sagar dam is guarded by the **CRPF** on the Centre's orders after an AP–Telangana stand-off).
[48:6:4] TABLE head: Body / dispute | Key fact
  [48:6:4.0] Bachawat Tribunal (KWDT-I) | Krishna; award 1976; 2,060 TMC at 75% dependability; AP 811 TMC
  [48:6:4.1] Brijesh Kumar Tribunal (KWDT-II) | Krishna; report 2010, further report 2013; 2016: only AP–Telangana sharing, no fresh distribution among all four riparian States – the Telugu States' grievance
  [48:6:4.2] GWDT | Godavari award 1980
  [48:6:4.3] Babli barrage | built by Maharashtra on the Godavari upstream of Sriramsagar, cutting its inflow; SC verdict 2013
  [48:6:4.4] Vamsadhara Tribunal | AP–Odisha; final award 2017
  [48:6:4.5] Banakacherla (Polavaram–Nallamala Sagar) | AP–Telangana dispute
  [48:6:4.6] Rayalaseema LIS | diverts Srisailam water – AP–Telangana dispute
[48:6:5] - **Objections:** Telangana objects to Pattiseema, Polavaram and Banakacherla (overuse of the Krishna share; breaks APRA 2014 and GWDT 1980); **AP objects to Kaleshwaram and Palamuru-Rangareddy**.
[48:6:6] ~~ Sources: APRA 2014 s.84-85 and Eleventh Schedule (src/ap-reorganisation/apra.txt); deccanchronicle.com (CRPF at Nagarjunasagar, 2 Dec 2023); app notes 4:48 (sub 10)

=== NOTES 4:49 | Andhra Pradesh – Climate, Rainfall Regions, Cyclone Vulnerability, Drought-prone Areas
## SUB 0 | Cyclone Vulnerability and Major Cyclones of AP
[49:0:0] # Why AP is cyclone-prone
[49:0:1] - **Coastline:** **1,053.07 km**, **3rd longest** in India after **Gujarat (2,340.62 km)** and **Tamil Nadu (1,068.69 km)** (PIB, 4 Dec 2025); the old figure **974 km ("2nd")** is still quoted in older reports such as the Flood Hazard Atlas 2021.
[49:0:2] - **Flood Hazard Atlas of AP (2021, NRSC):** AP is **more vulnerable to cyclones than to other disasters**; at risk of **at least one cyclone a year** on average; **moderate to severe cyclones every 2–3 years**; **most cyclones in October and November** – all four statements true.
[49:0:3] - **Bay cyclones** form between **8° N and 14° N**; on the AP coast they come mostly in the **last week of October** and in **October–December**.
[49:0:4] - **Month with most storms crossing the AP coast** (IMD count, 1891–2012): **October (about 30 of 73)**, then November (19); most fall in the NE-monsoon season.
[49:0:5] - About **44%** of the State is vulnerable to **tropical storms** and related hazards (AP Revenue Department).
[49:0:6] - **Storm surge** can flood villages up to **10 km inland**.
[49:0:7] - **IMD Cyclone Warning Centre** at **Visakhapatnam**.
[49:0:8] # Most exposed districts and stretch
[49:0:9] TABLE head: Item | Answer
  [49:0:9.0] Most vulnerable stretch | Ongole to Machilipatnam
  [49:0:9.1] Most exposed districts (long coast, Bay proximity) | Nellore and Srikakulam
  [49:0:9.2] Cyclone- and flood-prone coastal districts | Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Nellore
  [49:0:9.3] Drought-prone, not cyclone-prone | Rayalaseema – Anantapur, Kurnool (inland)
[49:0:10] - **Regional profile:** coastal Andhra = cyclones, storm surge, floods; Godavari–Krishna deltas = river floods; **Rayalaseema = drought** (arid, low rainfall); inland plains = heat waves – so AP needs **multi-hazard** planning.
[49:0:11] # Major cyclones
[49:0:12] TABLE head: Cyclone | Year | Landfall / AP impact
  [49:0:12.0] Diviseema | 19 Nov 1977 | Krishna delta (Krishna–Guntur); about 10,000 deaths – maximum loss of life in AP
  [49:0:12.1] 1990 AP cyclone | May 1990 | about 1,000 deaths; turning point for disaster management
  [49:0:12.2] Laila | 2010 | near Bapatla
  [49:0:12.3] Phailin | Oct 2013 | Gopalpur, Odisha; north coastal AP affected (not an AP landfall)
  [49:0:12.4] Hudhud | Oct 2014 | Visakhapatnam (north coastal AP); name given by Oman – Arabic for the hoopoe, a bird named in the Quran
  [49:0:12.5] Titli | Oct 2018 | near Palasa, Srikakulam
  [49:0:12.6] Phethai | Dec 2018 | Bay of Bengal storm; landfall near Kakinada/Yanam (East Godavari)
  [49:0:12.7] Michaung | Dec 2023 | near Bapatla
  [49:0:12.8] Montha | Oct 2025 | Kakinada coast; only 15 deaths with AWARE 2.0 (RTGS), which also handled Ditwah
[49:0:13] - Distractors in Hudhud/Phethai questions: **Gaja** (2018, Tamil Nadu), **Onil** (2004, Gujarat), **Hikaa** (2019, Oman), **Nilam**, **Mahasen** (2013).
[49:0:14] - **Hudhud lesson:** APSDMA linked IMD alerts quickly to district administration = **proactive risk governance integrating early warning with preparedness**.
[49:0:15] - Warning-led models: **Phailin, Fani** (Odisha evacuations), **Hudhud** (AP).
[49:0:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 02 p.6; Rocket AP Geography p.26; PIB 4 Dec 2025 (coastline, RUNBOOK settled fact); IMD 1891–2012 landfall count (news.fullhyderabad.com via web search); app notes 4:49 (sub 2, 6, 7)
## SUB 1 | Cyclone Mitigation – NCRMP and Shelters
[49:1:0] # National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP)
[49:1:1] - **World Bank**-assisted; run by **NDMA (MHA)**, project HQ **New Delhi**; launched **2011** (Phase I).
[49:1:2] - Aims: upgrade **forecasting, tracking and warning**, build capacity in **multi-hazard risk management**, and build **multipurpose cyclone shelters** and **embankments**.
[49:1:3] - **Phase I = Andhra Pradesh and Odisha** only; built **219 multipurpose cyclone shelters (MPCS)** in AP (Odisha 316).
[49:1:4] TABLE head: NCRMP category | States
  [49:1:4.0] Category I (higher vulnerability) | Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal
  [49:1:4.1] Category II (lower vulnerability) | Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala, Goa, Puducherry, Lakshadweep, Daman & Diu, A&N
[49:1:5] # Shelters and buildings
[49:1:6] - Coastal people are best saved by **building cyclone shelters**; in normal times MPCS serve as **community centres** (and schools).
[49:1:7] - **Roof:** a **pyramidal roof** (four slopes meeting at a point) best reduces wind force; a **hip roof** firmly anchored to the walls beats a **gable** roof; flat and gable roofs fare worst.
[49:1:8] - **NDMA Cyclone Guidelines 2008:** structural – shelters, raised platforms, cattle shelters, evacuation roads, **storm-surge barriers**; nature-based – **mangroves, bio-shields**, saline embankments, sand-dune restoration.
[49:1:9] - Tools: **Doppler radars**; **SCATSAT-1** (ISRO) for cyclone tracking; GIS mapping.
[49:1:10] ~~ Sources: Rocket Disaster Management p.36, p.51 (NCRMP World Bank, HQ New Delhi); PMF Internal Security & DM 02 p.56; ncrmp.gov.in "About NCRMP" (categories, via web search); app notes 4:49 (sub 8)
## SUB 2 | Climate and Rainfall – Two Monsoons
[49:2:0] # Climate and seasons
[49:2:1] - Climate **hot and humid**; summer **March to June**, when the **moisture level is quite high** (IMD report); Rayalaseema is **semi-arid**.
[49:2:2] TABLE head: Season | Period | Note
  [49:2:2.0] Winter | January–February | 13–30 °C
  [49:2:2.1] Summer | March to mid-June | mango showers in April–May (pre-monsoon)
  [49:2:2.2] SW monsoon | mid-June to September | onset in the 2nd week of June
  [49:2:2.3] Retreating / NE monsoon | October–December | October = transition from rains to winter
[49:2:3] - Order: **Winter → Summer → SW monsoon → Retreating monsoon**.
[49:2:4] - **Coldest place:** **Lambasingi** – "Kashmir of AP" (erstwhile **Visakhapatnam**, now **Alluri Sitharama Raju** district). **Hottest:** Rentachintala (Palnadu); heat-wave belt Palnadu, Kurnool, Anantapur.
[49:2:5] # Two monsoons
[49:2:6] TABLE head: Basis | SW monsoon | NE / retreating monsoon
  [49:2:6.0] Share of AP rain | about two-thirds (IMD 1989–2018: 57%) | about one-third (≈33%)
  [49:2:6.1] Wettest months | NextGen/Rocket: July; IMD 1989–2018 means: September (146 mm) > August (143) > July (128) > June (96) | October–November
  [49:2:6.2] Key region | most of AP, esp. north coast | Nellore and southern coastal districts; Rayalaseema depends on it
[49:2:7] - **"Most of AP's rain falls in August–September"** – the exam key; by IMD means August and September are the two wettest months.
[49:2:8] - **NE-monsoon maximum district:** **Nellore** (retreating monsoon brings heavy rain to Nellore and the south coast).
[49:2:9] - Normal annual rainfall about **860 mm** (574.7 SW + 285.3 NE); river floods mainly in the **SW monsoon (Jul–Sep)**, cyclones in Oct–Dec.
[49:2:10] - India gets about **75%** of its rain from the SW monsoon; the main exception is the **Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu** (max NE-monsoon rain); the Gujarat coast gets none.
[49:2:11] - 2026 El Niño year: SW-monsoon deficit **51.2%** (1 Jun–25 Aug), all 28 districts deficient.
[49:2:12] # Rainfall regions
[49:2:13] - **IMD "Observed Rainfall Variability and Changes over Andhra Pradesh State" (2020):** least rainfall = **south-western region (Rayalaseema)** – **Anantapur** lowest (558.5 mm a year); highest SW-monsoon rain in north coastal districts.
[49:2:14] - **Heavy rainfall:** **Sileru and Sabari valleys** (140–152 cm); **highest-rainfall district Visakhapatnam**.
[49:2:15] - **Low rainfall:** **Hagari valley** (< 51 cm); **lowest-rainfall district Anantapur**.
[49:2:16] # Agro-climatic zones (6, ANGRAU)
[49:2:17] TABLE head: Zone | Districts | RARS
  [49:2:17.0] North Coastal | Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam | Anakapalle
  [49:2:17.1] Godavari | Godavari delta | Maruteru
  [49:2:17.2] Krishna | Krishna, Guntur, Prakasam parts | Lam (Guntur)
  [49:2:17.3] Southern | Nellore, Chittoor, parts of Kadapa | Tirupati
  [49:2:17.4] Scarce Rainfall | Anantapur and Kurnool (entire districts) | Nandyal
  [49:2:17.5] High Altitude and Tribal | Eastern Ghats agency | Chintapalle
[49:2:18] ~~ Sources: IMD Met Monograph "Observed Rainfall Variability and Changes over Andhra Pradesh State" (2020) p.4-7 (imdpune.gov.in andhra_final.pdf); NextGen AP Geography 02 p.6; Rocket AP Geography p.28-29, p.48, p.50; app notes 4:49 (sub 0, 1, 3)
## SUB 3 | Drought-prone Areas and Drought Management
[49:3:0] # Drought-prone Rayalaseema
[49:3:1] - Rayalaseema lies in the **rain shadow** of the Western Ghats and the Karnataka–Telangana highlands → little SW-monsoon rain → depends on the **NE monsoon**; its failure causes **chronic drought** in Rayalaseema and southern Prakasam.
[49:3:2] - **Most frequently drought-affected district: Anantapur** (lowest rainfall); greatest rural distress in **Prakasam, Anantapur, Kurnool, Kadapa**.
[49:3:3] - Interior Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, AP and Tamil Nadu are **rain-shadow** areas.
[49:3:4] - Areas under **750 mm** a year = **chronically drought prone**; meteorological drought when seasonal rain < **75%** of normal.
[49:3:5] # Drought proofing
[49:3:6] - **Watersheds in arid areas** = prevention, i.e. stopping a hazard turning into a disaster (relief and assistance are response).
[49:3:7] - A watershed project that raises groundwater but leaves **yields flat** → the community **ignored crop diversification and soil management**.
[49:3:8] - **Ralegan Siddhi** (Maharashtra, Anna Hazare) overcame water crisis with **check dams and tanks**.
[49:3:9] - Drought prevention: **check dams, desilting village tanks, farm ponds**, **artificial recharge of groundwater**; **planting Eucalyptus is not** (water-hungry).
[49:3:10] - **WDC-PMKSY 2.0**: degraded and rain-fed land via **integrated natural-resource management**.
[49:3:11] - Projects: Pre-Monsoon Dry Sowing (Kurnool, Jul 2026); 100-day water plan launched at **Yadiki (Anantapur)**, 6 Apr 2026; **Gandikota** reservoir on the **Pennar** (Telugu Ganga, YSR Kadapa).
[49:3:12] # Drought management framework
[49:3:13] - **NDMA Drought Guidelines 2010**; **Manual for Drought Management revised 2016** – **multi-indicator**; **mandatory: rainfall deviation + dry spells**; impact indicators: crop sowing, NDVI, soil moisture, hydrology.
[49:3:14] - **Crop Weather Watch Group** (**Ministry of Agriculture**) meets **weekly** in the monsoon; uses **meteorological, hydrological and agricultural** parameters – **not geological**.
[49:3:15] - Nodal ministry for drought, pest attack, hailstorm, frost: **Agriculture**.
[49:3:16] - **Swaraj Abhiyan v. Union of India (2016)**: SC ordered the drought manual updated and a **National Disaster Mitigation Fund**.
[49:3:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 02 p.6; Rocket AP Geography p.29, p.53; IMD rainfall report (2020) p.7; app notes 4:49 (sub 4, 5)
## SUB 4 | Floods and Disaster Management Institutions
[49:4:0] # Floods
[49:4:1] - **Flood season (APSDMA):** with both monsoons, **1 June–31 October** in north coastal AP, Godavari and Krishna; **south of the Krishna it extends to 31 December** – both statements true.
[49:4:2] - **Rashtriya Barh Ayog (National Flood Commission):** set up **1976**, report **1980**; flood-prone area about **40 million ha**.
[49:4:3] - **CWC** flood forecasting since **1958**; Model Flood Plain Zoning Bill **1975**; NDMA Urban Flooding guidelines **2010**.
[49:4:4] - Flood management = **State subject**; Centre helps through **FMBAP**.
[49:4:5] TABLE head: Measure | Category
  [49:4:5.0] Dams, embankments, detention basins, channel improvement | Structural (flood)
  [49:4:5.1] Forecasting, floodplain zoning, insurance | Non-structural (flood)
  [49:4:5.2] Check dams, farm ponds, irrigation | Structural (drought)
  [49:4:5.3] Afforestation | Non-structural (landslide)
  [49:4:5.4] Seismic microzonation | Non-structural (earthquake)
[49:4:6] - Drainage planning → less urban waterlogging. **City Flood Alert** (Jul 2026): **RTGS + APSDMA + IIT Gandhinagar**, first in **Vijayawada**; **48-hour** rain forecasts, **6-hour** flash-flood warnings.
[49:4:7] - Godavari Anicut (Arthur Cotton) **1847–1852**; Krishna Anicut, Bezwada **1853–54** (Charles Orr); Polavaram spillway **48** radial gates; KRMB/GRMB advise releases for flood and drought mitigation.
[49:4:8] # Institutions
[49:4:9] - **AP State Disaster Management Rules: 2007** (under DM Act 2005).
[49:4:10] - **APSDMA**: chief nodal agency, chaired by the **Chief Minister**.
[49:4:11] - **NDMA** = policy and coordination; **NDRF/SDRF** = search, rescue, relief.
[49:4:12] - **2004 tsunami**: Tamil Nadu worst affected; **INCOIS, Hyderabad** – tsunami warning centre opened **2007**.

=== NOTES 4:50 | Andhra Pradesh – Natural Vegetation and Forests; Forest Cover and Types
## SUB 0 | Forest Cover and Recorded Forest Area – ISFR Data
[50:0:0] # Recorded (notified) forest area
[50:0:1] - **Recorded Forest Area (RFA): 37,258 sq km = 22.86%** of AP – **8th in India** (ISFR 2019, 2021, 2023; AP Forest Department, May 2024). "5th" is the usual wrong option.
[50:0:2] - Legal classes: Reserved **85.8%**, Protected **13.6%**, Unclassed **0.6%**; notified forest per APSES 2024-25: 37,221.11 sq km (22.84%); revised 37,421.11 sq km (~22.96%) in 2025-26.
[50:0:3] - Land-use statistics show **36.88 lakh ha (22.63%)** of AP as forest land – the figure some keys give as "area covered by forests".
[50:0:4] # Forest cover by ISFR edition (AP)
[50:0:5] TABLE head: ISFR | Forest cover | % of AP | Change
  [50:0:5.0] 2015 | about 26,006 sq km | ~15.96% | –
  [50:0:5.1] 2017 | 28,147 sq km | 17.27% | +2,141 (most improved State)
  [50:0:5.2] 2019 | 29,137.40 sq km | 17.88% | +990.40
  [50:0:5.3] 2021 | 29,784 sq km | 18.28% | +647
  [50:0:5.4] 2023 | 30,084.96 sq km | 18.47% | +95.59 (10 districts; Vizianagaram +35.35)
[50:0:6] - **ISFR 2023:** tree cover **5,340.02 sq km**; **forest + tree cover 35,424.98 sq km = 21.74%**.
[50:0:7] - The often-quoted **38,436.58 sq km (23.59%)** is forest cover **plus 8,351.62 sq km of scrub** – scrub is not forest cover.
[50:0:8] - India (ISFR 2023): forest + tree cover **25.17%**; gain 1,445 sq km of which true forest only **156 sq km**; **Madhya Pradesh** has the maximum forest area; India **3rd** in forest-area gain 2010–2020.
[50:0:9] # Density classes
[50:0:10] TABLE head: Class | Canopy | AP ISFR 2019 (sq km) | AP ISFR 2023 (sq km)
  [50:0:10.0] Very Dense (VDF) | 70% and above | 1,994.22 | 1,995.71
  [50:0:10.1] Moderately Dense (MDF) | 40–70% | 13,938.36 (largest) | 13,725.75
  [50:0:10.2] Open (OF) | 10–40% | 13,204.82 | 14,363.50 (largest)
  [50:0:10.3] Scrub (not forest) | < 10% | 8,254.84 | 8,351.62
[50:0:11] - **Largest class:** **Moderately Dense** up to ISFR 2021 (the 2017 exam answer); **Open Forest** since ISFR 2023.
[50:0:12] # District extremes (pre-2022 districts)
[50:0:13] TABLE head: Measure | Highest | Lowest
  [50:0:13.0] Forest cover (ISFR 2019) | East Godavari – 4,994.10 sq km | Krishna
  [50:0:13.1] Notified forest area | YSR Kadapa | Krishna
  [50:0:13.2] Forest % of district area | Visakhapatnam | Krishna
  [50:0:13.3] Rainfall | Visakhapatnam | Anantapur
[50:0:14] - **Trap:** "largest area under forest" – exam keys give **East Godavari** (ISFR forest cover); NextGen gives **Kadapa** for notified forest area.
[50:0:15] # Forest fires
[50:0:16] - **2023–24 fire season: AP first in India** in forest area burnt – **5,286.76 sq km**.
[50:0:17] - 2026 fire-prone zones: **Chittoor and Annamayya** (Horsley Hills, Mallappa Konda).
[50:0:18] - Critique of drives like "Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam": they add **tree cover, not natural forest**.
[50:0:19] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.79-80 (printed p.74-75: ISFR 2023 density classes, notified forest); NextGen AP Geography 02 p.9; web search (ISFR 2017: AP +2,141 sq km); app notes 4:50 (sub 2, 3, 5)
## SUB 1 | Forest Types and Natural Vegetation
[50:1:0] # Types by rainfall
[50:1:1] TABLE head: Forest type | Rainfall | Where
  [50:1:1.0] Moist deciduous | 125–200 cm (maximum rain; India: 100–200 cm) | erstwhile Srikakulam, Visakhapatnam, agency of East Godavari; Papikonda
  [50:1:1.1] Dry deciduous (largest) | 75–100 cm | erstwhile Kadapa, Kurnool; Seshachalam–Nallamala belt
  [50:1:1.2] Short thorn | < 70 cm | Kadapa, Kurnool, Chittoor, Anantapur
  [50:1:1.3] Tidal / mangrove ("Koringa forests") | coastal | mouths of the Godavari and Krishna – Coringa, Krishna WLS; coastal alluvial belt of Krishna district
[50:1:2] - **AP forests are mainly tropical deciduous**; most of the natural vegetation is **dry deciduous**.
[50:1:3] - **Seshachalam hills = dry deciduous** (not wet evergreen, desert or mangrove); **Papikonda NP = moist deciduous**.
[50:1:4] - **ISFR 2019 forest types:** **Southern Dry Mixed Deciduous** is the largest (15,128 sq km), then Dry Deciduous Scrub (12,551); Mangroves and Littoral 418 sq km.
[50:1:5] - **Coringa:** mangrove forest where the **Godavari** meets the Bay of Bengal backwaters; tidal forests were taken up on a large scale in the **6th Five-Year Plan**.
[50:1:6] - **Biggest forest: Nallamala** (dry deciduous; Gundlakamma forest zone part of it).
[50:1:7] - **Biotic provinces:** **Deccan Plateau** is AP's largest (about 53% of forests), then Central Plateau, Eastern Highlands, East Coastal Plains.
[50:1:8] - Forest extent: north **Simhachalam hills**; south **Palakonda and Nallamala**; west **Balaghat**.
[50:1:9] # Mangroves
[50:1:10] - Godavari–Krishna estuaries: called India's **2nd-largest mangrove ecosystem** (APSES) – true only on the **east coast**; by ISFR area AP is behind West Bengal, Gujarat and A&N.
[50:1:11] - ISFR 2023: AP mangrove cover **+13.01 sq km**; **MISHTI** launched **5 June 2023**.
[50:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 02 p.9-12; Rocket AP Geography p.29, p.41-42; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.80; app notes 4:50 (sub 0, 1)
[50:1:13] - **Dry deciduous species:** teak, *Terminalia*, red sanders and *Anogeissus*; moist deciduous hills give bamboo and sandalwood.
## SUB 2 | Tree Species, Forest Produce and Plantations
[50:2:0] # Species
[50:2:1] - **Red sanders (*Pterocarpus santalinus*)**: **endemic** to AP's **Seshachalam, Palakonda and Veligonda** ranges (southern Eastern Ghats); a **dry deciduous** tree, **not** a tropical rainforest tree; **greatest economic value**; IUCN **Endangered**, WPA **Schedule IV**, **CITES Appendix II**; thermal-imaging drones against smuggling (Feb 2026).
[50:2:2] - **Axlewood** = ***Anogeissus latifolia*** (dry deciduous).
[50:2:3] - **Eucalyptus** = family **Myrtaceae**; *Cylindrocladium* causes **dieback/blight of *Eucalyptus tereticornis***.
[50:2:4] - Teak – dry deciduous; **bamboo, sandalwood** – northern Eastern Ghats moist hill forests.
[50:2:5] - **Thimmamma Marrimanu:** giant **banyan** at Kadiri (erstwhile Anantapur, now **Sri Sathya Sai** district), about 70 km from Horsley Hills; **Guinness record 1989** as the **largest banyan (canopy) in the world**; about 550 years old; canopy usually quoted as "about 5–6 acres" (Guinness: about 4.7 acres).
[50:2:6] # Revenue and agencies
[50:2:7] - **Forest produce revenue:** older AP keys name **bamboo** as the top earner; red sanders auctions have earned more in recent years. Forest revenue ₹32.81 crore (2023-24), ₹19.63 crore (2024-25 to Dec); NTFP over ₹500 crore a year.
[50:2:8] - **GCC** (HQ Visakhapatnam) buys minor forest produce; **TRIFED** (1987, Multi-State Co-op Societies Act 1984; Tribal Affairs) – MSP for MFP; **APFDC** – export agent for **red sanders and beedi leaf**; **CAMPA** – compensatory afforestation through an Annual Plan of Operation.
[50:2:9] - Wood banks: teak **Kapavaram**, red sanders **Tirupati**, bamboo Rajamahendravaram; craft wood banks (Kondapalli, Etikoppaka, Udayagiri, Bobbili …) give timber to artisans at **no profit**.
[50:2:10] # APFDC plantations (to 2024-25)
[50:2:11] TABLE head: Species | Area (ha)
  [50:2:11.0] Eucalyptus (clonal) | 33,584 – largest; APFDC is the largest Eucalyptus grower among PSUs
  [50:2:11.1] Cashew | 5,664 (coastal districts, not only agency)
  [50:2:11.2] Coffee | 4,010 – Visakhapatnam and East Godavari
  [50:2:11.3] Bamboo | 2,359
[50:2:12] - **Coffee** in AP grows mainly in the **agency areas of Visakhapatnam (Araku, Paderu, Chintapalli) and East Godavari (Maredumilli)** – not West Godavari; Srikakulam has only small patches.
[50:2:13] # Trees outside forests and programmes
[50:2:14] - **TOFI = Trees Outside Forests in India**: **MoEFCC + USAID**, launched **8 Sep 2022**; AP one of **7** States; AP Forest Department launch **Nov 2022**.
[50:2:15] - **ISFR 2019 rural TOF in AP:** **mango (*Mangifera indica*)** is the most numerous species (about 28–29%).
[50:2:16] - **Vanam-Manam**: green cover outside reserved forests – **5.29 crore** seedlings (2024-25 to Dec).
[50:2:17] - Van Adhiniyam 1980: 26,924 ha diverted to 2017-18; 2026 changes allow commercial plantations on degraded forest land (33% goal). **16th FC** counts open forests with density weights. **Rekapalli revolt (1879)** against British forest laws.
[50:2:18] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.80, p.85 (APFDC, coffee, red sanders export); NextGen AP Geography 02 p.12; Testbook solution to APPSC Group-I 2024 coffee PYQ; The Hindu via inkl (ISFR rural TOF mango ~28%, via web search); app notes 4:50 (sub 6–9)

=== NOTES 4:51 | Andhra Pradesh – National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries and Ramsar Sites
## SUB 0 | Protected-Area Network and National Parks
[51:0:0] # At a glance (APSES 2024-25)
[51:0:1] - **3 national parks, 13 wildlife sanctuaries** (13 also in 2019, Jan 2020, Dec 2021), **4 deer parks**, **2 zoological parks**; **1 tiger reserve, 1 elephant reserve, 1 biosphere reserve**.
[51:0:2] - PA network (NPs + WLSs): **8,139.88 sq km** = 4.99% of AP, 21.87% of notified forest; notified forest ~22.96% of AP (2025-26 figure).
[51:0:3] - **Zoos (2):** **Indira Gandhi Zoological Park, Visakhapatnam** and **Sri Venkateswara Zoological Park, Tirupati** (managed by ZAAP); 1st ex-situ biodiversity park – Dolphin Conservation Society, Visakhapatnam.
[51:0:4] - **Deer parks:** **Kandaleru** (Rapur mandal, **SPS Nellore**, 25 ha), Chittoor reserve forest, Kotappakonda (Palnadu).
[51:0:5] # The three national parks
[51:0:6] TABLE head: National Park | District / place | Fact
  [51:0:6.0] Sri Venkateswara NP | Tirupati–Annamayya (erstwhile Chittoor and Kadapa); Seshachalam–Tirumala hills | First NP of AP, 1989; lies inside SV WLS; indicator species slender loris, golden gecko, red sanders, *Cycas beddomei*, giant squirrel; Talakona falls
  [51:0:6.1] Papikonda NP | near Rajamahendravaram; Godavari gorge (erstwhile East & West Godavari; now Eluru, ASR) | Largest NP (1,012.90 sq km); WLS 1978 → NP 2008; Godavari flows through it; moist deciduous; kanchu mekha dwarf goat; moth *Eucyclodes gavissima* recorded
  [51:0:6.2] Rajiv Gandhi NP (Rameswaram) | Kadapa, north bank of the Penna | Smallest NP (2.30 sq km); 2005
[51:0:7] - **Papikonda after 2014:** the Khammam (Telangana) part came to AP with the Polavaram mandals, so the park is now **wholly in AP** – a "three districts incl. Khammam" statement is outdated.
[51:0:8] - Tiger "Explorer" from **Tadoba** released into Papikonda (Feb 2026).
[51:0:9] - **NP vs WLS:** no rights and **no grazing** inside an NP; boundary changed only on **National Board for Wildlife** advice.
[51:0:10] - **Not AP:** Mrugavani NP, Kasu Brahmananda Reddy NP, Eturunagaram and **Manjira WLS** (Telangana); **Chinnar WLS** (Kerala); **Bhainsrorgarh WLS** (Rajasthan); Periyar (Kerala), Gir, Bandipur, Mudumalai.
[51:0:11] ~~ Sources: Rocket AP Geography p.30-32; NextGen AP Geography 02 p.9, p.12; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.80; en.wikipedia.org Sri Venkateswara National Park (1989, golden gecko, red sanders, Cycas beddomei); app notes 4:51 (sub 0, 1, 10)
## SUB 1 | Wildlife Sanctuaries – District, Flagship and Chronology
[51:1:0] TABLE head: Sanctuary | District (now; erstwhile) | Flagship / feature
  [51:1:0.0] Coringa | Kakinada (East Godavari) | Godavari mangroves; saltwater crocodile, fishing cat
  [51:1:0.1] Krishna | Krishna–Bapatla (Machilipatnam) | pristine mangroves of the Krishna estuary
  [51:1:0.2] Kolleru | Eluru (West Godavari) | freshwater lake; pelicans
  [51:1:0.3] Rajiv Gandhi (ex-Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam WLS) | Nandyal, Prakasam, Palnadu (Kurnool–Prakasam) | largest WLS, 2,131.67 sq km; tiger; core of NSTR
  [51:1:0.4] Gundla Brahmeswaram | Nandyal, Prakasam (Kurnool & Prakasam) | Nallamala, between Krishna and Penna; tiger corridor; *Euphorbia chalamensis* (2026)
  [51:1:0.5] Rollapadu | Nandyal (Kurnool) | grassland; Great Indian Bustard, blackbuck
  [51:1:0.6] Sri Lankamalleswara | Kadapa | Jerdon's courser
  [51:1:0.7] Sri Penusila Narasimha | Kadapa, Nellore | Penusila hills

## SUB 2 | Tiger, Elephant and Biosphere Reserves
[51:2:0] # Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam Tiger Reserve (NSTR)
[51:2:1] - Nallamala hills along the **Krishna**; AP + Telangana; declared **1983**; **3,727.50 sq km** – **India's largest tiger reserve** by area and by **core/critical tiger habitat** (Manas, Pakke, Periyar are smaller).
[51:2:2] - The **Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam WLS** was renamed **Rajiv Gandhi WLS**; it is the core. AP core: Nandyal, Prakasam, Palnadu.
[51:2:3] - Srisailam circle; NTCA core-buffer model; **tigers 63** (excl. 7 cubs, APSES 2024-25; AITE 2022: 63–67); Chenchus serve as protection watchers.
[51:2:4] - AP's only tiger reserve; NSTR is **not** a biosphere reserve.
[51:2:5] # Elephant reserve
[51:2:6] - **Koundinya WLS + Rayala Elephant Reserve** (Anantapuramu circle) – **Koundinya is AP's only sanctuary with Asian elephants**; nearest city **Chittoor**.
[51:2:7] - Elephants came into **Palamaner** in the **1980s** because of **drought in the Hosur–Dharmapuri reserve forests and Bannerghatta NP**.
[51:2:8] # Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve
[51:2:9] - **AP's first and only BR**, notified **2010**; **4,755.997 sq km**; Tirupati and Kurnool circles; Seshachalam (Tirumala) hills – the area of the **Sri Venkateswara** NP and WLS.
[51:2:10] - Endemic **red sanders**; fauna incl. **slender loris**, golden gecko; 1,756 flowering plants. Not "Sri Venkateswara BR".
[51:2:11] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.80; NextGen AP Geography 02 p.12; Rocket AP Geography p.32; app notes 4:51 (sub 4, 5, 6)

  [51:4:0.4] Uppalapadu | Guntur | pelicans, painted storks

## SUB 1 | AP's Share and Rank in India
[53:1:0] - AP = **"Ratna Garbha"** – the treasure house of minerals.
[53:1:1] - **IMYB (2017 state review):** AP is the **sole producer of apatite** in India; leading producer of **barytes**, ball clay, dolomite, garnet, laterite, **limestone**, quartz, silica sand, vermiculite.
[53:1:2] - AP's share of India's **resources**: **92% barytes**, 40% calcite, **41% mica**, **31% kyanite** and garnet, 19% titanium minerals, 16% bauxite, 15% dolomite, 13% sillimanite, 12% vermiculite and limestone.
[53:1:3] TABLE head: Mineral | AP's share / rank
  [53:1:3.0] Barytes | India's top producer; ~92–93% of India's reserves; nearly one-quarter of world output; a minor mineral since 2015
  [53:1:3.1] Mica | First in India – reserves 40.5% (~41%), production 70.2%; Rajasthan 2nd; Jharkhand, Rajasthan also produce, Goa does not
  [53:1:3.2] Heavy-mineral beach sands | ~327 Mt of India's 1,078 Mt = 30.4%; AP first in monazite
  [53:1:3.3] Limestone | production: Rajasthan > MP > AP (third); largest reserves: Karnataka
  [53:1:3.4] Diamonds (NMI) | 18,22,955 carats (18.23 lakh) of India's 319.22 lakh
  [53:1:3.5] Kyanite | ~30–31% of India (NMI 2020); tin reserves are in Chhattisgarh, not AP
  [53:1:3.6] Gold (IMYB 2021, 1.4.2020) | 47.17 tonnes resources; Chigargunta–Bisanattam (Chittoor, Kolar schist belt) reports handed to AP after the MMDR Amendment 2015
  [53:1:3.7] Asbestos | AP produces chrysotile (Kadapa) but holds only a few % of reserves – Rajasthan 59%, Karnataka 36% of India's asbestos resources
[53:1:4] - Barytes production share: keys give **92%** – strictly the IMYB 92% is AP's share of **resources**; nearly all of India's barytes output comes from Mangampet.
[53:1:5] - After beach sands, **bauxite** has the largest share of AP's major-mineral resources.
[53:1:6] - **APMDC** (AP Mineral Development Corporation) incorporated **1961**.
[53:1:7] - World mica (2022): **China first**, Madagascar second.
[53:1:8] ~~ Sources: Indian Minerals Yearbook 2017, State Reviews – Andhra Pradesh p.11-1; Indian Minerals Yearbook 2021, Asbestos p.1 (ibm.gov.in); NextGen AP Geography 03 p.13; app notes 4:53
## SUB 2 | Rock Systems and Basins of AP
[53:2:0] TABLE head: System | Nature | Region | Minerals
  [53:2:0.0] Archaean | oldest; no fossils; ~2/3 gneiss | Srikakulam, parts of Eluru | iron, manganese, copper, lead, gold
  [53:2:0.1] Dharwar | metamorphosed gneiss and schists | schist belts of Nellore (mica) and Chittoor–Anantapur (gold); NextGen also lists Vizianagaram–Visakhapatnam–East Godavari | mica, gold, crude iron
  [53:2:0.2] Cuddapah (Kadapa) | Proterozoic, ~1.6 billion years; crescent basin between the arching Nallamala–Velikonda branches of the Eastern Ghats | YSR Kadapa, Nandyal, Kurnool, Prakasam | barytes, asbestos, steatite, limestone, uranium, diamonds, copper, cobalt, nickel
  [53:2:0.3] Kurnool | sandstone, shale, limestone | Kurnool region | glass sand, ornamental stone; no metallic minerals
  [53:2:0.4] Gondwana | coal-bearing | Godavari valley | coal
  [53:2:0.5] Eastern Ghats (khondalites, charnockites) | Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt | Visakhapatnam Agency | bauxite, manganese, graphite
  [53:2:0.6] Deccan Trap | Cretaceous lava through fissures; basalt | Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur | basalt; black cotton soil
  [53:2:0.7] Pleistocene / coastal | recent coastal sediments | Srikakulam to Nellore – all coastal districts | oil and natural gas (KG basin) as keyed
[53:2:1] - **Kadapa basin** = the **mineral-rich** and **largest** sedimentary basin and the **oldest basin of AP** (APPSC Group-II 2019); Nagarjuna hill and Sanganakallu are sites, not basins – Sanganakallu (Neolithic) is in Ballari, Karnataka.
[53:2:2] - **⚠ Dispute:** keys put AP's oil and gas in the "**Pleistocene**" system; strictly the KG-basin hydrocarbons lie in **Cretaceous–Tertiary marine sediments** beneath the Pleistocene coastal cover.
[53:2:3] - Dharwar items: keys give **Chittoor and Nellore** (APPSC Group-I).
[53:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 02 p.2-4 (book p.29-31); Rocket AP Geography p.54; NextGen AP Geography 01 p.19 (PYQ key: Kadapa Basin); CDI APPSC Group-2 PYQs 2000-2025 Q28 (Group-II 2019); app notes 4:53
## SUB 3 | Gold, Uranium and Beach Sands
[53:3:0] # Gold
[53:3:1] - **Swarnagiri (Jonnagiri)** – **India's first (and largest) private-sector gold mine** after Independence; **Tuggali mandal, Kurnool**; **GeoMysore Services**, **30-year lease**; ~1,000 kg a year; opened 2026.
[53:3:2] - **Ramagiri (Anantapur)** – old gold field in the Dharwar greenstone belt; gold-bearing quartz in Anantapur, Chittoor, Kurnool.
[53:3:3] - India's **oldest gold field = Kolar** (Karnataka).
[53:3:4] # Uranium
[53:3:5] - **Tummalapalle (YSR Kadapa)**, **Kadapa basin**: principal AP uranium deposit, **low-grade** ore; **2011**: huge reserves confirmed – among the world's top 20; mine and plant working since **2012**.
[53:3:6] - Jaduguda, Narwapahar = Jharkhand; **radium** is extracted from **pitchblende**.
[53:3:7] # Beach sands and rare earths
[53:3:8] - Ilmenite, rutile, zircon, garnet, **sillimanite**, **monazite → thorium**; along the coast from **Srikakulam to Nellore** (Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Prakasam); **Bhavanapadu (Srikakulam)**; monazite at Bheemunipatnam.
[53:3:9] - **Kurnool** is inland – **no beach sands**.
[53:3:10] - NGRI found rare earth elements in syenite rocks of **Anantapur** (2023); critical-mineral mapping through **APMDC** (2026).
[53:3:11] # Dimension stones and minor minerals
[53:3:12] TABLE head: Stone | District
  [53:3:12.0] Black Galaxy granite | Chimakurthy, Prakasam
  [53:3:12.1] Srikakulam Blue | Srikakulam
  [53:3:12.2] Kashmir White | Visakhapatnam
  [53:3:12.3] Pista Green | YSR Kadapa
  [53:3:12.4] Chilli Red | Anantapur
  [53:3:12.5] Slate | Markapur (Prakasam)
[53:3:13] - **MMDR Act 1957**: major minerals → **Centre**; minor minerals (building stone, gravel, clay, sand) → **States**; **mica and barytes declared minor minerals in 2015**.
[53:3:14] - Policy: beneficiation plants for **low-grade iron ore and CDW-grade barytes**; **manganese processing clusters in Vizianagaram**.
[53:3:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP Geography 03 p.7, 10 (book p.61, 64); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.115-116; app notes 4:53 (sub 4-6)

[53:4:0] - AP's oil and gas basin = **Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin**, onshore (Konaseema, Godavari delta) and offshore; **Barmer–Sanchore** is in Rajasthan.

  [53:4:1.4] HPCL Visakhapatnam | AP's main refinery

## SUB 5 | Water, Marine and Forest Resources
[53:5:0] - Rivers: Godavari, Krishna, Pennar; north – **Vamsadhara and Nagavali**.
[53:5:1] - Coastline **1,053.07 km** (revised; **third** after Gujarat and Tamil Nadu; old figure 974 km, second); continental shelf ~**33,227 sq km**.
[53:5:2] - Fishing harbours: new at **Juvvaladinne (Nellore)** and Uppada; salt hub **Naupada (Srikakulam)**; **Gujarat** leads India's salt.
[53:5:3] - Forest cover **30,084.96 sq km = 23.59%**; **red sanders** endemic to **Seshachalam–Palakonda–Lankamalla** hills; **GCC** HQ **Visakhapatnam**.

=== NOTES 4:55 | World Population - Distribution, Density, Factors and Theories (malthus)
## SUB 0 | Population Theories – Malthus, Ehrlich and Others
[55:0:0] # Malthusian theory
[55:0:1] - **Thomas Robert Malthus**, *An Essay on the Principle of Population* (**1798**): population grows in **geometric progression** (1, 2, 4, 8), food only in **arithmetic progression** (1, 2, 3, 4).
[55:0:2] - Unchecked growth outruns food and ends in **scarcity, famine, disease and war** – the classic **overpopulation** theory (APPSC: the scientist who said population is too large with severe consequences = **Malthus**, not Darwin, Ehrlich or Einstein).
[55:0:3] TABLE head: Check | Acts on | Examples
  [55:0:3.0] Preventive | Lowers births | Moral restraint, late marriage, celibacy
  [55:0:3.1] Positive | Raises deaths | Famine, disease, war
[55:0:4] - **Criticism:** food production and living standards rose faster than he predicted – **technology, innovation and sustainable resource management**; Marxists and liberals say poverty comes from unequal distribution, not numbers.
[55:0:5] # Neo-Malthusian works
[55:0:6] TABLE head: Book / report | Author | Year
  [55:0:6.0] An Essay on the Principle of Population | Thomas Malthus | 1798
  [55:0:6.1] The Population Bomb | Paul R. Ehrlich | 1968
  [55:0:6.2] The Limits to Growth (World3 computer model) | Donella Meadows and others, for the Club of Rome | 1972
  [55:0:6.3] The Population Explosion | Paul and Anne Ehrlich | 1990
[55:0:7] - **"The battle to feed all of humanity is over"** is the opening line of **The Population Bomb (1968)** – not Malthus's Essay or the 1990 sequel.
[55:0:8] - **"New Population Bomb"** = rapid **urban growth in the Third World**.
[55:0:9] # Other theories
[55:0:10] TABLE head: Theory | Thinker | Idea
  [55:0:10.0] Demographic transition | Warren Thompson (1929) first; Frank Notestein named and formalised it (1945, three stages) | Death rates fall first with development, birth rates later
  [55:0:10.1] Optimum population | Edwin Cannan | The size giving the highest output (income) per head for given resources and technology
  [55:0:10.2] Marxian (anti-Malthusian) | Karl Marx | Hunger and "surplus population" come from exploitation / capitalism, not nature
[55:0:11] > Exam angle: book–author and quote–book pairs; preventive vs positive check; geometric (population) vs arithmetic (food).
[55:0:12] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society 03 p.58 (Malthus); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 04 p.1; NextGen Indian Economy P1 04 p.23 (Thompson, Notestein), p.57 (New Population Bomb); app notes 4:55 (sub 0, 1), 4:59 (sub 3)
## SUB 1 | Distribution of World Population and Its Factors
[55:1:0] # Pattern
[55:1:1] - **90%** of the world's people live on about **10%** of its land; most live in the **Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes and the tropics of Asia**.
[55:1:2] - Crowded regions: **East Asia, South and South-east Asia, Europe, north-eastern North America**; two great clusters = **East Asia** and **South Asia**; the **Ganges–Brahmaputra delta** is among the densest areas on Earth.
[55:1:3] - Sparse: high latitudes, tropical deserts, high mountains, equatorial forests.
[55:1:4] # Factors
[55:1:5] TABLE head: Factor | Effect | Example
  [55:1:5.0] Water | River valleys densest | Nile valley
  [55:1:5.1] Landform | Plains favoured, mountains sparse | Ganga plains
  [55:1:5.2] Climate | Moderate climates attract; hot and cold deserts repel | Sahara, polar lands
  [55:1:5.3] Soil | Fertile loamy alluvium supports dense farming | Java, eastern China
  [55:1:5.4] Minerals | Mining draws workers | Katanga–Zambia copper belt
  [55:1:5.5] Industry, urbanisation | Jobs concentrate people | Kobe–Osaka
  [55:1:5.6] Social-cultural | Religious centres attract; unrest repels | Varanasi, Vatican
[55:1:6] # The odd one out
[55:1:7] - **North-eastern USA** (New York, Philadelphia, Boston, Pittsburgh) is dense because of **industry and urbanisation** – it does **not depend directly on agriculture**, unlike the lower Nile valley, Java and the eastern plains of China (MPPSC 2021).
[55:1:8] # Religion
[55:1:9] - **China** has the world's **largest Buddhist population** (about half of all Buddhists); Thailand is second, then Myanmar and Japan.
[55:1:10] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 03 p.10-11; PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.31-32; app notes 4:55 (sub 2, 3); general knowledge, not checked (Buddhist population)

[55:2:0] # Continents (UN, 2022)
[55:2:1] TABLE head: Region | Population (mn) | Density (per sq km) | World share
  [55:2:1.0] Asia | 4,017 | 146 (densest) | 59%
  [55:2:1.1] Africa | 1,152 | 43 | 17.2% (highest growth)
  [55:2:1.2] Europe | 748 | 34 | 9.7%
  [55:2:1.3] Latin America | 658 | 32 | 8.5%
  [55:2:1.4] Northern America | 368 | 20 | 4.8%
  [55:2:1.5] Oceania | 45 | 5 | 0.6%
[55:2:2] - Of South America, North America, Europe and Africa, the **lowest density is North America** (Oceania is lower still but is a separate option).
[55:2:3] # Countries
[55:2:4] TABLE head: Rank (2023) | Country | Density
  [55:2:4.0] 1 | India (1,428.6 mn, 17.76%) | 481
  [55:2:4.1] 2 | China | 152
  [55:2:4.2] 3 | United States | 37
  [55:2:4.3] 4 | Indonesia (most populous Muslim-majority country) | 153
  [55:2:4.4] 5 | Pakistan | 312
  [55:2:4.5] 6 | Nigeria | 246
  [55:2:4.6] 7 | Brazil (most populous in South America) | 26
  [55:2:4.7] 8 | Bangladesh | 1,329
[55:2:5] - **India overtook China in April 2023** (UN); until then India was **second**. India: **1.46 billion** (UNFPA SOWP 2025).
[55:2:6] - Top 10 countries hold about **60%** of people; **6 of the 10 are in Asia**; the top six hold about **half** – in 2011 China, India, USA, Indonesia, **Brazil**, Pakistan; now **Nigeria** has passed Brazil.
[55:2:7] - Pakistan is projected to pass the USA as 3rd by 2054. Asia about **59%** and Africa about **18%** of world population (2024).
[55:2:8] - Densest country: **Monaco**; sparsest sovereign country: **Mongolia** (~2 per sq km).
[55:2:9] - **Latin America:** **Puerto Rico** (small densely settled island) has the highest density among Puerto Rico, Brazil, Panama and Mexico.

=== OWN MCQs of 4:55 (56)
[na70c9b6d881] sub0
  According to Thomas Malthus, in what progression does population increase?
  *Geometrical progression, while food supply increases arithmetically | Arithmetical progression, while food supply increases geometrically | Constant proportion, while food supply remains unchanged | Linear progression, while food supply increases geometrically
  x: Malthus argued that population tends to grow geometrically or exponentially, whereas food and resources increase only arithmetically.
[n8e3f7330b68] sub0
  Which one of the following is a preventive check in Malthusian population theory?
  Epidemic disease | Famine | *Late marriage | War
  x: Preventive checks reduce the birth rate and include moral restraint, late marriage and celibacy. Famine, disease and war are positive checks because they increase mortality.
[n65353cea984] sub0
  Which one of the following is a major criticism of the Malthusian prediction?
  Population has declined continuously because of famine | *Technology, innovation and sustainable resource management have exceeded his predictions | Industrialisation eliminated all regional differences in population distribution | Food production has remained completely static since the eighteenth century
  x: Technological progress, innovation and sustainable resource management have enabled resources and food production to grow faster than Malthus anticipated.
[f12c909c82be1] sub0

  x: Thomas Malthus (1798) held that population grows geometrically and food arithmetically, so overpopulation brings famine.

=== NOTES 4:57 | India - Population Distribution and Density; State-wise and District-wise Patterns
## SUB 0 | Population Density – Measures and Census 2011 Pattern
[57:0:0] # Measures
[57:0:1] TABLE head: Measure | Formula
  [57:0:1.0] Arithmetic (crude) density | Total population ÷ total area (persons per sq km)
  [57:0:1.1] Physiological density | Total population ÷ net cultivated (arable) area
  [57:0:1.2] Agricultural density | Agricultural population ÷ net cultivable area
[57:0:2] - Physiological density is the **better index** of pressure on land because it uses arable land, while arithmetic density uses total area – so in the CDS 2009 A–R both are true and **R explains A**.
[57:0:3] - Density **rises** with natality and immigration; **falls** with mortality and emigration.
[57:0:4] # India
[57:0:5] - **117 (1951) → 382 per sq km (2011)**; 325 in 2001. India is among the densest large countries (only Bangladesh and Japan higher among big ones).
[57:0:6] # Census 2011 density (per sq km)
[57:0:7] TABLE head: Unit | Density
  [57:0:7.0] NCT of Delhi (highest overall) | 11,297 (11,320 final)
  [57:0:7.1] Chandigarh | 9,252
  [57:0:7.2] Puducherry | 2,598
  [57:0:7.3] Bihar (highest State) | 1,102 (1,106 final)
  [57:0:7.4] West Bengal | 1,029
  [57:0:7.5] Kerala (highest in the South) | 859–860
  [57:0:7.6] Uttar Pradesh | 828
  [57:0:7.7] Tamil Nadu | 555
  [57:0:7.8] Karnataka | 319
  [57:0:7.9] Undivided Andhra Pradesh / residual AP | 308 / 304
  [57:0:7.10] Himachal Pradesh | 123
  [57:0:7.11] Sikkim | 86
  [57:0:7.12] Mizoram | 52
  [57:0:7.13] Andaman and Nicobar | 46
  [57:0:7.14] Arunachal Pradesh (lowest; 2001 and 2011) | 17
[57:0:8] - **Ascending:** Arunachal (17) < Mizoram (52) < Sikkim (86) < Himachal Pradesh (123); of Sikkim, Nagaland (119), Manipur (122) and Mizoram, the lowest is **Mizoram**.
[57:0:9] - **Lowest density State = Arunachal Pradesh**, not Sikkim – so "Sikkim has the lowest density among States" is the **wrong** statement.
[57:0:10] - **Census 2001:** highest density State = **West Bengal (904)**, ahead of Bihar (880).
[57:0:11] - Southern States: undivided AP had the lowest density, Kerala the highest.
[57:0:12] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.45-47 (State table, 117→382, measures); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 03 p.12-14; NextGen Indian Geography 15 p.16 (Bihar 1,106, Delhi 11,320, Arunachal 17); Economic Survey 2001-02 Table 9.2 (indiabudget.gov.in, 2001 densities)
## SUB 1 | Population Size of States – Census 2011 and 2001 Ranking
[57:1:0] TABLE head: Rank (2011) | State | Population / share
  [57:1:0.0] 1 | Uttar Pradesh | 19.96 crore, 16.49%
  [57:1:0.1] 2 | Maharashtra | 11.24 crore, 9.29%
  [57:1:0.2] 3 | Bihar (12th in area) | 10.38 crore, 8.58%
  [57:1:0.3] 4 | West Bengal | 7.55%
  [57:1:0.4] 5 | Undivided Andhra Pradesh | 7.00%
  [57:1:0.5] 6 / 7 / 8 / 9 | Madhya Pradesh 7.26 cr / Tamil Nadu / Rajasthan / Karnataka 6.11 cr | 6.00 / 5.96 / 5.67 / 5.05%
[57:1:1] - **Census 2001:** UP 1st, **Maharashtra 2nd, Bihar 3rd** (same order).
[57:1:2] - **Residual AP** (4.95 crore, 4.09–4.10%) is the **10th** most populous State; **7th** by area (1,62,970 sq km).
[57:1:3] - Comparisons asked: Karnataka < MP < Bihar < Maharashtra; **Punjab** (2.77 cr) < Odisha < MP < Maharashtra; **Jammu and Kashmir** (1.25 cr) < Haryana < Gujarat < Rajasthan.
[57:1:4] - **Small States:** Sikkim 6.08 lakh (least populous State) < Mizoram 10.9 lakh < Arunachal 13.8 lakh < Goa 14.6 lakh < Nagaland < **Meghalaya 29.6 lakh** – so Meghalaya is the most populous of Goa, Mizoram, Meghalaya and Sikkim.
[57:1:5] - **Least populous units:** **Lakshadweep (64,429)**, Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Sikkim, Chandigarh; Lakshadweep was also the least populous UT in **2001**.
[57:1:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.45-46; NextGen Indian Geography 15 p.8, p.14; NextGen AP Geography 01 p.8 (AP 10th, 4.10%); app notes 4:57 (sub 5)
## SUB 2 | Area of States, UTs and Districts
[57:2:0] TABLE head: Feature | Answer
  [57:2:0.0] India's share of world area | 2.4% (32.87 lakh sq km)
  [57:2:0.1] Largest State by area | Rajasthan (capital Jaipur)
  [57:2:0.2] Smallest State by area | Goa (3,702 sq km)
  [57:2:0.3] Smallest UT by area | Lakshadweep (about 32 sq km)
  [57:2:0.4] Largest district by area | Kutch, Gujarat (45,674 sq km)
  [57:2:0.5] Smallest district by area | Mahe (about 9 sq km) – a Puducherry district enclaved in Kerala
  [57:2:0.6] State with most districts | Uttar Pradesh (75)
  [57:2:0.7] State bordering the most States | Uttar Pradesh (8 States + Delhi)
[57:2:1] - **Descending area:** Chhattisgarh (1.35 lakh) > Jharkhand (79,716) > Himachal Pradesh (55,673) > Uttarakhand (53,483) sq km; Uttarakhand is far smaller than UP, MP and Rajasthan.
[57:2:2] - Big but thinly peopled: Rajasthan (largest, only 5.5% of people), J&K, Arunachal, Uttarakhand.
[57:2:3] > Dispute: Kutch is the usual answer for the largest district; Leh's official area including territory under foreign occupation is larger, but Census 2011 gave Leh 45,110 sq km.
[57:2:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Geography p.102 (Kutch, Rajasthan), p.104 (Goa, Lakshadweep, Mahe, Sikkim); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 03 p.10-11; app notes 4:57 (sub 5); general knowledge, not checked (areas of Goa, Lakshadweep, Mahe; UP borders and districts; Leh)
## SUB 3 | Factors, Regions of High Density and BIMARU
[57:3:0] # Factors
[57:3:1] TABLE head: Factor | Dense | Sparse
  [57:3:1.0] Water | River valleys | Thar desert (lack of water)
  [57:3:1.1] Soil | Loamy alluvium | Thin, rocky soils
  [57:3:1.2] Relief | Plains | Hills, mountains (except valleys like Kashmir, parts of Himachal)
[57:3:2] # High-density regions
[57:3:3] - **Ganga plain and Ganges–Brahmaputra delta**; **Godavari–Krishna deltas** (intensive **rice farming**); Kerala coast.
[57:3:4] - **Dhanbad** is the densest district of the **Chotanagpur plateau** because of the **development of mining industries and industrialisation** (coal; BCCL); its red soil is poor for farming, and mere availability of minerals is not the reason (UPPSC 2007).
[57:3:5] - Growing **population pressure** hinders government efforts to improve the quality of life (APPSC Group II 2011).
[57:3:6] # Population–resource regions
[57:3:7] TABLE head: Type | Meaning
  [57:3:7.0] Progressive | Resource-developed: Ganga–Yamuna Doab, Tamil Nadu
  [57:3:7.1] Problem | Population pressure on limited or degraded resources
  [57:3:7.2] Deficit | Resources exceed their use
[57:3:8] # BIMARU
[57:3:9] - **BI**har, **MA**dhya Pradesh, **R**ajasthan, **U**ttar Pradesh ("bimar" = sick); coined by demographer **Ashish Bose** in **1986** (not Odisha).
[57:3:10] - High growth and weak indicators; their faster growth than the southern States feeds the **delimitation debate**.
[57:3:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.32 (factors); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 03 p.11-14; app notes 4:57 (sub 1, 2, 3, 4); general knowledge, not checked (Ashish Bose 1986)
## SUB 4 | Census Town Criteria
[57:4:0] - A **Census Town** needs population **at least 5,000**, density **at least 400 per sq km**, and **at least 75% of male workers** in non-farm work – unchanged since **1981**.
[57:4:1] - 17 Sep 2026: MoHUA told a parliamentary panel the criteria are outdated; the **RGI keeps them for Census 2027**.
[57:4:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.80; app notes 4:57 (sub 6), 4:58 (sub 1)
