=== NOTES 4:61 | India - Literacy: Levels, Gender and Regional Gaps, Trends
## SUB 0 | Education Policy and School Schemes
[61:0:0] # Policies
[61:0:1] - **NPE 1986** launched **Operation Blackboard (1987)** – at least **two rooms and two teachers**, teaching aids, for primary schools; also stressed ST education. **Ramamurti Committee (1990)** reviewed NPE; NPE **revised 1992** (Programme of Action) gave more weight to tribal education.
[61:0:2] - **NEP 2020:** replaced NPE 1986 after **34 years**; **5+3+3+4** – Foundational **3-8**, Preparatory 8-11, Middle 11-14, Secondary 14-18.
[61:0:3] - NEP targets: **100% school GER by 2030**; **50% higher-education GER by 2035**; **100% youth and adult literacy by 2030**.
[61:0:4] - **NIPUN Bharat:** foundational literacy by **Grade 3**; deadline moved to **2026-27**.
[61:0:5] # Schemes
[61:0:6] TABLE head: Scheme | Fact
  [61:0:6.0] Samagra Shiksha (2018) | Subsumes SSA, RMSA, Teacher Education
  [61:0:6.1] Unnat Bharat Abhiyan | Higher education – institutions adopt villages
  [61:0:6.2] SEMIS | Secondary Education MIS – nodal agency NUEPA, New Delhi
  [61:0:6.3] Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu (AP) | 14 Nov 2019; English labs (not Operation Blackboard)
[61:0:7] # Learning and enrolment data
[61:0:8] - **FLN Index** (Institute for Competitiveness for **EAC-PM**): 2nd edition – **Punjab** highest (64.19) among **small States**; Jharkhand was **not** the lowest small State in the web summaries. 2021 edition – West Bengal top among large States.
[61:0:9] - **AISHE 2023-24:** GER about **30**, female GER **31.2**, GPI **1.08**; female GER 28.5 → **30.2** (2021-23), above male; gender parity at all school levels.
[61:0:10] - **UDISE+ 2024-25** dropout: preparatory **2.3%**, middle **3.5%**, secondary **8.2%** (from 3.7, 5.2, **10.9**).
[61:0:11] - NFHS-5: women with **10+ years** of schooling **41%** (NFHS-4 35.7%).
[61:0:12] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:61 (sub 8, 9); web search summary of the FLN 2nd-edition report (competitiveness.in, Morung Express); SEMIS, Unnat Bharat Abhiyan, NPE 1992: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 1 | Andhra Pradesh – Literacy
[61:1:0] # Census 2011 – two series
[61:1:1] TABLE head: AP series | Total | Male | Female
  [61:1:1.0] Undivided AP (final) | 67.02% | 74.88% | 59.15%
  [61:1:1.1] Undivided AP (provisional) | 67.66% | 75.56% | 59.74%
  [61:1:1.2] Residual AP (13 districts) | 67.35% | 74.77% | 59.96%
  [61:1:1.3] India (final) | 72.98% | 80.88% | 64.63%
[61:1:2] - AP stays **below** the national average.
[61:1:3] - Residual AP trend: **29.94% (1981) → 45.86% (1991) → 62.07% (2001) → 67.35% (2011)**; 2001 male 71.28%, female 52.72%.
[61:1:4] - Undivided AP 1991-2001: female literacy rose about **18.45 points** (32.72% → 51.17% provisional 2001; final 50.43%); **rural females** gained **20.44 points**, the largest gain of any group.
[61:1:5] # Surveys
[61:1:6] - **NSS 75th round (2017-18):** AP **lowest State, 66.4%** (male 73.4%, female **59.5%**).
[61:1:7] - **PLFS:** 69.1% (2018-19) → **72.60% (2023-24)** → **71.40% (2025**, published 2 Jul 2026).
[61:1:8] # Districts
[61:1:9] TABLE head: District map | Highest | Lowest
  [61:1:9.0] 28 districts (2011 data recast) | Visakhapatnam 79.05% | Alluri Sitarama Raju 44.67%
  [61:1:9.1] 13 districts (Census 2011) | West Godavari 74.6% | Vizianagaram 58.9%
[61:1:10] - Female literacy **above** All-India (64.63%): **West Godavari, Krishna, East Godavari**. Literacy gap widest in tribal **ASR district**.
[61:1:11] # AP drives
[61:1:12] - **ULLAS in AP:** 41,500 SHG volunteers from **5 Nov 2024**; target-oriented drive for districts **below the State average**.
[61:1:13] - **Akshara Andhra (2025):** **100% literacy** drive for about **25 lakh** illiterate adults; universal literacy by **2027**.
[61:1:14] - **Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu:** launched **14 Nov 2019** – **nine** facilities (toilets, drinking water, furniture, paint, repairs, lights and fans, green chalkboards, **English labs**, compound walls).
[61:1:15] > Exam angle: 59.15% = undivided AP female (final); 59.96% = residual AP female; 67.02% = undivided total; 74.88% = undivided male.
[61:1:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 15 p.6 (book p.202: residual AP 67.35 / 74.77 / 59.96, India 72.98 / 80.88 / 64.63); web search summary of NSS 75th round reports (onmanorama, Drishti, 8 Sep 2020); app notes 4:61 (sub 5, 8); undivided-AP figures and the 1991-2001 gains: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 2 | Adult Literacy Programmes and Literacy Days
[61:2:0] TABLE head: Programme | Year | Note
  [61:2:0.0] Farmers' Functional Literacy Programme | 1967-68 | Early adult education
  [61:2:0.1] NAEP | 2 Oct 1978 | Age 15-35
  [61:2:0.2] National Literacy Mission | 5 May 1988 | Total Literacy Campaign = its main mass-campaign strategy
  [61:2:0.3] Total Literacy Campaign | 1989-90 | Ernakulam – first totally literate district (1990); Kottayam – first fully literate town (1989)
  [61:2:0.4] Saakshar Bharat | 8 Sep 2009 (International Literacy Day) | Adults 15+, focus on women; Centre : State 75 : 25 (NE 90 : 10); planned up to March 2012, extended to 31 March 2018, then wound up
  [61:2:0.5] ULLAS (Nav Bharat Saaksharta Karyakram / New India Literacy Programme) | 2022 | FY 2022-23 to 2026-27; Ministry of Education; non-literates 15+
[61:2:1] - ULLAS = **Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society**; five components – FLN, critical life skills, basic education, vocational skills, continuing education.
[61:2:2] - Fully literate (ULLAS): **Ladakh** (first UT, 2024) → **Mizoram** (first State, 2025) → Goa, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim → **Uttarakhand 6th (Jul 2026)**.
[61:2:3] - **Velland (Kerala)** is the exam answer for India's first fully **computer-literate panchayat**; Chamravattom (Malappuram) was declared the first 100% computer-literate village (2003).
[61:2:4] - **International Literacy Day: 8 September** (UNESCO, declared 1966, first observed 1967). **2017 theme: "Literacy in a digital world"**; 2026: "Literacy for people, the planet and prosperity".
[61:2:5] - **Information literacy:** the skill of defining, locating, accessing and using information.
[61:2:6] > NAEP = 15-35; Saakshar Bharat and ULLAS = 15+.
[61:2:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:61 (sub 6, 7, 9); web search summary of Saakshar Bharat parliamentary replies (extension to 31.03.2018); web search summary on Chamravattom / Vellanad (Wikipedia, The Hindu)
## SUB 3 | Census 2011 – India, Gender Gap and States
[61:3:0] # Definition
[61:3:1] - **Literate** = aged **7 and above**, can **both read and write with understanding** in any language; reading only = **not literate**.
[61:3:2] - Censuses 1951-1971 used age **5+**; **7+ from 1981**. PLFS uses the same 7+ definition but a **sample** – not directly comparable.
[61:3:3] - Full literacy (ULLAS) = **95%+** among persons aged **15+**. **Census 2027** adds a **digital literacy** question.
[61:3:4] # National figures
[61:3:5] TABLE head: Census | 1951 | 1961 | 1971 | 1981 | 1991 | 2001 | 2011
  [61:3:5.0] Literacy % | 18.33 | 28.30 | 34.45 | 43.57 | 52.21 | 64.83 | 74.04
[61:3:6] # Census 2011 – provisional vs final
[61:3:7] TABLE head: India 2011 | Total | Male | Female
  [61:3:7.0] Provisional | 74.04% | 82.14% | 65.46%
  [61:3:7.1] Final | 73.0% (72.98%) | 80.9% (80.88%) | 64.6% (64.63%)
[61:3:8] - **Largest decadal gain: 1990s**. Males about 27% → 82% in 60 years; women from less than 1 in 10 (1951) to 2 in 3.
[61:3:9] - **Gender gap 2011:** about **16-17 points** (82.14 − 65.46 = 16.68 provisional); widest in **Rajasthan (about 28 points)**; under **5 points** in **Meghalaya** (about 76 vs 73).
[61:3:10] - Rural / urban (provisional): **68.9% / 85.0%**; largest deficit: **rural women**. Causes of the gap: distance and safety, early marriage, dowry, son preference, poverty.
[61:3:11] - SC literacy **66.1%**, ST **59.0%**; low literacy is one of the **four PVTG criteria**.
[61:3:12] # States
[61:3:13] TABLE head: Measure | Highest | Lowest
  [61:3:13.0] Total | Kerala 94.0% > Lakshadweep 91.8% > Mizoram 91.3% | Bihar 61.8%
  [61:3:13.1] Female | Kerala 92.1% | Bihar 51.5% (final); Rajasthan 52.7% (provisional)
  [61:3:13.2] AP / MP / Uttarakhand / UP (final) | Uttarakhand 78.8% is highest of the four | AP 67.02%, UP 67.7%, MP 69.3%
[61:3:14] > Lowest female literacy: Bihar in the final data, Rajasthan in the provisional data – keys use both.
[61:3:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 15 p.16 (book p.212: 74.04%, Kerala highest, Bihar lowest, Rajasthan gap 28, national gap 16); app notes 4:61 (sub 0-3); Meghalaya figures: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 4 | Surveys Beyond the Census – NSS 75th Round and PLFS
[61:4:0] TABLE head: Survey | India | Ranking
  [61:4:0.0] NSS 75th round (Jul 2017-Jun 2018, NSO) | 77.7% | Kerala top (96.2%); AP lowest (66.4%), then Rajasthan 69.7%, Bihar 70.9%
  [61:4:0.1] PLFS 2023-24 (7+) | 80.9% (M 87.2, F 74.6; gap 12.6 points) | Top: Mizoram, Lakshadweep, Nagaland; bottom: AP, Bihar, MP
[61:4:1] - NSS 75th: lowest **female** literacy **Rajasthan 57.6%** (male 80.8% – widest gap); **AP female 59.5%**, AP male **73.4%** – the lowest male figure in the reported data, not Rajasthan.
[61:4:2] - PLFS 2023-24 rural / urban: **77.5% / 88.9%**.
[61:4:3] - "UP has the lowest female literacy" is **wrong** in every series (APPSC 2022 FRO: the keyed "NOT correct" statement).
[61:4:4] > Lowest State: Bihar (Census 2011) vs AP (NSS 2017-18, PLFS 2023-24).

=== NOTES 4:66 | Racial Groups of India – Risley and Guha Classifications
## SUB 0 | World Races and Physical Traits
[66:0:0] # Three (four) major races
[66:0:1] TABLE head: Race | Main distribution | Notes
  [66:0:1.0] Caucasoid | Europe, North Africa, Middle East, parts of Central and South Asia | Europeans, Arabs, Persians, many North Indians; Nordic, Alpine, Mediterranean sub-types
  [66:0:1.1] Mongoloid | China, Japan, Korea, Mongolia, SE Asia, Arctic (Inuit/Eskimo), Native Americans | North-East India (hill and forest tribes)
  [66:0:1.2] Negroid | Sub-Saharan Africa; Pygmies (Congo Basin), Bushmen (Kalahari), Bantu, Zulu, Maasai | Negrito sub-race in the Andamans
  [66:0:1.3] Australoid | Australian Aborigines, Melanesians | Proto-Australoid tribes of central and south India
[66:0:2] - **Largest group:** exam keys say **Caucasoid** (Europe + West and South Asia counted together); NextGen notes call the **Mongoloid** the most populous – the count depends on how South Asians are classed.
[66:0:3] - **Native Americans** of North America = **Mongoloid** stock; their name = **Amerinds** (American Indians). **Mestizo** = European-Amerind mix; Mulatto = European-African; Zambo = Amerindian-African.
[66:0:4] - Humans share **over 99%** of genes; race is subjective – all belong to *Homo sapiens*.
[66:0:5] # Criteria of classification
[66:0:6] - Criteria: **skin, eye and hair** (colour, form), **face, nose**, stature, head form – **cephalic, nasal, stature indices**; blood groups – **not the ear**.
[66:0:7] - **Cephalic index** = maximum breadth ÷ maximum length × 100.
[66:0:8] TABLE head: Index | Value | Type
  [66:0:8.0] Cephalic | 82+ / 77–81.99 / 76.99 and below | Brachy (round) / Meso / Dolicho (long)
  [66:0:8.1] Nasal | 85+ / 70–84.9 / below 70 | Platyrrhine (broad) / Mesorrhine / Leptorrhine
  [66:0:8.2] Stature (Topinard) | 170 cm+ / under 160 cm | Tall / small
  [66:0:8.3] Hair | leio / cymo / ulotrichi | Straight (Mongoloid) / wavy (Caucasoid) / woolly (Negroid)
  [66:0:8.4] Type | Diagnostic traits | 
  [66:0:8.5] Mongoloid | Yellowish complexion, oblique eyes (epicanthic fold), high cheek bones, sparse hair, flat face | 
  [66:0:8.6] Negrito | Dark skin, woolly/frizzy hair, short stature, broad flat nose | 
  [66:0:8.7] Proto-Australoid | Dark skin, wavy hair, long head, depressed nasal root | 
  [66:0:8.8] Dravidian (Risley) | Long head, broad nose, dark skin | 
  [66:0:8.9] Caucasoid / Negroid | High bridge, narrow nose / low bridge, broad nose | 
[66:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 13 p.9-12 (pp.177-180); NextGen Indian Geography 14 p.1-4 (pp.183-186); Rocket World Geography #27 p.44; app notes 4:66 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Racial Stock of Indian Tribes
[66:1:0] - **Andaman tribes** (Onge, Jarawa, Great Andamanese, Sentinelese) = **Negrito**, a branch of the **Negroid** race (UPSC 1997; "aborigine tribes of Andaman" → Negroid); traces among Kadar, Irula.
[66:1:1] - **Nicobar Shompen = Mongoloid**, like the Nicobarese.
[66:1:2] - **North-East hills and forests** = **Mongoloid** (Naga = Indo-Mongoloid).
[66:1:3] - **Proto-Australoid** = central and south Indian tribes – **Santhal**, Munda, Oraon, Ho, Bhil, Chenchu, Yeruva (Khasi and Tharu are Mongoloid).
[66:1:4] - **AP**: **Chenchus (Nallamala) = Proto-Australoid**; AP plains = mainly **Mediterranean**, Dravidian-speaking.
[66:1:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.28-29; NextGen Indian Geography 14 p.12-13 (Naga); Rocket World Geography #27 p.44; app notes 4:66 sub 4
## SUB 2 | Risley Classification – 7 Types (1901 Census)
[66:2:0] - **H.H. Risley**: Census Commissioner, **1901**, ran its ethnographic survey and divided Indians into **seven** racial types; **The People of India (1908)**.
[66:2:1] - Basis: **nasal index**; dictum: caste status varies inversely with nasal index – **racial theory of caste**, rejected.
[66:2:2] TABLE head: Type | Region
  [66:2:2.0] Turko-Iranian | Baluchistan, NWFP
  [66:2:2.1] Indo-Aryan | Punjab, Rajasthan, Kashmir
  [66:2:2.2] Scytho-Dravidian | Western India – Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Coorg
  [66:2:2.3] Aryo-Dravidian | Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, parts of Rajasthan
  [66:2:2.4] Mongolo-Dravidian | Lower Bengal, Odisha
  [66:2:2.5] Mongoloid | Himalaya, Assam, north-east
  [66:2:2.6] Dravidian | South India, Chota Nagpur, central India (Paniyan, Santals)
[66:2:3] - "Dravidian" properly names a **language family** (Indo-Aryan + Dravidian = main groups).
[66:2:4] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Society 01 p.1 (1901 Census, Risley); app notes 4:66 sub 2
## SUB 3 | B.S. Guha Classification – 6 Groups (1931 Census)
[66:3:0] - **1931 Census** data: **6 groups, 9 sub-types**; most cited.
[66:3:1] TABLE head: Group | Region / peoples
  [66:3:1.0] Negrito | Andaman – Onge, Jarawa, Great Andamanese, Sentinelese; traces Kadar, Irula
  [66:3:1.1] Proto-Australoid | Central and south tribes – Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Ho, Bhil, Chenchu, Yeruva
  [66:3:1.2] Mongoloid | Palaeo-Mongoloid (Sema Nagas, Lepchas) + Tibeto-Mongoloid (Tibetans of Sikkim); Shompen
  [66:3:1.3] Mediterranean | Palaeo-Mediterranean (Dravidian south) + Mediterranean (Punjab, Ganga plain) + Oriental (Punjab, Rajasthan)
  [66:3:1.4] Western Brachycephals | Alpinoid, Dinaric, Armenoid (Parsis)
  [66:3:1.5] Nordic | North-West Frontier, Punjab, Rajasthan
[66:3:2] - Only Guha lists Negrito and Proto-Australoid separately.
[66:3:3] - **Western Brachycephals – regions:** Alpinoid and Dinaric types are found in Gujarat, Bengal, Odisha and Coorg; the Armenoid type in the Parsis.

## SUB 4 | Anthropological Survey of India and Modern Criticism
[66:4:0] - **AnSI**: founded **1945 at Varanasi**, moved to **Kolkata (HQ) 1948**; first Director **B.S. Guha**.
[66:4:1] - **People of India project (1985)**: **K.S. Singh**, about **4,635 communities**; the book *The People of India* (1908) = Risley.
[66:4:2] - AnSI classified **268** DNT communities for NITI Aayog.
[66:4:3] - **2009** genetics: Indians = mix of **Ancestral North Indians (ANI)** + **Ancestral South Indians (ASI)**; Rakhigarhi DNA – no **Steppe Pastoralist** gene.
[66:4:4] - **Criticism of old schemes:** Risley and Guha relied on visible physical traits and colonial ethnography; modern genetics shows rigid racial categories are not scientific.
[66:4:5] - India ratified **ICERD 1968**; UN CERD review first since **2007**.
[66:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 14 p.1 (99% shared genes); app notes 4:66 sub 6

  Which of the following correctly represents the cephalic index?

  x: Cephalic index is calculated as (maximum breadth / maximum length) × 100.
[n6c50dfedb7d] sub0
  A person has a nasal index of 86. Under the stated classification, this person would belong to which nasal category?
  Dolichocephalic | Mesorrhine | Leptorrhine | *Platyrrhine
  x: Platyrrhine refers to a broad nose with a nasal index of 85 or above. Leptorrhine is below 70 and mesorrhine is 70–84.9.
[n5390ef01deb] sub0
  The cephalic index of a living person is 83. What is this head type under the standard classification?
  Dolichocephalic | Mesocephalic | *Brachycephalic | Platyrrhine
  x: For a living head, a cephalic index of 82 and above is brachycephalic (round-headed), 77-81.99 is mesocephalic and 76.99 and below is dolichocephalic (long-headed), so 83 is brachycephalic. Platyrrhine is a nasal-index class (85 and above), not a head type.
[naab781ce5ba] sub0

  x: Straight, coarse hair, termed leiotrichi, is associated with the Mongoloid group. Woolly or frizzy hair, termed ulotrichi, is associated with the Negroid group.

## SUB 1 | Metropolitan Cities, Megacities and Urban Terms
[71:1:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning | Coiner / source
  [71:1:0.0] Metropolitan city | 10 lakh (1 million) to 1 crore (10 million) | Census usage; NCERT XII: 1-5 million
  [71:1:0.1] Megacity | 1 crore (10 million)+ | UN / Census usage; NCERT XII: over 5 million
  [71:1:0.2] Metropolitan area (Constitution) | 10 lakh or more – Art. 243P (74th Amendment) | –
  [71:1:0.3] Megalopolis | Chain of merged metropolitan areas (US north-east seaboard, Boston-Washington) | Jean Gottmann (1961)
  [71:1:0.4] Umland | Area surrounding a town, linked to it | German term
  [71:1:0.5] Conurbation | Continuous urban area of merged towns | Patrick Geddes
  [71:1:0.6] Primate city | Several times larger than the next city | Mark Jefferson
[71:1:1] - **Rakesh Mohan**: three processes of Indian urbanisation.
[71:1:2] - **Mumbai** is the large city built on an **island** (Salsette and the seven islands of Bombay).
[71:1:3] > Exam angle: 1-10 million = metropolitan city; above 10 million = megacity; Class I = only 1 lakh+.

## SUB 2 | Slums and Problems of Large Cities
[71:2:0] TABLE head: Measure | Place
  [71:2:0.0] Slum population (2011) | 6.54 crore = 17.4% of urban
  [71:2:0.1] Largest number (State) | Maharashtra
  [71:2:0.2] Highest share (State) | Undivided AP (~36%)
  [71:2:0.3] Largest number (city) | Greater Mumbai; Dharavi (Mumbai) – India's best-known largest slum
  [71:2:0.4] Highest share (million-plus city) | Greater Visakhapatnam (~44%) vs Mumbai (~41%)
[71:2:1] - World Bank: **177 million** slum dwellers (broader definition).
[71:2:2] - **UN World Habitat Award 2023: Odisha** – **JAGA Mission** (land titling and slum upgrading).
[71:2:3] - **Air pollution:** IQAir World Air Quality Report 2019 – **6 of the world's 10** most polluted cities were Indian; **IQAir 2025 report (24 Mar 2026): 5 of the top 10**, **Loni** (Ghaziabad) most polluted (112.5 µg/m³), India 6th most polluted country. **Delhi** – most polluted capital; repeatedly hits "**severe plus**" AQI in winter.
[71:2:4] - **Waste**: ~**62 million tonnes** MSW a year; **70% collected, 30% processed**. **Noida** was billed as India's first **zero-discharge city** (sewage reuse).
[71:2:5] - **Congestion**: 1.5-2 hours a day lost; **one planner per 1 lakh** (developed countries 1:5,000).
[71:2:6] - **Urban flooding**: building over lakes, wetlands, floodplains; blocked drains – building **basements** is NOT a flood-control measure. **Urban heat island**: dense construction, asphalt, lost tree cover.

=== NOTES 4:75 | Andhra Pradesh – Sc and St Population; Major Tribal Groups and Pvtgs
## SUB 0 | Major Tribes and Their Regions
[75:0:0] # Northern hills and agency tracts
[75:0:1] TABLE head: Tribe | Area
  [75:0:1.0] Savara (Sora) | Srikakulam, Vizianagaram
  [75:0:1.1] Jatapu | Srikakulam–Vizianagaram
  [75:0:1.2] Gadaba | Salur, Parvathipuram
  [75:0:1.3] Bagata (Bhagata) | Visakhapatnam, ASR
  [75:0:1.4] Konda Dora (Kubi) | Northern Eastern Ghats; Mutadars (hill chiefs) of Rampa agency
  [75:0:1.5] Kondh | Eastern Ghats on the Odisha border
  [75:0:1.6] Kotia | Visakhapatnam highlands
  [75:0:1.7] Porja | Araku Valley
  [75:0:1.8] Valmiki, Nayak, Andh | Agency and other notified areas
  [75:0:1.9] Konda Kapu, Manna Dora, Kulia, Malis, Goud, Rona | Northern agency tracts
[75:0:2] # Godavari valley
[75:0:3] - **Koya** – Godavari basin (Chintoor, Polavaram, Eluru, ASR); call themselves **Koyi Toor**.
[75:0:4] - **Konda Reddi** – Godavari hills, **Rampa** (East and West Godavari); **PVTG**; podu.
[75:0:5] # Southern forests and plains (plains tribes)
[75:0:6] TABLE head: Tribe | Area
  [75:0:6.0] Chenchu | Nallamala forests around Srisailam, Ahobilam – the "aboriginal tribe" of AP; name = "those who live under trees"; Ahobilam Narasimha married Chenchita
  [75:0:6.1] Yanadi | Nellore plains, Chittoor; original home near Pulicat Lake
  [75:0:6.2] Yerukula | Almost every plains district (Korava in TN)
  [75:0:6.3] Sugali (Lambadi, Banjara) | Rayalaseema and central Andhra; settlements = thandas
[75:0:7] - **Boya** is a BC community in AP, **not** a plains ST.
[75:0:8] - **Not AP tribes:** **Munda, Santhal, Bhil, Asur** (Jharkhand/central India).
[75:0:9] > Exam angle: odd-one-out – Asur, Munda, Santhal; plains-tribe odd one – Boya.
[75:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 15 p.3 (book p.199, AP tribes, 1976 Act list) and p.2 (Chenchu in the State-wise tribe list); app notes 4:75 (sub 3)
## SUB 1 | PVTGs of Andhra Pradesh
[75:1:0] - **12 PVTGs** (list for AP and Telangana together): Bodo Gadaba, Gutob Gadaba, Bondo Poraja, Khond Poraja, Parengi Poraja, **Chenchu**, Dongria Khond, Kutia Khond, **Kolam**, **Konda Reddi**, Konda Savara, **Thoti**. About 7 lie in residual AP.
[75:1:1] - Criteria: **pre-agricultural technology**, **extremely low literacy**, economic backwardness, **stagnant or declining population** – not caste or sex ratio.
[75:1:2] - **Dhebar Commission 1973** → PTG; renamed **PVTG in 2006**. India **75** PVTGs (18 States + 1 UT); **Odisha 13** (most).
[75:1:3] - Konda Reddis and Kolams are the "tribes on the verge of extinction" of the TSPSC 2017 question; **Chenchus** work as forest watchers in the **Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve**.
[75:1:4] - **Yerukula is NOT a PVTG**.
[75:1:5] TABLE head: Cluster | PVTGs | Habitat
  [75:1:5.0] Gadaba / Poraja | Bodo, Gutob Gadaba; Bondo, Khond, Parengi Poraja | Araku Valley / Visakhapatnam agency
  [75:1:5.1] Khond | Dongria, Kutia Khond | North coastal Khond belt
  [75:1:5.2] Hill / forest | Chenchu, Konda Reddi, Konda Savara | Nallamala; Godavari hills; Srikakulam hills
[75:1:6] - 2024 ST Order amendment added 7 PVTG communities to ST lists (4 Odisha, 3 AP); total stays 75.
[75:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 15 p.3 (book p.199, PTG list and characteristics); app notes 4:75 (sub 4)
## SUB 2 | SC and ST Population – Census 2011
[75:2:0] TABLE head: Indicator | Value
  [75:2:0.0] ST population | 27.39 lakh = 5.53% of residual AP (4.39% in 1971; undivided AP 7.0%)
  [75:2:0.1] SC population | 84.69 lakh = 17.08%
  [75:2:0.2] Highest ST population | Visakhapatnam (6.18 lakh; now mostly ASR)
  [75:2:0.3] Highest SC share | Prakasam (23.19%), then SPS Nellore (22.49%)
  [75:2:0.4] Lowest ST share, 26-district map | West Godavari (HQ Bhimavaram) – agency mandals went to Eluru
[75:2:1] - SC literacy, undivided AP 2001: **53.5%**.
[75:2:2] - India 2011: **698** STs counted; largest tribe **Bhil**; **Odisha** most notified tribes (62).
[75:2:3] - **Art. 342:** **President** notifies STs after consulting the Governor; only **Parliament** amends the list. **Art. 366(25)** defines STs.
[75:2:4] - **1976 SC and ST Orders (Amendment) Act:** **33 STs** in undivided AP; 5 area-restricted (**Goudu, Mali, Nayak, Thoti, Valmiki**); **Goudu, Nayak, Valmiki** only in the **Agency tracts**. Present AP: **34** ST communities.
[75:2:5] - Feb 2024: Porja and Savara sub-groups added (Bondo Porja, Khond Porja, Konda Savara).
[75:2:6] - **Polavaram district** (HQ **Rampachodavaram**) carved from ASR on **31 Dec 2025**.
[75:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 15 p.3-5 (book p.199-201, 1976 Act; SC/ST population table); app notes 4:75 (sub 0, 1); lowest-ST district: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 3 | Livelihoods, GCC and Araku Coffee
[75:3:0] TABLE head: Tribe | Occupation
  [75:3:0.0] Chenchu | Hunting, food gathering; semi-nomadic
  [75:3:0.1] Konda Reddi, Koya, Porja, Savara | Podu and hill agriculture
  [75:3:0.2] Yanadi | Fishing, rice, herbal medicine
  [75:3:0.3] Yerukula | Basket and rope making, fortune-telling, pig-rearing
  [75:3:0.4] Lambada | Once traders/transporters; now farming
[75:3:1] - **Podu** = slash-and-burn; erosion and forest fires; in **ASR and Parvathipuram Manyam** (not Nallamala).
[75:3:2] - **GCC** (Girijan Cooperative Corporation, **1956**): buys **MFP**, runs PDS depots; trademark "**GCC Araku Valley Coffee**" – the coffee brand of Visakhapatnam's tribals.
[75:3:3] - Coffee grows in the **Araku Valley** (Paderu ITDA); the ITDA Paderu coffee project targeted **expansion by 1,00,000 acres** – Araku coffee now about **1 lakh acres**.
[75:3:4] - Van Dhan Vikas Kendras 415 sanctioned (258 working); annatto at Maredumilli.
[75:3:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:75 (sub 5)

## SUB 6 | Laws, Institutions and Movements
[75:6:0] TABLE head: Year | Law / event

=== NOTES 4:76 | Andhra Pradesh – Religious and Linguistic Composition; Rural-urban Components
## SUB 0 | Official Languages of AP and Urdu
[76:0:0] - First official language: **Telugu** (**AP Official Languages Act, 1966**).
[76:0:1] - **Urdu** = **second official language**: in joint AP it applied to **15 districts** – six now in AP (**Anantapur, Kadapa, Chittoor, Guntur, Nellore, Kurnool**) and nine in Telangana.
[76:0:2] - **AP Official Languages (Amendment) Bill, 2022:** tabled and passed in the Assembly on **23–24 March 2022**; extends Urdu to **all districts**; the government order bringing it into force came in **June 2022** – so "in force on 25 April 2022" is wrong.
[76:0:3] - So the official languages of AP = **Telugu and Urdu**; **Urdu** is also the **second most widely spoken** language of AP (about 3.7% in 2011).

## SUB 1 | Cropping Seasons – Kharif, Rabi, Zaid
[81:1:0] TABLE head: Season | Sown | Harvested | Crops
  [81:1:0.0] Kharif | June-July (SW monsoon) | Sep-Oct / Oct-Nov | Rice, jowar, maize, bajra, ragi, tur, moong, cotton, soybean, groundnut, sugarcane, jute, red chilli
  [81:1:0.1] Rabi | October-November | March-April | Wheat, gram, peas, mustard, lentil (masoor), linseed, lathyrus, French bean, barley
  [81:1:0.2] Zaid | Short summer between rabi and kharif (April-June) | – | Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, bitter gourd, vegetables, fodder, sunflower; irrigated moong and urad
[81:1:1] - **Not kharif:** gram, masoor, mustard. **Not rabi:** lady's finger (summer/kharif vegetable), moong. Carrot, radish, pea are rabi.
[81:1:2] - **Maize** – grown **throughout the year** (mainly kharif, also rabi in Bihar); "**Queen of Cereals**".
[81:1:3] - **Rice in West Bengal:** three crops – **aus, aman, boro** (all **paddy**). **Aman** sown **June-July**, harvested Nov-Dec.
[81:1:4] - **Pulses in both seasons:** kharif (tur, moong, urad) and rabi (gram, masoor, pea); **black gram** grows as kharif and rabi.
[81:1:5] - **Transplanted crops:** **rice** (less seed, more labour) and **onion** (nursery seedlings).
[81:1:6] - Rabi in **Punjab, Haryana** (north-west) depends on winter rain from **western disturbances** – **temperate (extra-tropical) cyclones** from the Mediterranean, 10-15 cm of rain.
[81:1:7] > Exam angle: cotton, groundnut, rice = kharif; wheat = rabi (UPSC 2013).
[81:1:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Geography p.80 (crop–season table), p.81-82 (moong NOT rabi; zaid crops in irrigated areas); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 05 p.5 (seasons, aus–aman–boro), p.7 (maize also rabi); NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.4 (western disturbances, rabi); app notes 4:81 (sub 0)
[81:1:9] - **AP seasons:** maize, rice – kharif (also rabi); **sugarcane – perennial**; **sunflower – rabi** (also zaid).
## SUB 2 | Production, Area and World Position
[81:2:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [81:2:0.0] Foodgrains 2024-25 | Record 357.73 MT; horticulture higher at 367.72 MT
  [81:2:0.1] Order of output | Rice 150.2 > wheat 117.9 > coarse grains 63.9 > pulses 25.7 MT
  [81:2:0.2] Rice | India now world's largest producer (150.18 MT vs China 145.28 MT, Jan 2026; earlier 2nd); largest exporter since 2014-15 (~40% of world trade); largest rice area in the world
  [81:2:0.3] Wheat | 2nd (China > India > Russia); 109.5 MT (2020-21, 4th AE); 117.94 MT (2024-25)
  [81:2:0.4] Largest-area crop | Rice (51.27 MH); wheat 32.80 MH
  [81:2:0.5] Pulses | India = world's largest producer, consumer and importer; pulses are not usually exported
  [81:2:0.6] Millets | India ~42.75% of world output; 18.59 MT
  [81:2:0.7] Bananas | India largest producer
[81:2:1] - Max growth after Independence: **wheat** (Green Revolution); wheat 2006-07 → 2009-10: **75.81 → 78.57 → 80.68 → 80.80 MT** (upward trend).
[81:2:2] - Record **oilseeds** in **1992-93** (20.11 MT).
[81:2:3] - India short of **pulses**, not of protein, because of high demand (keyed: R explains A).
[81:2:4] - Kharif area (UPSC 2019): **rice largest**; **cotton > sugarcane**; jowar < oilseeds; sugarcane area fluctuates.
[81:2:5] - Rice area roughly **stagnant** in the 2000s decade (UPSC 2010 key).
[81:2:6] # Land and irrigation
[81:2:7] TABLE head: Item (2021-22) | Value
  [81:2:7.0] Net sown area | 141 MH
  [81:2:7.1] Gross cropped / net irrigated / gross irrigated | 219.16 / 77.9 / 120.3 MH
  [81:2:7.2] Cropping intensity | 155.4%
[81:2:8] - **56.4%** of net sown area irrigated (not 60%); wells and tube wells **over 63%**; drip/sprinkler only **~12%**; India has the **world's largest irrigated area**.
[81:2:9] - Most irrigated crops (2023-24): **sugarcane 96.8%**, wheat 95.5%, rice 69.5%, oilseeds 43.9%.
[81:2:10] - Arable land: India **2nd after USA**, **more than China**; China has the higher irrigated share and higher yields (UPSC 2023: only one statement correct).
[81:2:11] - Indian agriculture: dependent on monsoon, low productivity, crop diversity, **small and marginal holdings** (not large farms); low productivity from overcrowding, small holdings, traditional practices; efficient **irrigation** is the main pathway to higher productivity.
[81:2:12] - World leaders: maize **USA > China > Brazil** (**US Corn Belt** = maize); potato **China > India**, Russia, Ukraine (**not Brazil**); wheat **China > India**.

## SUB 3 | Food Crops – Growth Conditions and Crop Types
[81:3:0] TABLE head: Crop | Season / rank | Temperature | Rainfall | Soil / area
  [81:3:0.0] Rice | Kharif; chief food crop, 1st cereal | Above 25°C, high humidity | Above 100 cm (100 cm isohyet ≈ western limit) | Clayey/loamy deltaic and coastal alluvium
  [81:3:0.1] Wheat | Rabi; 2nd cereal | Cool growing season, 10-15°C winter; bright warm sun at ripening | 50-75 cm (moderate) | Ganga-Satluj plains; black soil of the Deccan also suits wheat
  [81:3:0.2] Maize | Year-round | Warm | Moderate | Semi-arid, inferior soils
  [81:3:0.3] Jowar | Kharif/rabi | Warm, drought tolerant | Rainfed | Peninsular, semi-arid
  [81:3:0.4] Bajra | Kharif | Hot, dry | Driest | Sandy
  [81:3:0.5] Ragi | Kharif | Warm, dry | Low | Red soils
  [81:3:0.6] Pulses | Both | – | Rainfed | Fix atmospheric nitrogen – improve soil
[81:3:1] - Wheat needs **moderate temperature and moderate rainfall**; **macaroni (durum) wheat** suits **rainfed** conditions.
[81:3:2] - **Origins:** rice – **South-East Asia**; red gram (arhar) – **India**; **maize** – the Americas (New World), so it is **not an ancient cereal** of the Old World (rice, wheat, barley are).
[81:3:3] - **Maize** is a **C4** plant (paddy, wheat, soybean are C3) and the best fodder for **silage**.
[81:3:4] - Cereals and millets are mainly **starch**. Wheat, rice, maize, jowar = cereals; **wheat is not a millet**.
[81:3:5] - **Rajma** is the pulse that does **not** fix nitrogen (poor nodulation); **paddy** does not help N-fixation; **black gram (urad)** improves soil fertility.
[81:3:6] - Black soil grows **cotton, wheat, jowar, pulses** (APPSC dropped its "not grown in black soil" item).
[81:3:7] # Crop types
[81:3:8] - **Cash/commercial:** sugarcane, cotton, jute, tobacco, groundnut, **banana** – **not bajra**, jowar, millets.
[81:3:9] - **Stimulant crops:** **tea**, coffee, tobacco, opium poppy, betel nut.
[81:3:10] - **Subsistence-farmed:** **coarse cereals and rice**.
[81:3:11] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Geography p.81 (rice ~25°C, >100 cm, 100 cm isohyet; wheat cool, dry; jowar, bajra, ragi); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 05 p.5 (rice tropical humid crop), p.7 (wheat 2nd cereal), p.8 (pulses fix nitrogen); app notes 4:81 (sub 1); maize origin, C4, silage, rajma: general knowledge, not checked
[81:3:12] - **Dicot / monocot:** groundnut, pulses = **dicots**; wheat, rice, maize (grasses) = **monocots**.
## SUB 4 | Green Revolution
[81:4:0] TABLE head: Person | Role
  [81:4:0.0] Norman Borlaug | Father of the Green Revolution (world); Mexican dwarf wheat; Nobel Peace 1970
  [81:4:0.1] M.S. Swaminathan | Father of the Green Revolution in India; HYV wheat; Evergreen Revolution
  [81:4:0.2] C. Subramaniam | Union Agriculture Minister who backed it
  [81:4:0.3] William Gaud | Coined the term (1968)
  [81:4:0.4] B.P. Pal | First DG of ICAR
[81:4:1] - **New Agricultural Strategy (mid-1960s, sixties)** after the 1965-67 droughts and **PL-480** imports; **HYV Programme from Kharif 1966**.
[81:4:2] - **Green Revolution = High Yielding Variety programme**; aim: **food-grain output through HYV seeds**, not land redistribution or exports.
[81:4:3] - Components: **HYV seeds**, fertilisers, pesticides, **irrigation**, mechanisation, MSP, **rural electrification, rural roads and marketing** (all four in the code).
[81:4:4] - Main crop: **Mexican dwarf wheat** (Lerma Rojo 64-A, Sonora-63/64, Kalyan Sona). **Wheat** benefited most in **production and productivity** (output about 2.5 times), then **rice**; pulses, oilseeds, millets lagged. Wheat yield touched about **2,000 kg/ha** (3,595 kg/ha in 2024-25).
[81:4:5] - First stage: **Punjab, Haryana, western UP**; eastern belt lagged. Phases: early 1968-81 (growth 2.3%), later 1981-92 (spread east, 3.4%).
[81:4:6] - **Limitations:** **regional disparities** (A and R both true, R not the explanation), **income disparities** (farmers with 10+ ha gained most), **soil degradation** from fertiliser, groundwater depletion; it did **not** raise all crops equally; N:P:K 10.9:4.1:1 vs ideal 4:2:1.
[81:4:7] - Procurement confined to rice, wheat, sugarcane – these use over two-thirds of urea; MSP + free power favour paddy in Punjab.
[81:4:8] - Small and marginal farmers **86.2%** of farmers, 47.3% of area (2015-16).
[81:4:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy 20 p.5 (PL 480, 1965-67 droughts, New Agricultural Strategy, HYV seeds, fertilisers), p.6 (HYV from 1966; wheat gained maximum; farmers with 10+ ha; phases 2.3% / 3.4%; eastern region lagged); app notes 4:81 (sub 4)
## SUB 5 | Cropping Systems
[81:5:0] TABLE head: System | Meaning
  [81:5:0.0] Double / multiple cropping | Two crops at different times (in succession) on the same land in a year (paddy then wheat)
  [81:5:0.1] Mixed cropping | Two or more crops simultaneously on the same land, seeds mixed, no row pattern
  [81:5:0.2] Intercropping | Crops together in definite rows (tur + jowar or maize)
  [81:5:0.3] Parallel cropping | Crops of different habit, no competition – wheat + mustard, maize + green gram
  [81:5:0.4] Sequential cropping | Crops in sequence on the same field in a year – no intercrop competition
  [81:5:0.5] Relay cropping | Next crop sown into the standing crop
  [81:5:0.6] Ratoon | Regrowth from stubble
  [81:5:0.7] Crop rotation | Planned sequence; pulse–cereal leaves fixed nitrogen
  [81:5:0.8] Mixed farming | Crops + rearing animals
[81:5:1] - **Rice–wheat** = major cropping system **by area** (Indo-Gangetic plains); UP's largest pattern too. Best cycle for eastern UP: **paddy – maize – wheat**.
[81:5:2] - **Monocropping does not protect soil fertility**; rotation, mixed cropping and fallowing do.
[81:5:3] - **Land Equivalent Ratio (LER)** measures the advantage of **intercropping over sole cropping**; sole cropping = one crop variety.
[81:5:4] - Agro-ecological cell models fit crop cycles to the **length of growing period**, with turn-around times and intercropping levels.
[81:5:5] - **Cereal yield** = output per unit of **harvested area** (kg/ha), not total production.
[81:5:6] - Wheat irrigation: **CRI (crown root initiation) stage**, 20-25 days after sowing, is the most critical – not flowering.
[81:5:7] - AP cropping intensity: **1.21 (2023-24) → 1.88 (2024-25)**; AP diversifying to **fruits, vegetables, spices, oil palm**.
[81:5:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:81 (sub 7); NCERT Class 9 definition of mixed cropping, LER, CRI stage: general knowledge, not checked
[81:5:9] - **AP practice pairs (APPSC key):** monocropping – **rice**; mixed cropping – **sorghum**; crop rotation – **cotton**; intercropping – **sugarcane**.
## SUB 6 | Millets and Dryland Farming
[81:6:0] TABLE head: Group | Millets
  [81:6:0.0] Major | Bajra (pearl; ~60% of millet output), jowar (sorghum), ragi (finger)
  [81:6:0.1] Minor | Foxtail (kangni), little (kutki), kodo, proso (chena)
[81:6:1] - Millet group: **sorghum, kodo, kangani, ragi** – not maize or moong; tur and gram are pulses.
[81:6:2] - **2023 = UN International Year of Millets** (proposed by India); brand **Shree Anna**.
[81:6:3] - **Dryland farming: annual rainfall below 75 cm** (NCERT; NDA 2020) – wetland farming in high-rainfall areas.
[81:6:4] - Best dryland crop: **groundnut** (50-125 cm; needs gypsum). Predominantly **rainfed: groundnut, sesamum, pearl millet** (UPSC 2012).
[81:6:5] - Sorghum and pearl-millet based cropping systems: keyed **Andhra Pradesh** (APPSC Panchayat Secretary).
[81:6:6] - Millets are mainly **kharif** crops of dryland and rainfed tracts; rainfed areas grow mostly **millets, pulses and oilseeds**.
[81:6:7] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 04 p.17 (dryland farming below 75 cm); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 05 p.7 (millets jowar, bajra, ragi; bajra hot dry); testbook.com NDA 2020 dryland question (75 cm); app notes 4:81 (sub 6)

## SUB 8 | Shifting Cultivation
[81:8:0] TABLE head: Local name | Region
  [81:8:0.0] Jhum | North-East (Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland)
  [81:8:0.1] Pamlou | Manipur
  [81:8:0.2] Podu / Penda | Andhra Pradesh
  [81:8:0.3] Pama Dabi / Koman / Bringa; Pondu | Odisha
  [81:8:0.4] Dipa | Bastar (Chhattisgarh), Andaman
  [81:8:0.5] Bewar / Dahiya | Madhya Pradesh
  [81:8:0.6] Kumari | Western Ghats
  [81:8:0.7] Poonam | Kerala
  [81:8:0.8] Valre / Khil / Kuruwa | SE Rajasthan / Himalayan belt / Jharkhand
  [81:8:0.9] Milpa / Ladang / Roca / Masole / Chena / Conuco | Mexico–Central America / Indonesia–Malaysia / Brazil / Central Africa / Sri Lanka / Venezuela
[81:8:1] - **Fazenda** = Brazilian (coffee) plantation, **not** shifting cultivation; **Mashan–MP** is the wrong pair.
[81:8:2] - Also called **slash and burn**; leaves hills barren (Nagaland). AP practitioners: Konda Reddi, Koya, Savara.
[81:8:3] - **Terrace farming**: steps cut on **hill slopes**.
[81:8:4] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 05 p.1 (Indian and world names of shifting cultivation); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography 04 p.17 (slash and burn); app notes 4:81 (sub 8)
[81:8:5] - **Jhum practitioners:** Khasi and Garo (Meghalaya) and other hill tribes of the North-East.

## SUB 10 | Varieties, Diseases and Biofertilisers
[81:10:0] TABLE head: Crop | Disease | Cause
  [81:10:0.0] Wheat | Black rust; loose smut; Karnal bunt | *Puccinia*; *Ustilago*; *Tilletia indica*
  [81:10:0.1] Rice | Tungro; Khaira | Virus; zinc deficiency
  [81:10:0.2] Bajra | Green ear (green hair is a millet disease – not rice) | *Sclerospora*
  [81:10:0.3] Maize | White bud | Zinc deficiency
[81:10:1] - Varieties: **Kalyan Sona, Sonalika**, UP-308, Kundan (wheat); Jaya, Padma (rice); Mahi Sugandha (basmati); Pant-114 (gram); UPAS-120 (arhar); Pitambari (yellow mustard); **Triticale** = wheat × rye.
[81:10:2] - Rice biofertiliser: **blue-green algae**, **Azolla-Anabaena**; **cobalt** needed for Rhizobium N-fixation in pulses.
[81:10:3] - Wheat **ear cockle** – nematode *Anguina tritici*. **Aflatoxins** – toxins of moulds in badly stored grain, not destroyed by cooking.
[81:10:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:81 (sub 10)
[81:10:5] - **BGA biofertilisers:** *Nostoc, Anabaena, Tolypothrix, Aulosira* – not *Agaricus* (mushroom) or *Spirogyra*.
[81:10:6] - **Green manure:** **sunhemp** (most common), **dhaincha** (saline/usar soils), **lobia/cowpea** (dry land; highest N in the book table 0.49%).
[81:10:7] - **Rice varieties (UP keys):** **Barani Deep**, Narendra Shushk Samrat, Lalmati; hybrid basmati **Pusa RH-10**; aromatic **Pusa Sugandh-5**. **Jawala** is not a rice variety.
[81:10:8] - **Arhar (pigeon pea) varieties:** **Bahar**, Amar, Azad, Malaviya Chamatkar; **UPAS-120** (early) suits double cropping with wheat.
[81:10:9] - **Pulse + fodder + green manure:** **cowpea and green gram** (UPSC 2012) – not pigeon pea.
[81:10:10] - **Wheat varieties:** **Pusa Sindhu Ganga (HD 2967)**; **Sharbati Sonora** – gamma-ray mutant of Sonora-64 (IARI, 1967).
[81:10:11] - **Shaktiman-1, 2:** quality-protein **maize** hybrids (conventionally bred, not GM).
[81:10:12] - **Rajasthan varieties:** **Mahi Kanchan – maize**; **RCB 911 – bajra** (RPSC 2023).
[81:10:13] - **Rice tungro:** complex of **two viruses** (RTBV + RTSV), spread by green leafhopper; blast – *Pyricularia*; bacterial blight – *Xanthomonas*.

[82:0:1] - **Bt cotton** covers **over 90%** of India's cotton area.
[82:0:2] - **Gujarat** once led cotton, groundnut, salt and milk; now it leads groundnut and salt (cotton: Maharashtra; milk: UP).
[82:0:3] - Correct pairs: **Maharashtra – cotton, West Bengal – jute, Gujarat – groundnut**; Kerala – tapioca was also true in the 1990s (Kerala then the leading tapioca State; now Tamil Nadu).
[82:0:4] - **Karnataka** grows coffee, rubber and tobacco together.
[82:0:5] - **Andhra Pradesh:** tobacco on a large scale (Guntur, Prakasam: FCV tobacco); **chillies 1st** in India; AP is **not** a jute State; tea only in **Araku** (ASR district).
[82:0:6] - **Statements:** "Tea is the main crop of Assam" and "Tobacco is grown on a large scale in AP" are true; "Coffee – Tamil Nadu" and "Jute – Chhattisgarh" are false.
[82:0:7] > Exam angle: older keys follow the data of their year; check the "now" column before answering a "largest producer" question.

## SUB 1 | Spices – States, Varieties and Nicknames
[82:1:0] TABLE head: Spice (2024-25) | Leading State | Next
  [82:1:0.0] All spices (output) | Madhya Pradesh (38.4 lakh t) | Rajasthan, Gujarat, AP
  [82:1:0.1] Chilli | Andhra Pradesh (11.5 lakh t; Guntur) | Telangana, MP
  [82:1:0.2] Turmeric | Maharashtra | Tamil Nadu, Telangana (AP only about 6th)
  [82:1:0.3] Black pepper | Karnataka (66,028 t) | Kerala (29,503 t)
  [82:1:0.4] Small cardamom | Kerala (about 88%) | Tamil Nadu, Karnataka
  [82:1:0.5] Large cardamom | Sikkim | Arunachal Pradesh
  [82:1:0.6] Clove | Tamil Nadu (about 89%) | Karnataka, Kerala
  [82:1:0.7] Nutmeg | Kerala | –
  [82:1:0.8] Saffron | Jammu and Kashmir – the only producer (UT since 31 Oct 2019) | –
[82:1:1] - **Kerala = "Spice Garden of India"**, famous for spices since ancient times; it grows **black pepper and cardamom** – but by output MP is the largest spice State (Gujarat was keyed in 2012).
[82:1:2] - With Karnataka absent from the options, **Kerala** is the answer for "largest producer of cardamom and pepper".
[82:1:3] - **Odisha** is not a cardamom State (cardamom: Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu).
[82:1:4] - **Black pepper = "Black Gold / Black Diamond"** of spices; it needs a hot moist climate, **over 200 cm** rain, hill slopes of about **1,100 m**, 15-30°C – the Western Ghats.
[82:1:5] - **Lakadong turmeric** (high curcumin) – **Meghalaya**. Turmeric's used part is the **rhizome**, not the leaf.
[82:1:6] - **National Turmeric Board** – **Nizamabad** (Telangana), launched January 2025.
[82:1:7] > Exam angle: "spice garden" / fame = Kerala; output = MP; pepper output = Karnataka.
[82:1:8] ~~ Sources: Spices Board, State-wise area and production of spices 2021-22 to 2025-26 and Major spice-wise State tables 2024-25 (indianspices.com); app notes 4:82 (sub 2, 7)
## SUB 2 | Growth Conditions – Climate and Soil
[82:2:0] TABLE head: Crop | Temperature | Rainfall | Soil / site
  [82:2:0.0] Cotton | 21-30°C (up to 37°C); 210 frost-free days; hard frost harmful; subtropical | 50-100 cm (light to moderate) | Black (regur) soil of the Deccan; light, well-drained, moisture-retaining; deep alluvium in the north
  [82:2:0.1] Jute | 24-35°C, hot and humid; kharif | 125-200 cm | Fresh alluvium of flood plains; Ganga-Brahmaputra delta; low plain land
  [82:2:0.2] Tea | 20-30°C, frost-free | 150-300 cm (150-250 cm in many books), evenly spread | Deep, well-drained, acidic (not lime-rich), humus- and iron-rich hill slopes; no waterlogging; below 1,800 m
  [82:2:0.3] Coffee | 15-28°C, shade; no frost or strong sun | 150-250 cm | Well-drained loams with humus; Western Ghats
  [82:2:0.4] Rubber | 25-35°C, hot humid, equatorial | Over 200 cm | Laterite of the Western Ghats; not delta flood plains
  [82:2:0.5] Sugarcane | 21-27°C, hot humid; 10-15 months (Adsali about 18) | 75-150 cm or irrigation | Alluvial / black soil
  [82:2:0.6] Groundnut | Warm, tropical | 50-125 cm | Light sandy loam; gypsum (calcium) for pod filling
[82:2:1] - **Cotton** is mainly a **kharif** crop; "100 frost-free days" is **not** its requirement (it needs about 210); rainfall 50-75 cm in some books (R.C. Tiwari).
[82:2:2] - Hot humid area, **200 cm rain, hill slopes up to 1,100 m, 15-30°C** → **black pepper**.
[82:2:3] - **Lower Gangetic plain** (hot, humid, floods with fresh silt) → **paddy and jute**.
[82:2:4] - Over 200 cm rain on sloping hills → **tea**.
[82:2:5] - **Black soils** (moisture-retentive) → **cotton, chillies, tobacco**, jowar, oilseeds; red soils → groundnut, ragi, tobacco; laterite (with manure) → tea, coffee, rubber, cashew.
[82:2:6] - **Sugarcane** = **least water-efficient** crop (1,400-2,300 mm subtropics; 2,000-3,500 mm tropics); millets, pulses and oilseeds are water-efficient.
[82:2:7] - **Red chilli:** kharif, warm climate; Andhra Pradesh. Soybean needs a warm season – being an oilseed does not explain it.
[82:2:8] - In **Maharashtra's black-soil belt** sugarcane competes with cotton because **irrigation** has expanded.
[82:2:9] > Exam angle: 210 frost-free days and 50-100 cm = cotton; 150-300 cm, acidic slopes = tea; over 200 cm = rubber.
[82:2:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 05 p.34 (200 frost-free days), p.67 (tea: 20-30°C, 150-300 cm, humus- and iron-rich soils, below 1,800 m), p.73 (coffee: 15-28°C, 150-250 cm); NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.6-7 (black soil: cotton, chillies, tobacco; laterite: plantation crops); Rocket Indian Geography p.81 (crop table); app notes 4:82 (sub 1)
## SUB 3 | Cash, Fibre, Food and Plantation Crops
[82:3:0] - **Cash crops** (grown for sale): **cotton, sugarcane, jute, tobacco, oilseeds (groundnut/peanut), tea, rubber, bananas**.
[82:3:1] - **Food crops:** wheat, rice, maize, **jowar, millets**, gram, peas – the usual "not a cash crop" answer.
[82:3:2] - **Soybean** is a commercial oilseed too; in the tobacco–cotton–soybean–rubber set it is keyed as "not a cash crop".
[82:3:3] - **Fibre crops:** **cotton, jute, sunhemp** (also flax/mesta); jute–wheat–cotton mixes a food crop.
[82:3:4] - **Plantation crops** (tea, coffee, rubber, coconut): high-value, **labour- and capital-intensive**; colonial plantations (tea, coffee, rubber, indigo) were **European-dominated and export-oriented**.
[82:3:5] - **Medicinal crop:** **aloe vera** (not sugarcane, cotton or mahua).
[82:3:6] - **Tea** earns the most foreign exchange among tea, tobacco, flax and wheat.
[82:3:7] - Tea and coffee are **substitutes**: if tea gets cheaper, **coffee consumption decreases**.
[82:3:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:82 (sub 0); Rocket Indian Geography p.80 (crop seasons)
## SUB 4 | Tea and Coffee – Regions, History and Araku
[82:4:0] - **First tea plantations:** **Brahmaputra valley, Assam**, first half of the 19th century (1830s, after Robert Bruce found wild tea), before Darjeeling.
[82:4:1] - **Barak Valley** (Cachar, south Assam): **tea**.
[82:4:2] - **Tea-producing States:** Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, **Tripura, Himachal Pradesh (Kangra)**, Uttarakhand; **AP** only in **Araku** – UPSC 2022 official key counts **all four** (AP, Kerala, HP, Tripura).
[82:4:3] TABLE head: Area | Crop | State
  [82:4:3.0] Brahmaputra valley, Barak valley | Tea | Assam
  [82:4:3.1] Darjeeling, Dooars | Tea | West Bengal
  [82:4:3.2] Nilgiris | Tea, coffee | Tamil Nadu
  [82:4:3.3] Munnar, Wayanad, Idukki | Tea | Kerala
  [82:4:3.4] Kangra | Tea | Himachal Pradesh
  [82:4:3.5] Baba Budan hills (Chikkamagaluru), Kodagu | Coffee (first introduced; Arabica) | Karnataka
  [82:4:3.6] Araku valley (ASR district) | Arabica coffee | Andhra Pradesh
[82:4:4] - **Africa:** tea first grown at the **Durban Botanical Garden (1850)**; now Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda – so "no tea plantations in Africa" is false.
[82:4:5] - Coffee varieties: **Arabica** and **Robusta**.
[82:4:6] - **Araku coffee:** first retail store in **Paris** (August 2017); **Araku Valley Arabica coffee GI** (2019).
[82:4:7] - **GI:** a sign on products of a specific geographical origin; **Darjeeling Tea = India's first GI**; GI protection is **not** granted through a "Paris Agreement and Protocol".
[82:4:8] - India is a **major tea exporter** (3rd-4th; Kenya 1st) but **consumes about 80%** of its tea at home – domestic consumption is not poor.
[82:4:9] - **Supreme Court:** **tea** is **not a "foodstuff"** under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (AIR 2005 SC 218).
[82:4:10] - **Green Gold** = tea.
[82:4:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.13 (Robert Bruce, Assam tea); PMF Human & Economic Geography 05 p.71 (India 2nd tea producer, ~10% export share), p.75 (coffee in Baba Budan hills); gktoday.in (UPSC 2022 official final answer: all four States); web search summary of S. Samuel v. Union of India, AIR 2005 SC 218; app notes 4:82 (sub 3)
## SUB 5 | Sugarcane – Tropical vs Sub-tropical
[82:5:0] TABLE head: Point | Tropical (south) | Sub-tropical (north)
  [82:5:0.0] States | Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, AP | UP, Bihar, Punjab, Haryana
  [82:5:0.1] Yield and sucrose | Higher | Lower
  [82:5:0.2] Area | Smaller | Larger
  [82:5:0.3] Crushing season | October to May/June (longer) | November to February
  [82:5:0.4] Why | Cool nights with clear skies, latitude, long sunshine, no frost or loo, maritime influence | Alluvium rich in lime and potash, level land, dense market
[82:5:1] - **Sugar industry is shifting south**: higher yield and juice per hectare explain it (A and R true, R explains A).
[82:5:2] - **UP** produces more cane and sugar than Maharashtra but has **lower productivity**; most Maharashtra mills are **cooperatives** (true, but not the explanation).
[82:5:3] - **Frost** at ripening **lowers sucrose**; excess rain lowers sugar content.
[82:5:4] - **Adsali** cane (Maharashtra): planted July-August, ripens in about **18 months** (normal crop 10-12).
[82:5:5] - **Sustainable Sugarcane Initiative (SSI):** fewer seed setts (**low seed cost**), suits **drip irrigation**, more **intercropping**; it does **not** ban chemical fertilisers.
[82:5:6] - Pest **Pyrilla** (leafhopper); disease **red rot**; variety **Co. 1148**.
[82:5:7] - **UP = "Sugar Bowl of India"**; western UP is the mill belt; mills sit near fields because cane is **weight-losing**.
[82:5:8] - **Pricing: FRP**, not MSP.
[82:5:9] > Exam angle: "southern cane yields more – why" = cool clear nights, latitude, long sunshine (APPSC G-1).
[82:5:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography 10 p.10 (higher yields and sucrose in the south; crushing seasons); PMF Human & Economic Geography 05 p.64 (north vs south, shift south), p.63; app notes 4:82 (sub 4)
## SUB 6 | Oilseeds – Seasons, Varieties, Production
[82:6:0] TABLE head: Kharif | Rabi | Both
  [82:6:0.0] Groundnut, soybean, sesamum, castor, nigerseed | Rapeseed-mustard, linseed, safflower | Sunflower
[82:6:1] - **Rabi-only oilseed = mustard**.
[82:6:2] - **Varieties:** mustard **Varuna, Pusa Bold, Pitambari** (yellow mustard); groundnut **Kaushal**, Chitra; linseed (not "Surya"); field pea Sapna.
[82:6:3] - **Groundnut:** **pegging** (the peg enters the soil and the pod grows there); needs **gypsum**; came from **Brazil**; "poor man's cashew". **Punjab** – small area but very high yield (when asked).
[82:6:4] - **Soybean** = "vegetable meat"; MP has the **largest area**.
[82:6:5] - **Yellow Revolution** = oilseeds (not jute or pulses).
[82:6:6] - **Order of output:** 1990s **groundnut > mustard > soybean > sesamum**; 2024-25 **soybean 15.27 > rapeseed-mustard 12.67 > groundnut 11.94 > sesamum 0.83** MT.
[82:6:7] - **Import dependence:** farmers prefer foodgrains with support prices; oilseeds are mostly **rain-fed**; tree-borne oilseeds and rice bran remain unexploited.
[82:6:8] - **India** = largest producer and exporter of **castor** (Gujarat about 86%).
[82:6:9] - **MSP:** **23** commodities – 7 cereals, 5 pulses, **7 oilseeds** (groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, soybean, sesamum, sunflower, safflower, nigerseed) + commercial crops; coffee, areca nut, turmeric are not MSP crops.
[82:6:10] - **Oilseeds 2025-26:** area, production and productivity all rose; **NMEO-Oilseeds** + **NMEO-Oil Palm**; **AP leads oil palm** (area, production, productivity).
[82:6:11] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Geography p.80 (kharif/rabi table), p.53 (Yellow Revolution); app notes 4:82 (sub 5); oilseed figures 2024-25 as quoted in the app's PYQ explanation (Economic Survey 2025-26); variety names: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 7 | World Producers and India's Rank
[82:7:0] TABLE head: Crop | World leaders | India
  [82:7:0.0] Jute | India, Bangladesh, China | 1st (raw jute and jute goods)
  [82:7:0.1] Tea | China (about 47%), India, Kenya, Sri Lanka | 2nd
  [82:7:0.2] Cotton | China, India, Brazil, USA | 2nd (3rd in 2004, behind China and USA)
  [82:7:0.3] Sugarcane | Brazil, India, China, Thailand | 2nd; but 1st in sugar since 2021-22
  [82:7:0.4] Coffee | Brazil, Vietnam (also 2nd exporter), Colombia, Indonesia, Ethiopia | 7th
  [82:7:0.5] Rubber | Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam | 6th
  [82:7:0.6] Tobacco | China, India, Brazil | 2nd
  [82:7:0.7] Castor | India | 1st
  [82:7:0.8] Coconut | India (31.24%) | 1st
[82:7:1] - **Cotton yield:** **China** highest among China, USA, Pakistan, India; India's yield is low.
[82:7:2] - **Long-staple cotton:** the classic answer is **Egypt** (Nile valley, **Giza**); USA grows **Pima**; but the Nile delta now grows little of it and **India leads ELS + LS output** (ICAC 2025/26: 110,000 t, then USA, Egypt, China). India mostly grows **medium staple**.
[82:7:3] - **India first developed hybrid cotton** (H-4, 1970) and the Indian subcontinent is an original home of cultivated cotton.
[82:7:4] - **India is the largest producer of jute** – but the Yellow Revolution (oilseeds) has nothing to do with it.
[82:7:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 05 p.34 (Nile delta little long-staple cotton now), p.44 (cotton producers 2023: China, India, Brazil), p.51 (jute producers: India, Bangladesh, China), p.63 (India largest sugar producer 2021-22), p.71 (China 47% of tea, India 2nd); ICAC Specialty Cotton Report 2025 p.10; PIB coconut backgrounder Aug 2026; app notes 4:82 (sub 8)

## SUB 11 | Horticulture Link
[82:11:0] - Horticulture output exceeds foodgrains (since **2012-13**); about **30.4%** of agricultural GDP from under 14% of cropped area; India **2nd** in fruits and vegetables.
[82:11:1] - **MIDH:** 60:40 (**90:10** for NE and Himalayan States); sub-schemes NHM, HMNEH, National Bamboo Mission.
[82:11:2] - **AP = largest fruit producer (15.6%)**; **Bihar** – litchi; **Arunachal** – over 50% of kiwi; **West Bengal** – pineapple.
[82:11:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 4:82 (sub 9)
